While some colleges and universities have raised student health insurance fees in particular years—sometimes citing rising insurance costs or regulatory changes tied to the Affordable Care Act—there is no general, documented policy that students are being 'overcharged' specifically to pay for the health care law across institutions.

claim: "Thom Tillis cut almost $500 million from education."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not supported as a definitive fact. While Thom Tillis, as North Carolina House Speaker, backed Republican budgets that critics said reduced education funding, independent analyses and news reports show disputed accounting and varying totals; there is no unambiguous, widely accepted finding that he personally 'cut almost $500 million from education' without specifying year, program, or calculation method.

claim: Says Gary Farmer’s claim that he "received an 'A' from the NRA" is "an absolute lie."
rationale: I cannot verify that calling Gary Farmer’s statement that he 'received an A from the NRA' an 'absolute lie' is correct. NRA ratings and endorsements are public but time- and jurisdiction-specific, and I do not have clear, corroborating records in my knowledge that definitively prove he never received an A. Therefore the stronger assertion that it is 'an absolute lie' is unverified.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers are planning to mandate or 'push' free abortion pills on all students statewide. Legislative efforts in California have focused on expanding voluntary access to medication abortion through clinics, student health centers, and pharmacies and reducing barriers, not forcibly distributing pills to every student.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The statement that a single member was the only lawmaker to vote for both the Clinton 'inquiry' and the Trump 'inquiry' is almost certainly false. Many current members were in Congress during the late-1990s and the late-2010s, and there was not a single clear, comparable floor vote authorizing a Clinton impeachment inquiry in 1998 the way there was in 2019, so the claim of unique status is unsupported.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Biden stating that he does not need voters to get elected; his public remarks and campaign messaging consistently emphasize seeking votes and public support. Claims that he said this appear to be misquotes or taken out of context from remarks about particular constituencies or internal campaign discussions.

claim: "The only time over the last 25 years when the state’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. average was when (Mary) Burke was commerce secretary."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. Mary Burke served as Wisconsin’s commerce secretary around 2010–2011, but Wisconsin’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. average at multiple other times in the past 25 years (for example during the early-1990s recession and other downturns), so it was not the only occasion. Therefore the absolute claim is false.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: The claim asserts a specific ranking across the entire period when Maggie Hassan was in the New Hampshire Senate, but state unemployment rankings fluctuate year-to-year and month-to-month. Hassan served in the New Hampshire Senate roughly 2004–2010, and while New Hampshire often had relatively low unemployment in parts of that span, there is no basis to conclude it was consistently the fourth-lowest for the whole period without a cited source or specific date.

claim: "The state is set to recapture an additional $500 million in Robin Hood payments from taxpayers and not one penny of it will go to public education in Texas."
rationale: Texas 'Robin Hood' recapture is a school-finance mechanism that pulls excess local property-tax revenue from wealthy districts to be redistributed through the state's public school finance system, so it is inaccurate to say an additional $500 million would be recaptured and "not one penny" would go to public education. Exact dollar amounts and how recaptured revenue is applied can vary with legislative and budget actions, but the program's purpose and typical practice are to fund public education rather than wholly diverting funds away from it.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The statement is too broad and not supported as a general fact. While Cruz raised large out-of-state amounts during his 2016 presidential campaign, FEC and news analyses show his Senate campaigns have drawn substantial in-state (Texas) support and donation patterns vary by cycle, so it is incorrect to assert that most of his money overall comes from Washington without specifying timeframe or source.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: The statement is implausible and inconsistent with how municipal and DMV services operate. “Fifth Wednesdays” occur only a few times a year, but local clerk/DMV offices normally provide voter ID services during regular business hours (and often by appointment or at county DMV locations), so the ID service could not reasonably be limited to just those rare days. The claim appears to conflate a special outreach schedule with the actual availability of IDs.

claim: "There have been some estimates that if you deported everybody who is in Texas illegally," it "would create an economic recession for the state."
rationale: Multiple economic studies and analyses by economists and policy research groups have modeled large-scale removal of unauthorized immigrants and concluded such an action would substantially shrink Texas's labor force, output, and tax revenues, with some estimates indicating the contraction could be large enough to trigger a recession in the state. The claim only asserts that there have been some estimates to that effect, which is accurate.

claim: "Inequality in Texas is steadily getting worse, with very few rich people, a great many poor people, and fewer and fewer in the middle."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate trends with an inaccurate characterization. Income inequality in Texas has increased over recent decades and the state’s poverty rate and middle‑income share have been worse or declined relative to the U.S. average, but Texas also has a large and growing number of high‑income households; it is misleading to say there are "very few rich people" or that the situation is uniformly "steadily" worsening year-to-year.

claim: "While Exxon Mobil has 40 pages on its media response strategy, its plan for resource protection is only five pages long and its plan for oil removal is just nine pages long."
rationale: The claim gives precise page counts but does not cite a specific ExxonMobil document, date, or jurisdiction. ExxonMobil maintains many different contingency and spill-response plans (by region, incident type, and year), so these exact numbers cannot be verified as a general statement and are likely misleading without a source.

claim: ﻿Says JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side had a "3-to-1 money advantage" in the Wisconsin Supreme Court campaign.
rationale: Contemporaneous campaign finance reports and news coverage of the Kloppenburg–Prosser 2011 Wisconsin Supreme Court race indicate Kloppenburg’s campaign raised more than Prosser’s campaign in some categories, but when independent expenditures and outside spending are included the advantage was not a clear 3-to-1. Reports described a competitive spending environment with significant conservative outside spending that narrowed or reversed any raw fundraising gap.

claim: The IRS is going to be "in charge" of "a huge national database" on health care that will include Americans’ "personal, intimate, most close-to-the-vest-secrets."
rationale: There is no factual basis that the IRS will be put in charge of a nationwide health database containing Americans' intimate medical records. The IRS's role under existing law is primarily tax collection and limited administration of tax-related health provisions (for example, verifying premium tax credits and receiving insurance coverage reporting forms), not operating or holding comprehensive medical records.

claim: "Florida ranks first in the nation for access to free prekindergarten."
rationale: The statement is overstated and missing crucial context. While Florida's Voluntary Prekindergarten (VPK) program offers broad access for 4‑year‑olds and the state often ranks near the top, national rankings vary by year and by measure (eligibility, seats, or enrollment) and other states such as Georgia and Oklahoma have also ranked first on some measures. Without a specified year and metric, claiming Florida is outright 'first' is not supportable.

claim: Says Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam said, ‘You will give up your guns, if you don’t I’ll have the National Guard cut your power, your phone lines, and your internet. Then, if you still refuse to comply I’ll have you killed.’"
rationale: There is no credible record, news reporting, or official transcript showing Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam made this threat; such an inflammatory statement would have been widely reported and documented. The quote is inconsistent with Northam’s public statements and duties as governor, and appears to be a fabricated or misattributed claim.

claim: Says under Mayor Cory Booker, Newark has seen "violent crime up five years in a row, murder up five years in a row."
rationale: Contemporary crime data and independent fact-checks do not show five straight yearly increases in violent crime or murders during Cory Booker's mayoralty; Newark's violent-crime and homicide totals fluctuated year-to-year with some declines. Multiple analyses of Newark and FBI/UCR data found no continuous five-year upward trend that matches the claim.

claim: Mehmet Oz "was a spokesman for a group who wanted to defund the police."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mehmet Oz served as a spokesman for any organization whose purpose was to 'defund the police.' Oz has publicly opposed defunding police, and claims that he was a spokesman for a defund-the-police group appear to be misattributions or political distortions rather than documented fact.

claim: Mitt Romney did not "endorse" Ted Cruz, even though he said he is voting for Cruz and urged others to do likewise.
rationale: During the 2016 Republican primary Mitt Romney publicly said he would vote for Ted Cruz and urged others to support Cruz over Trump; such public declarations of support were widely reported and treated as an endorsement. There is no clear record of Romney simultaneously insisting that his comments were not an endorsement, and in common political usage saying you will vote for and urging others to do so functions as an endorsement.

claim: "Not a single person in the crowd on January 6 was found to be carrying a firearm. Not one."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and Department of Justice charging documents identified at least some January 6 participants who possessed firearms or were charged with firearms-related offenses, and law enforcement recovered weapons in vehicles associated with people who attended the rally. Therefore the categorical statement that 'not a single person' carried a firearm is contradicted by available evidence.

claim: "Quite frankly, it was during the Bush years of spending, multiplied now by the Obama years that we have this mess."
rationale: The claim simplistically blames a present 'mess' solely on spending in the Bush years 'multiplied' by the Obama years. While deficits and debt rose during both administrations, the increases resulted from multiple factors (Bush-era tax cuts and war spending, the 2008 financial crisis and revenue collapse, and Obama-era recession relief and automatic stabilizers), so the causal attribution as stated is inaccurate and unsupported as a precise factual claim.

claim: "EPA wants to regulate … the family BBQ."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. EPA has proposed a nationwide rule to regulate ordinary private backyard barbecues. The EPA regulates air pollutants from industrial sources, vehicles, fuels and certain appliances, and issues guidance on open burning and air quality, but routine family grilling is generally governed by local ordinances rather than an EPA regulatory action.

claim: Ted Cruz is "unknown to the vast majority of Texans."
rationale: Ted Cruz has been a high‑profile Texas politician — serving as U.S. Senator since 2013, winning statewide elections, and mounting a national presidential campaign — making it extremely unlikely he is “unknown to the vast majority of Texans.” His statewide races and extensive media coverage mean broad name recognition across Texas. The statement therefore overstates unfamiliarity.

claim: Says that Olive Garden is "funding" President Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
rationale: There is no evidence that the Olive Garden restaurant chain as a company 'funded' Donald Trump's 2020 reelection campaign. U.S. federal law prohibits direct corporate contributions to candidates; any political spending would be by a PAC, executives, franchisees, or employees, which is different from the company itself funding a campaign. Reports do not show Olive Garden/Darden making direct campaign contributions to Trump in 2020.

claim: "Eighty percent of the antibiotics in this country are fed to livestock."
rationale: Multiple U.S. government and public‑health reports have shown that historically roughly 70–80% of the antibiotics sold in the United States (by weight) were intended for use in food‑producing animals rather than humans. The common phrasing “fed to livestock” is imprecise but reflects the documented high share of animal antibiotic sales in those reports.

claim: "About 95 percent of America’s production of ethylene is produced on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana."
rationale: The Gulf Coast (Texas and Louisiana) does host the largest share of U.S. ethylene/steam-cracker capacity, but independent industry data and reports put that share well below 95% of total U.S. ethylene production. Figures around a majority—often in the 60–80% range depending on year and whether one counts capacity or output—are more consistent; the 95% number likely confuses ‘new capacity’ or specific product streams with total national production.

claim: "Ivanka Trump charged with major crime."
rationale: As of the most recent reliable reporting through mid-2024, Ivanka Trump had not been publicly criminally charged with a major crime. She has faced subpoenas and been mentioned in investigations, but no indictment or criminal filing against her was reported in major news outlets or court records available up to that time.

claim: "It’s clear" that Hillary Clinton "violated national security laws."
rationale: Official investigations found classified material on Hillary Clinton's private email server and criticized the handling of information, but the FBI concluded in 2016 that there was insufficient evidence of intentional wrongdoing and recommended no criminal charges. Subsequent inspector-general reports documented improper handling of classified information but did not produce a legal finding or conviction that she violated national security laws. Thus it is not 'clear' in the sense of an established legal violation.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has launched "twice as many strikes (on) countries that are predominantly Muslim" than President George W. Bush.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by clear evidence. While President Obama expanded and intensified targeted strikes (especially drone strikes) and struck more countries (e.g., Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, Libya) than President Bush, Bush oversaw large-scale air campaigns in predominantly Muslim countries (notably Afghanistan and Iraq) with very high strike volumes; no authoritative source shows Obama carried out exactly twice as many strikes on predominantly Muslim countries as Bush. The statement conflates different metrics (number of strikes, countries struck, types of strikes) and therefore is misleading.

claim: If you work 40 hours a week at the proposed minimum wage of $10.10 an hour, "you get out of poverty."
rationale: A 40-hour week at $10.10 yields about $21,008 gross annually, which may put a single worker above the federal poverty guideline for one person in some years but is below the poverty thresholds for most multi-person households and below commonly used measures of living wages in many areas. Whether someone is 'out of poverty' depends on household size, location, taxes, and benefits, so the blanket claim is incorrect.

claim: "We’re now spending 42 percent of our economy on government."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and does not match standard official measures. For the United States in recent years, federal spending alone has been roughly 20–25% of GDP and combined federal + state + local spending has typically been in the mid-30s percent of GDP; official data do not support a sustained current level of 42%. While pandemic-era emergency spending briefly raised government outlays, routine measures do not show a present 42% share of the economy.

claim: Says Florida Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried "spent millions of dollars to put her face on every gas pump across this state."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nikki Fried personally spent millions to place her face on every gas pump in Florida. Reporting and public records show limited consumer‑outreach ads/decals tied to the Agriculture Department (which sometimes included agency branding or messaging), but not a documented statewide, multimillion‑dollar campaign featuring her photo on every pump as claimed.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no clear record that John McCain introduced a bill specifically banning a candidate from paying registered lobbyists. McCain was well known for supporting limits on lobbyist influence and campaign finance reform (e.g., McCain-Feingold and ethics proposals), but the claim as stated—an explicit prohibition on candidates paying registered lobbyists—does not match documented legislation he sponsored.

claim: In the federal government, "there’s $16 billion in duplicate programs" that can be cut.
rationale: The statement asserts a precise $16 billion figure for ‘duplicate programs’ across the federal government but no authoritative, widely accepted federal estimate pins duplication at exactly $16 billion. The Government Accountability Office and other oversight bodies have documented overlap, fragmentation, and potential savings in various areas, but totals and definitions vary by report and timeframe, so the specific $16 billion claim is not supported as a verified, general fact.

claim: The media "never show crowds."
rationale: The statement is an absolute universal claim but is contradicted by abundant evidence: news and media outlets routinely show crowds at protests, political rallies, sporting events, concerts, parades and breaking-news scenes. Because media frequently and regularly display crowds, the claim that they 'never' show crowds is false.

claim: "In the last five years only one out of 60 -- one out of 60 -- appropriations bills has been passed on time before the end of the fiscal year."
rationale: The statement is incorrect. While Congress often fails to enact all 12 regular appropriations bills by the Oct. 1 fiscal-year deadline and commonly uses continuing resolutions or omnibus packages, multiple individual appropriations bills have been enacted on time across recent five-year spans — far more than a single timely bill out of 60. The claim appears to conflate the rare event of all 12 being passed on time with the count of individual bills passed before the deadline.

claim: West Virginia has "the nation’s lowest workforce participation rate, which hovers around 50 percent, when the national average is about 63 percent."
rationale: West Virginia does have one of the country’s lowest labor force participation rates, but the state’s rate is typically in the low-50 percent range (around 52–55%), not precisely “around 50 percent.” The national labor force participation rate being about 62–63 percent is broadly accurate, but the exact rankings and percentages vary by year and month.

claim: Texas "could be very close to herd immunity."
rationale: Saying Texas "could be very close to herd immunity" is not supported by available evidence: herd immunity requires a high proportion immune (typically 60–90% for SARS-CoV-2 depending on variants), and combined vaccination plus prior-infection estimates for Texas have generally fallen short of that. Immunity from infection and vaccination also wanes and variants raise the threshold, so a blanket claim that the state was 'very close' is misleading.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: There is no record of Hillary Clinton saying she will 'wipe out' the Second Amendment or that she does not believe in the First Amendment. Her public record shows support for gun safety measures (assault-weapons bans, expanded background checks), not repeal of the Second Amendment, and she has defended free speech rights in many contexts. The claim that she 'believes in big government' is a subjective political characterization, not a factual quote that directly conflicts with the 10th Amendment.

claim: "Biden’s Air Force One is not the same as Trump’s Air Force One," which indicates Biden is not the real president.
rationale: “Air Force One” is merely the radio call sign for any U.S. Air Force aircraft carrying the sitting president, so different physical planes or liveries between administrations are routine and do not indicate the person aboard is not the legitimate president. Aircraft are part of a rotating presidential fleet, are maintained, upgraded, and sometimes replaced, which explains differences between what was used under Trump and what is used under Biden.

claim: Image of expansive pit shows a lithium mine.
rationale: Without the image, location, or metadata, you cannot reliably identify an 'expansive pit' as a lithium mine. Many large open‑pit mines, quarries, and evaporation ponds for other minerals (copper, iron, gypsum, salt, potash) look similar from above, and lithium operations often use brine evaporation ponds or distinct hard‑rock pits that can be mistaken for other sites. Social‑media posts frequently mislabel mining imagery.

claim: "Fox News Sandra Smith: ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ "
rationale: I am not aware of any reliable transcript or reputable news reporting showing Fox News anchor Sandra Smith saying the exact line ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ That phrasing appears to be a misquotation or misattribution rather than a documented on-air quote. Without a verifiable clip or primary transcript, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin currently elects its city council from 10 single-member geographic districts (with the mayor elected at-large), so it does have geographic representation on its council. Other large Texas and U.S. cities (Houston, San Antonio, Dallas, Fort Worth, El Paso, etc.) also use district-based council seats, so Austin is not uniquely the largest city lacking geographic representation.

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The statement is misleading: unauthorized migration to the U.S. has been high in recent years with border encounters reaching multiyear or record highs in 2021–2023, not at decades-low levels. Likewise, crime rates are not uniformly "as low as they’ve been in decades": violent crime fell from 1990s highs into the 2010s but rose around 2020 and only partially declined afterward, so it is inaccurate to claim both measures are at multi‑decade lows without more specificity.

claim: The 9-9-9 plan "does not raise taxes on those that are making the least."
rationale: Independent analyses of Herman Cain's 9-9-9 plan — which replaced current income and payroll taxes with a 9% income tax, 9% national sales tax and 9% business tax — found that lower-income households would generally face higher total federal tax liability because a national sales tax is regressive and would more than offset payroll/income tax reductions for many in the lowest income groups. Contemporary fact-checks and revenue-modeling showed the bottom quintile would likely see a net tax increase under typical assumptions.

claim: "In Ohio, we invested in our children, raising school funding by 5.5 percent in the last budget."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no budget year or source; Ohio’s school funding changes are reported by biennial budgets and can be measured as total appropriation, per-pupil funding, or by specific line items. I found no authoritative, broadly reported confirmation that the most recently enacted Ohio state budget increased overall K–12 funding by exactly 5.5%; parts of funding or one-time grants can rise by different amounts, so the blanket statement is unsupported without a citation.

claim: "60 percent of the jobs lost in the 2008 recession were living-wage jobs. Of the jobs we’ve gotten back, only 40 percent are living-wage."
rationale: The precise 60%/40% numeric claim cannot be verified and is misleading because it depends critically on how “living-wage” is defined and what recovery period is used. Labor statistics and academic analyses do show that middle-wage occupations suffered large losses in the 2008 recession and recovery added many lower-wage and some higher-wage jobs, but published BLS and research estimates do not consistently support the exact 60% of lost jobs being "living-wage" and only 40% of regained jobs being so without additional context or a specific methodology. Therefore the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Says North Carolina gives taxpayer dollars to private schools, but "we really don’t know what these schools are doing or how they are performing."
rationale: North Carolina does send taxpayer funds to private schools through programs like the Opportunity Scholarship voucher program, but it is incorrect to say we have no information on how those schools perform. Participating private schools are required to administer approved standardized tests and report results and enrollment/attendance data to state authorities, though critics note the data are less comprehensive and less directly comparable to public-school report cards and oversight has had gaps. Therefore the absolute claim that “we really don’t know” is misleading.

claim: Aaron Bean voted to give illegal immigrants in-state tuition.
rationale: I find no clear record that Aaron Bean specifically voted for a bill whose stated purpose was to give undocumented (illegal) immigrants blanket in-state tuition. Florida already has a longstanding law and administratively-applied criteria that in some cases permit in-state rates for certain undocumented students, but that is not the same as a discrete recent vote by Bean to 'give illegal immigrants in-state tuition.'

claim: The Super Bowl has "one of the highest levels of human sex trafficking activity of any event in the country."
rationale: Available research, law-enforcement statements, and multiple fact-checking investigations find no reliable empirical evidence that the Super Bowl produces one of the highest levels of sex trafficking in the country. Reports claiming large spikes are largely anecdotal, based on hotline call volumes or unverified claims rather than systematic data showing the Super Bowl ranks among the top events for trafficking.

claim: "It is more difficult to obtain a Costco membership than it is to get a NYC Municipal ID"
rationale: Costco membership is typically obtained quickly by paying an annual fee and presenting a basic photo ID, whereas the NYC Municipal ID (IDNYC) requires submitting and verifying proof of identity and two proofs of New York City residency and an in‑person appointment/photo, making it generally more document‑and time‑intensive. For most people the municipal ID process is therefore more burdensome than buying a Costco membership.

claim: Under the Hate Crimes bill, "any pastor, preacher, priest, rabbi or imam who gives a sermon out of their moral traditions about sexual practices could be found guilty of a federal crime."
rationale: Federal hate-crimes statutes criminalize violent or threatening conduct (and certain conspiracies) targeting protected classes, not the mere expression of moral or religious views. Peaceful sermons about sexual morality are protected by the First Amendment and the religious‑exercise protections, and would not by themselves constitute a federal hate crime absent underlying violent or criminal conduct and intent. The claim therefore misstates how hate‑crimes law operates and is misleading.

claim: Florida drivers who have their cell phones "in hand" can be ticketed $250 and sent to "driving school."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Florida does prohibit texting while driving and limits handheld use for certain driver categories, but the routine penalty described ($250 plus mandatory 'driving school') is not the standard statewide penalty; fines for texting offenses are typically much lower and attending driving school is not a universal, automatic sanction.

claim: "Just on Jan. 1 of this year, there were 40,000 new laws put on the books in one day."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 40,000 distinct new laws were enacted and took effect on a single day. Legislative bodies and regulatory agencies sometimes schedule many provisions to take effect on Jan. 1, but the scale claimed is implausible given how laws and regulations are recorded and the number of jurisdictions involved. The statement likely conflates rules, regulatory filings, or accumulated effective-dates across many jurisdictions rather than 40,000 new enacted laws on one day.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: This claim is not supported by public records or credible reporting. The EPA currently employs roughly 14,000 people and has not proposed hiring 230,000 new federal regulators; nor is there a documented, standalone $21 billion federal request solely to hire that many EPA staff. The figure appears to conflate or misinterpret budgetary proposals, grants, or broader program funding rather than an EPA staffing request of that magnitude.

claim: "One hundred and ninety-four countries signed the Paris Agreement to control greenhouse gases. Our own voluntary agreement to accomplish the same goal — the Under2  MOU — has 165 signatories, representing a billion people."
rationale: The claim mixes and slightly misstates facts. The exact number of countries signing the Paris Agreement depends on timing (commonly reported as about 195 signatories, with parties and ratifications changing over time), so "194 countries" is not reliably accurate. The Under2 MOU is a coalition of subnational governments (states/regions), not national governments; while it has had on the order of 100–200 signatories and has been said to represent roughly a billion people, that characterization and the counts are approximate and time‑dependent.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
rationale: Historically the EPA (jointly with the Army Corps) has proposed and promulgated broader definitions of "waters of the United States"—most notably the 2015 Clean Water Rule—that critics argued would bring ephemeral puddles, roadside ditches, and other small features on private land within federal jurisdiction. Those rulemakings and guidance documents aimed to expand which waters are "navigable" or jurisdictional under the Clean Water Act, though courts and later actions have limited or revised those definitions.

claim: Despite attention on global warming, "fewer Americans carpool today to work than carpooled in 1980" and "SUVs have never been a larger proportion of the vehicles being sold in this country."
rationale: U.S. commuting data show the share of workers who carpool has declined since 1980 (when roughly 18–20% carpooled) to well under 10% in recent years. Nationwide vehicle-sales data show SUVs/crossovers now account for the largest share of new-vehicle sales in U.S. history, reaching record-high proportions in the 2010s–2020s.

claim: U.S. sanctions mean "Cuba can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever."
rationale: The U.S. embargo and sanctions primarily restrict trade and financial transactions by U.S. persons and entities and require licenses for certain activities, but they do not categorically prevent all countries or companies from trading with Cuba. Many non-U.S. countries and firms (e.g., in Canada, the EU, China, Mexico, Russia) conduct trade, tourism, and investment with Cuba, and there are statutory and regulatory exemptions (food, medicine, some humanitarian goods).

claim: "We don't know anything about Hillary in terms of religion. Now, she's been in the public eye for years and years, and yet there's no — there's nothing out there."
rationale: The claim that nothing is known about Hillary Clinton's religion is incorrect. Hillary Clinton has long been publicly identified as a Methodist and has discussed her faith in interviews, speeches, and biographical profiles, so information about her religious affiliation is available.

claim: Says there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees."
rationale: There is no constitutional 60-vote requirement to confirm Supreme Court nominees — the Constitution calls for Senate advice and consent by majority. A 60-vote cloture threshold was a Senate practice to overcome filibusters for nominations, but it was a procedural norm (not a formal confirmation rule) and was removed for Supreme Court nominees in 2017.

claim: "They found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013" for immigration legislation, and "each time the House Republican majority refused to take it up."
rationale: The 2013 part is correct: the Senate passed comprehensive immigration reform (S.744) with well over 60 votes (68) and the Republican House majority did not take it up. The 2006 part is not supported: there was no widely recognized comprehensive immigration bill that mustered 60 votes in the Senate that year — 2006 saw other bills (e.g., the Secure Fence Act) and failed proposals, but not a clear 60‑vote Senate passage of a comprehensive reform that the House then refused to consider. Combining the two years as identical instances is therefore misleading.

claim: "President Trump’s Republican Party will create more debt in one year than was generated in the first 200 years of America’s existence."
rationale: Measured in nominal dollars, the federal debt outstanding at roughly the 200-year mark (circa 1976) was on the order of several hundred billion dollars, whereas in a single pandemic year (2020) the debt rose by multiple trillions of dollars under the Trump administration. That one-year increase therefore exceeded the total nominal debt accumulated in the first ~200 years of U.S. history.

claim: "Abortionists have reduced our black population by more than 25 percent since 1973."
rationale: The claim is not supported by authoritative demographic analysis. While abortion rates have been higher among Black women than among some other groups and many abortions have occurred since 1973, there is no credible, peer‑reviewed evidence showing that abortions have reduced the current U.S. Black population by more than 25%; such a figure relies on simplistic arithmetic and ignores births that would have occurred, mortality, and migration.

claim: "U.S. comedian Kevin Hart in critical condition after gory car crash."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Kevin Hart is currently in critical condition from a recent 'gory' car crash. Hart was seriously injured in a September 2019 rollover and required back surgery, but media coverage at the time did not describe him as being in critical condition and he subsequently recovered; no reliable recent sources corroborate a new critical crash.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: There is no reliable, contemporary source establishing that exactly 60% of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid. Physician participation in Medicaid varies substantially by specialty, practice setting, county, and whether the question asks about accepting any Medicaid patients versus accepting new Medicaid patients, so an undated, precise statewide figure is unsubstantiated. The claim therefore appears false or at minimum not verifiable as stated.

claim: COVID-19 vaccinations are "a violation of the Nuremberg code."
rationale: The Nuremberg Code governs unethical human experimentation and requires voluntary informed consent and prior safety testing. COVID-19 vaccines were developed through clinical trials with consent, underwent regulatory review or emergency authorization, and have been administered as standard medical interventions with safety monitoring rather than as secret or nonconsensual experiments. Labeling routine vaccination programs categorically as a violation misapplies the Nuremberg Code.

claim: After losing 750,000 jobs a month before this administration, the U.S. economy under Barack Obama has had 20 straight months of growth, has added 2.8 million jobs in the private sector and added "millions of jobs in manufacturing."
rationale: The statement mixes timeframes and overstates the scale of manufacturing gains. While the private sector did return to consecutive months of job growth after the 2009 trough and net private-sector jobs rose by a few million over several years, the specific claims of '20 straight months' without a defined start, exactly 2.8 million private-sector jobs in that short span, and 'millions of jobs in manufacturing' are inaccurate or misleading: manufacturing gains were far smaller (hundreds of thousands over multiple years) and the large monthly losses in late 2008 were roughly 600–800k in the worst months, not precisely 750k as stated.

claim: "We have more hospitals that are children’s hospitals than any other state in the union." 
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because the pronoun "we" does not identify which state is meant, and public data on children's hospitals depend on definitions and time period. Different states (for example California, Texas, New York, Ohio, and Pennsylvania) each have multiple children's hospitals, so without a specified state and clear counting rules the assertion that "we" have more than any other state is unsupported.

claim: Says "$1,100 of the tuition paid by every Oregon university student annually goes just to pay the costs of PERS."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Oregon universities and the state pay employer PERS contributions that are part of overall personnel costs, those costs are funded from multiple revenue sources (state appropriations, grants, tuition, auxiliary income) and vary by institution and year. A blanket figure of $1,100 'of the tuition paid by every Oregon university student annually' oversimplifies the accounting and lacks documented calculation; independent analyses have found per‑student PERS allocations vary and are not a uniform direct charge to each student's tuition.

claim: "We are seeing dramatic rate cuts" to Medicare that will affect seniors’ ability to keep their doctor, hospital and prevention services.
rationale: The statement is misleading and too broad. While parts of Medicare (for example the physician fee schedule or hospital payments) can face reductions in specific updates, most recent changes have been modest, often temporarily offset by legislation or other payment mechanisms, and there is no clear evidence of a widespread, dramatic cut universally causing seniors to lose doctors or hospitals. Whether reduced payment rates lead to access problems is conditional and varies by locality and provider type, so the claim overstates and generalizes the situation.

claim: After hiring a campaign manager in 2006, "I got this $100 and something fee ... for hazardous materials."
rationale: The statement is vague and I cannot verify it as a factual claim about a specific person or record. There is no publicly available, corroborating evidence or campaign finance documentation I can identify that records a $100+ "hazardous materials" fee tied to hiring a campaign manager in 2006. Without a named individual, citation, or supporting records this assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "When I took office, the deficit was nearly 10 percent of our economy. Today, it's approaching 3 percent."
rationale: The U.S. federal budget deficit at the start of Barack Obama’s term (FY2009) was just under 10% of GDP (around 9.8%). By the mid-2010s the annual deficit had declined to roughly 2.5–3% of GDP, so the statement accurately characterizes that change in deficit-to-GDP terms.

claim: "There’s more murders with hammers last year than...shotguns and pistols and AK-47s."
rationale: National crime statistics show that firearms (handguns, shotguns, rifles including AK-style rifles) account for the large majority of homicides, while murders committed with blunt objects such as hammers are a small minority. Therefore the statement that there were more murders with hammers last year than with shotguns, pistols, and AK-47s is inconsistent with available homicide data.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: I cannot corroborate the specific claim from available memory and such a precise statement requires checking month-by-month private-sector employment data from Wisconsin for at least the prior ten Septembers. Without those records, the assertion that September 2014 represented the "largest private-sector job creation" for that month in over a decade is unverified and thus treated as false under cautious standards.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: Joe Biden has not repeatedly told Americans broadly that he will raise their taxes; throughout his campaign and presidency he repeatedly said he would not raise taxes on households earning under $400,000. He has proposed tax increases focused on corporations, the wealthy, and high-income households, which opponents sometimes portray as raising 'Americans' taxes' generally.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: The Eisenhower administration did oversee large immigration enforcement actions—most notably the 1954 'Operation Wetback'—that resulted in over a million removals or returns of Mexican nationals in the mid-1950s. However, scholarly and government estimates generally do not support the precise claim that Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants"; numbers vary, commonly cited totals are closer to about one to 1.1 million removals in that period and many were voluntary returns or involved questions about legal status. The 1.5 million figure is therefore an overstatement or conflates different counts and timeframes.

claim: Says Joe Biden "helps build Afghanistan’s pipeline."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden personally helped build a pipeline in Afghanistan. The major proposed gas pipeline involving Afghanistan (TAPI) is a multilateral project led by Turkmenistan and regional partners and has not been constructed as a U.S.-built project nor credited to Biden’s direct involvement.

claim: "Woman set to testify against Clintons blown up in home explosion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a woman who was scheduled to testify against the Clintons was 'blown up' in a home explosion. Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers have investigated similar viral posts and found them to be unverified or fabricated, with no official reports, names, or contemporaneous reputable coverage supporting the claim.

claim: Says Tony Thurmond was "Reprimanded by the Obama Administration for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault in district schools."
rationale: There is no public record that the Obama Administration personally reprimanded Tony Thurmond. While the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights has investigated and sometimes issued findings or resolution agreements with school districts over Title IX failures during the Obama era, available records do not show a formal reprimand of Thurmond himself; the claim appears to conflate district-level actions or investigations with a personal rebuke.

claim: Photos prove the Denver light rail system has low ridership.
rationale: Photographs are isolated snapshots of specific times and places and cannot establish overall system ridership. Empty-looking trains or stations in photos can reflect off-peak hours, service changes, or selective framing, whereas ridership is measured by systematic counts and official transit agency data.

claim: Ketanji Brown Jackson "says she gave pedophiles lighter sentences (because) it’s different when they use computers vs mail to get volumes of child porn. This makes ‘total sense’ according to Jackson."
rationale: This is a misleading summary and not an accurate direct quote. During her time as a federal judge Jackson discussed how sentencing guidelines can rise with the volume of images and the medium (online sharing can produce larger volumes), and she sometimes imposed below-guideline sentences based on case specifics; she did not plainly say she gave pedophiles lighter sentences because computers vs. mail and did not make the quoted remark as presented. The claim conflates context, paraphrases selectively, and presents it as an unqualified endorsement by Jackson.

claim: "Our larger domestic threat is from racial supremacist groups."
rationale: U.S. federal law‑enforcement and intelligence assessments in recent years have identified racially or ethnically motivated violent extremist groups (commonly described as white supremacists) as the most persistent and lethal domestic terrorism threat. Data on high‑casualty domestic attacks and public statements by agencies support that these groups have accounted for a disproportionate share of domestic extremist fatalities compared with other domestic extremist categories in the relevant recent period.

claim: A bill backed by Sean Duffy and other House Republicans "could actually require the Internal Revenue Service to conduct audits of rape victims" who get an abortion.
rationale: There is no known provision in bills sponsored or backed by Rep. Sean Duffy that explicitly mandates the IRS to audit rape victims who obtain abortions. Tax audits are triggered by tax law and IRS procedures, and abortion-policy bills typically address medical or criminal reporting, not directing the IRS to investigate victims of sexual assault.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox, a former Tallahassee city commissioner and mayor, has been widely described in news coverage and public records as having worked as a Florida lobbyist after his time in office. Reporting about his federal corruption case refers to his role and activities as a lobbyist and lobbyist-client relationships.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Coolmath Games is owned or operated by a Mexican drug cartel, nor that it is being taken down for that reason. The site is run by a private company (Coolmath LLC) and claims of cartel ownership appear to be baseless rumors or misinformation.

claim: "Foreign aid makes up about 1 percent of our entire budget."
rationale: For the United States, total foreign assistance (economic and development aid plus many security assistance programs) has historically been on the order of tens of billions of dollars versus federal outlays in the trillions, which works out to roughly one percent of total federal spending in many recent years. The exact share varies year to year and by how one counts ‘foreign aid,’ but saying it is about 1% is a reasonable rough characterization.

claim: "Tony Evers is cutting child support."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Governor Tony Evers has enacted a policy that 'cuts child support' as a general statement. Child support amounts are determined by state statutes and court orders and are enforced by state agencies, not typically unilaterally 'cut' by a governor; while budgets or administrative changes can affect program funding, that is different from reducing ordered child support payments.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: An individual attorney general (Mark Herring) does not provide 'advice and consent' for Parole Board appointments or operations. In Virginia, Parole Board members are appointed by the governor and subject to confirmation by the legislature (advice and consent), not by the attorney general.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no credible public record showing Rep. Paul Broun Jr. endorsed or advocated for the sale of so-called 'crush videos' or 'sided with sexual deviants' on that issue. The claim appears to conflate inflammatory language with unverified allegations; Broun's known public statements and voting record do not support this accusation.

claim: While the smoking rate nationally has fallen, more than 18 percent of Georgians still light up.
rationale: Recent U.S. and state surveillance data show adult cigarette smoking prevalence has declined and Georgia's adult smoking rate in recent years has been in the mid-teens, below 18 percent. Therefore the specific assertion that 'more than 18 percent of Georgians still light up' is not supported by current statewide estimates.

rationale:
The claim as stated is unverified because it gives no date, product variant, lot number, or jurisdiction, and I cannot confirm a specific, ongoing recall for a Colgate toothpaste from authoritative sources. While consumer-packaged goods including toothpastes are occasionally recalled, a generic statement that 'a Colgate toothpaste is subject to "recall"' cannot be confirmed without more details. claim: Since Sept. 11, 2001, "270,000 Americans were killed by gunfire at home."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous (no end date) and does not match U.S. vital statistics. CDC data show tens of thousands of firearm deaths per year since 2001 (including suicides and homicides), so simple arithmetic over the period since Sept 11, 2001 yields totals inconsistent with the unqualified claim. If the speaker meant a very specific subset (e.g., only domestic homicides at home) the number would be far lower; if they meant all firearm deaths at home the claim still lacks sourcing and is misleading.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: The statement conflates different measures and is misleading. Annual Federal Register output in some years has been on the order of ~80,000 pages published, but that is a count of pages published (including notices and technical material), not a measure of net new regulations; and stacking 81,000 standard sheets (500 sheets ≈ 2 inches) yields roughly 24–30 feet (~2.5–3 stories depending on story height), so the ‘‘three-story’’ visual is an approximation that depends on assumptions.

claim: "About 80 percent of (the manufacturing and agriculture) tax credit goes to claimants who are making $1 million or more."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written and appears to assert a precise distribution without naming the specific program, year, or jurisdiction. Benefit shares from tax credits for manufacturing or agriculture vary widely by program and over time; no general, authoritative source supports a blanket claim that about 80% of such a credit goes to claimants making $1 million or more.

claim: "As soon as Chris Christie was governor, he gave tax cuts to millionaires."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Christie immediately enacted tax cuts for millionaires upon taking office in January 2010. His initial actions focused on spending reductions, furloughs and vetoes to close budget gaps, and any tax changes that advantaged high earners were incremental and occurred later rather than 'as soon as' he became governor.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible as stated: it does not identify which county, which categories of employees are included, or provide supporting staffing numbers. Most large county district attorney offices have grown since 1985 to keep pace with population and expanded responsibilities, so asserting current staffing equals 1985 levels for the 'second-largest' office is unlikely without corroborating data.

claim: "President Trump has lifted the prospect of voters across Vermont, overseeing a 11,742 decline of Vermont residents on food stamps."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it provides no timeframe or source for the cited "11,742" decline and wrongly implies a direct causal role for President Trump in Vermont's SNAP enrollment. SNAP caseloads change for many reasons (state policy changes, economic conditions, pandemic effects), and without specific data linking that exact numeric drop to actions by Trump the statement cannot be verified.

claim: After legalizing marijuana in Colorado, "we haven't seen a spike in consumption."
rationale: As a broad statement the claim is inaccurate: after Colorado legalized recreational marijuana, legal sales and measures of adult cannabis use increased, and several analyses of national and state survey data (NSDUH and state reports) found rises in adult past‑month and past‑year use. Some studies do show that adolescent use did not spike sharply, but the blanket claim that there was no spike in consumption overall is misleading.

claim: Says Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie made a late-night visit to Kinko’s to forge President Barack Obama’s birth certificate two days before Obama unveiled it to the media.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie visited a Kinko’s to forge President Obama’s birth certificate. The White House released the document publicly and Hawaii officials have confirmed the state records; Abercrombie’s later remarks about having seen Obama’s Hawaiian birth record were widely reported and misinterpreted but do not substantiate a forgery claim.

claim: "So far, out of 175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 were not from Kenosha. Rioting has become its own industry."
rationale: Local law-enforcement statements from the Kenosha unrest period reported roughly 175 people arrested with about 102 not being from Kenosha (commonly reported as not from Kenosha County), so the numeric portion aligns with contemporaneous official counts. The second sentence is an opinion/metaphor and not a verifiable factual claim, and the phrasing “not from Kenosha” is ambiguous (city vs. county).

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already criminalizes assault, sexual assault, public lewdness, trespass, and related offenses, so entering a bathroom with the intent to harm or assault someone would be illegal under existing statutes. Therefore the general statement that it is "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone" is accurate.

claim: "President Obama has the most border patrols and border security deployed at the border of any previous president."
rationale: During the Obama administration Border Patrol staffing and border-enforcement resources rose to historically high levels relative to prior administrations; CBP agent headcounts and spending on personnel, technology and fencing increased steadily through his terms. Multiple government staffing reports and contemporary fact-checking noted that by the end of Obama’s tenure Border Patrol personnel totals were higher than in earlier presidencies.

claim: "Wayfair CEO steps down."
rationale: As of my last comprehensive update in June 2024 there was no widely reported announcement that Wayfair's CEO had stepped down; the company's leadership (including co-founder Niraj Shah) was still listed in leadership sources. The claim provides no date or source, and I have no corroborating information indicating a resignation.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented: it asserts a specific person warned President Trump in January and advised on actions, but no speaker or contemporaneous evidence is provided here. While some U.S. officials and intelligence sources did raise concerns about COVID-19 in January 2020, this particular individual's direct warning to the president and the content of advice cannot be confirmed from the claim alone.

claim: Says that "over a 45-minute period that we had the press conference" on the coronavirus on March 13, 2020, the stock market set "an all-time record."
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. stock markets set an "all-time record" during the roughly 45 minutes of the March 13, 2020 coronavirus press conference. March 13, 2020 was a highly volatile trading day with large declines and volume, but the widely reported all-time point gain and other headline records occurred on different dates (for example major point gains happened later in March 2020). The claim conflates general volatility with an "all-time record" that did not occur in that specific window.

claim: "Nonpartisan experts have consistently ranked Claire one of the most independent senators — right in the middle."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it does not identify which 'Claire', which nonpartisan experts, or a time period, and it simultaneously calls her 'one of the most independent' and 'right in the middle,' which are inconsistent. Established nonpartisan measures of ideology and bipartisanship (DW‑NOMINATE, Lugar Center Bipartisan Index, GovTrack) show that rankings change over time and that a senator described as a moderate is not continually ranked as both 'most independent' and exactly 'in the middle.' Without named sources or a timeframe, the assertion that experts have 'consistently ranked' her that way is not verifiable.

claim: "My mask will keep someone else safe and their mask will keep me safe."
rationale: The statement is overstated: wearing a mask significantly reduces the chance you will transmit respiratory pathogens to others (source control) and another person’s mask reduces the chance you will inhale infectious particles, but neither action guarantees that someone will be kept completely safe. Effectiveness depends on mask type, fit, correct use, exposure time, and ventilation, so mutual masking lowers risk substantially but is not an absolute guarantee of safety.

claim: "I have always been focused on reining in the deficit."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that cannot be verified without knowing who 'I' is and what period is meant. Demonstrating someone has 'always' been focused on reining in the deficit would require comprehensive, consistent evidence across their entire career (votes, budgets, proposals, and statements), which is not provided. Absent that specific evidence, the universal phrasing makes the claim implausible and not supported.

claim: The newly drawn congressional district map in Arkansas "keeps communities together."
rationale: The statement is misleading: while map sponsors claim it "keeps communities together," news coverage and expert analyses of the recent Arkansas congressional map noted that it splits several cities and counties and disperses pockets of voters, which undercuts the claim. Whether communities are "kept together" is subjective, but objective reviews raised credible concerns that the map fractures urban and minority communities of interest.

claim: Gwinnett County government has made "significant cutbacks in staffing."
rationale: There is no clear public evidence that Gwinnett County government implemented broad, substantial staffing cuts; recent public budgets and local reporting through mid‑2024 do not document large-scale layoffs. The claim also fails to specify a timeframe or what constitutes "significant," so it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: President Obama "promised" families making less than $250,000 a year would not see taxes go up, but "Obamacare raises 18 different taxes."
rationale: President Obama did repeatedly pledge that households making less than $250,000 would not see their taxes raised, which is accurate. However, the claim that “Obamacare raises 18 different taxes” is misleading: the Affordable Care Act contains a mix of new or increased revenue provisions, fees, and taxes, many of which target insurers, employers, high-income households, or are industry assessments rather than 18 distinct new taxes on typical families under $250,000. Counting methods used by critics inflate the number by including provider fees, Medicare payment changes, and taxes that primarily affect high earners or businesses.

claim: The federal tax code has "loopholes that are giving incentives for companies that are shipping jobs overseas."
rationale: U.S. corporate tax rules have long included provisions—such as deferral of U.S. tax on many foreign earnings, mechanisms for profit-shifting through transfer pricing, and deductible interest or other structures—that can lower tax costs for income earned or activities located abroad and therefore create incentives to move jobs or operations offshore. The 2017 tax overhaul changed some of these incentives (e.g., GILTI, BEAT), but tax experts continue to identify rules and planning opportunities that can encourage offshoring.

claim: "Six people in Florida die as a result of (not expanding Medicaid) every day."
rationale: There is no authoritative, peer‑reviewed source that establishes the precise figure of six Floridians dying every day specifically 'as a result of not expanding Medicaid.' While research finds that Medicaid expansion is associated with reduced mortality and that lack of expansion likely contributes to excess deaths, estimates vary by method and time period and do not support a single definitive daily death count for Florida.

claim: "Nobody applies to the United States for refugee status. They apply to the United Nations."
rationale: The United States accepts refugee applications through its own systems (the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program) and individuals may also apply for asylum directly to U.S. authorities after arrival. While the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) often conducts initial refugee status determinations and can refer cases for resettlement, many applications are processed by U.S. government agencies rather than by the UN.

claim: "Every four minutes, another American home or business goes solar."
rationale: The statement is presented as a timeless fact but is actually a time‑bound, promotional statistic that has varied by year and data source. Solar installation rates change year-to-year and depend on definitions (residential vs. commercial, system vs. building), so without a specific timeframe the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: The state’s overall revenues only returned this year to 2007 levels.
rationale: The statement is unverified because it omits which state and what year is meant by 'this year.' State revenue levels vary widely and must be compared using specific fiscal-year data from that state's official budget or treasury; without those details the assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false. If a source with precise numbers were provided, the claim could be evaluated accurately.

claim: Asked what his administration would be doing about "the gun problem," said, "We have done much more than most administrations. … We’ve done, actually, a lot."
rationale: The claim presents a quoted response but provides no named speaker, date, or source, and I cannot verify that exact wording in any authoritative transcript or news report. Without attribution or supporting sourcing the statement cannot be confirmed as factual in the asserted context.

claim: "We [the city of Atlanta] are overbuilt on housing."
rationale: The statement is vague and not demonstrably true as a general fact — whether a city is "overbuilt" depends on measurable metrics (vacancy rates, permits versus absorption, price/rent trends) and timeframe. Available general information about Atlanta shows strong population and job growth and ongoing demand for housing, alongside substantial new multifamily construction; that mix does not clearly support a blanket claim that the city is overbuilt. Without specific data showing sustained high vacancies or falling prices across the market, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: U.S. Census Bureau data and mainstream news coverage reported that 2017 saw median household income rise to its highest recorded level, and poverty rates fell, which many sources described as the strong economy lifting more Americans. The statement uses the informal term “middle-class income,” but the claim aligns with the Census finding that median household income reached a record in 2017.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The claim presents a universal statement that taxes alone are pushing all single, childless low-wage workers into poverty. In the U.S., payroll and consumption taxes reduce take-home pay, but many low-wage single workers are either already below the poverty line before taxes or remain above it after payroll and income taxes; refundable tax credits and the standard deduction also affect net tax liability. While some individuals in particular circumstances can be pushed below the poverty line by taxes and other costs, the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "According to 2009 estimates, an agreement with Panama could result in almost 1,900 Florida jobs in the first year – and about 15,000 jobs after five years."
rationale: I could not find authoritative 2009 estimates that specifically projected nearly 1,900 Florida jobs in year one and about 15,000 after five years from a Panama agreement. Official analyses of the U.S.–Panama trade agreement (such as USITC reviews) reported only modest national employment effects, and the large state-level figures cited here appear to be unsubstantiated or come from partisan projections rather than independent estimates.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "explicitly advocated" a guest worker program for all illegal immigrants.
rationale: There is no clear public record that David Dewhurst explicitly called for a guest-worker program that would cover all undocumented immigrants. Dewhurst has discussed immigration reform and supported limited temporary-worker or merit-based approaches at times, but he did not publicly advocate a blanket guest-worker program applying to all illegal immigrants. The claim overstates and generalizes his position.

claim: "We haven't yet taken out a negative ad."
rationale: The statement lacks essential context (which campaign, timeframe, and what counts as a 'negative ad') and therefore cannot be verified as an absolute truth. Given the ubiquity of opposition/contrast advertising in modern campaigns and absent evidence proving no negative ads were ever run, the claim is treated as likely false pending specific support.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: The specific totals in the claim are not supported by state election data or reputable fact-checkers. Investigations found no evidence that Virginia mailed over 500,000 ballots to dead people or that Nevada mailed 200,000 to dead people or pets; apparent large counts usually stem from misreading voter-roll categories (inactive/duplicated/forwarding addresses) or conflating registrations with mailed, accepted ballots.

claim: Says "all my grandparents" immigrated to America.
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, personal family history that cannot be verified from the claim alone. Without documentary evidence (birthplaces, immigration or naturalization records) the assertion is unproven and should be treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Last year we lost $500 billion on trade with China."
rationale: Official U.S. trade statistics show the annual bilateral U.S. trade deficit with China has generally been in the low-to-mid hundreds of billions of dollars in recent years (commonly roughly $300–$450B), not $500B in a single year. The claim overstates commonly reported figures and does not specify whether it means goods only or goods plus services, which affects totals.

claim: Says YouTube removed Tucker Carlson’s interview with Tony Bobulinski.
rationale: There are no widely reported or documented credible sources showing YouTube permanently removed Tucker Carlson’s interview with Tony Bobulinski; the interview and reuploads were available across multiple platforms and outlets. Claims of removal appear to be based on isolated repost takedowns or misstatements rather than an official, verifiable platform-wide removal.

claim: Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas and his wife Ginni posted a photo of themselves enjoying a $5,135 bottle of wine "as American women despair about abortion rights being taken away from them."
rationale: There is no evidence that Clarence Thomas and his wife posted a photo with that quoted line. While Ginni Thomas did briefly share an image of the couple with a bottle of wine around the time of the Dobbs decision, the attribution that the bottle cost $5,135 and that they posted it “as American women despair about abortion rights being taken away from them” conflates media commentary and unverified price estimates with the couple’s own post. Fact-checkers and news reports found the caption/quote and the exact $5,135 valuation are unsupported.

claim: "We know dangerous criminals can slip through immigration at airports just like ours. Yet Joe Donnelly stood right here with the radical left against all efforts to secure our most vulnerable entry points."
rationale: The statement bundles a plausible general risk (individuals can sometimes evade airport immigration controls) with a broad, unsupported attack that Joe Donnelly "stood ... with the radical left against all efforts" to secure entry points. Public record shows Donnelly is a moderate Democrat and there is no evidence he opposed every or all security efforts for airports; the phrase "radical left" is a partisan label rather than a factual descriptor of specific votes or actions.

claim: "Trump's Cabinet is more white and more male than any first Cabinet since President Ronald Reagan’s."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and news analyses found that President Trump's initial Cabinet had a higher share of white men and fewer women and racial minorities than the first Cabinets of presidents since Ronald Reagan. Comparisons of the heads of the 15 executive departments (and typical Cabinet-level posts) show Trump's team was the least gender- and racially-diverse among first-term Cabinets after Reagan's 1981 lineup.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no record from official Joe Biden accounts or reputable fact-checkers of him tweeting that exact phrasing; the language and tone are inconsistent with Biden's public communications and would have been widely reported if authentic. Claims like this commonly originate from parody or fake screenshots and social accounts misattributing statements to public figures.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsubstantiated generalization. 911 response times vary by county, jurisdiction, call priority and remoteness, and available public data and reporting for Curry County (no single county specified) do not support that an hour-long wait is the normal or 'likely' outcome for 911 calls; while some remote calls can take longer, typical emergency dispatch/response times are substantially shorter.

claim: If COVID-19 was real, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge wouldn’t have been "allowed to join 50,000 other football fans inside a stadium."
rationale: This is false because COVID-19 was real and public‑health rules varied over time; by mid‑2021 UK authorities had begun permitting large crowds at venues with mitigations in place, and senior royals attended large sporting events (for example the Euro 2020 final at Wembley). The fact that people were allowed into a stadium under government rules does not imply the virus was not real.

claim: "The government does not need a warrant to read your old emails."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and therefore false: whether a warrant is required to read emails depends on jurisdiction and circumstances. In the U.S., the Stored Communications Act historically allowed prosecutors to obtain older emails with a subpoena or §2703(d) court order in some cases, but Fourth Amendment protections, Department of Justice policy updates, and many providers’ policies now often require a warrant based on probable cause; laws and practices vary internationally.

claim: "FREE HORSES!!!! 52 thoroughbred horses need homes. Will go to Sugarcreek this Sat. for slaughter. Gentleman died due to COVID-19 and his son wants nothing to do with them."
rationale: This reads like a viral social-media alert and there is no corroborating reporting from local news, animal welfare groups, or public records about 52 thoroughbreds being freed for slaughter in Sugarcreek after an owner's COVID-19 death. Large, specific claims about mass animal disposals typically generate verifiable records (shelter intake, police reports, auction or transport manifests) and credible outlets; none are evident based on common verification patterns.

claim: "A strong bipartisan majority" in the House of Representatives "voted to defund Obamacare."
rationale: Multiple votes in the House to repeal or 'defund' the Affordable Care Act have overwhelmingly passed along party lines with Republican majorities; they did not command a strong bipartisan majority. Only a small number of Democrats occasionally voted with Republicans, but those defections were not large enough to constitute a strong bipartisan majority.

claim: The Obama administration’s "own Environmental Protection Agency" has said its Clean Power Plan "will have a marginal impact on climate change."
rationale: The EPA's regulatory analyses for the Clean Power Plan projected only a very small reduction in global mean temperature attributable solely to the rule by the end of the century and described the direct global temperature effect as modest. The agency nonetheless emphasized the Plan's domestic emissions reductions and health co-benefits, but its own modeling showed the isolated climate-temperature impact would be small.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The claim asserts a blanket absence of provisions benefiting 'big Wall Street bankers' in an unspecified text; without specifying the bill or document this cannot be verified and is therefore implausible as stated. Historically many financial-sector provisions have appeared in large legislative packages, and sweeping negative claims about all provisions require textual evidence. Absent the actual text, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "The Republican from Georgia [U.S. Rep. Jack Kingston], he hasn’t even been to a NASCAR race."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Representative Jack Kingston has 'never' been to a NASCAR race, and the claim is implausible given his Georgia constituency where NASCAR is popular. Politicians from that region commonly attend motorsports events for campaigning and constituent outreach, so an absolute statement that he has never attended is unlikely to be true.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: The claim asserts SunTrust cancels an account solely because a company sells guns, but there is no evidence of a broad SunTrust corporate policy to close accounts just for lawful firearm sales. Banks may close individual accounts for a variety of risk, compliance, or legal reasons, and isolated news reports of specific account closures exist, but that does not support the blanket claim as stated.

claim: A photo shows Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing and smiling in front of a Trump 2020 sign.
rationale: This claim is false: the circulated photo was manipulated or miscaptioned and does not legitimately show Reps. Maxine Waters and Nancy Pelosi posing in front of an authentic 'Trump 2020' sign. Multiple independent fact-checks found the image was altered or taken out of context rather than showing the two Democrats endorsing a Trump campaign sign.

claim: "Business spirit is the highest it's ever been, according to polls."
rationale: The statement is too vague and unsupported: it does not name a country, time period, or specific poll. Business confidence (or 'business spirit') varies by country and index and has hit different highs at different times, so a blanket claim that it is the highest ever "according to polls" cannot be verified and is likely false without a cited source.

claim: "For the second quarter in a row, my campaign has raised more money than any other challenger in the nation and brought our fundraising total to over $800,000."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it omits the candidate name, the specific quarter/year, and the comparator set of 'challengers in the nation.'
