rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that SpaceX’s Starlink constellation was used to guide the fire or an attack on the Russian ship Moskva. Public reporting and statements from SpaceX and U.S. officials say Starlink provided internet connectivity in Ukraine but did not provide targeting data, and independent investigations did not corroborate claims that Starlink guided the incident. Russian authorities and state media alleged Starlink’s involvement, but those assertions remain unproven and contradicted by available technical and official statements.

claim: "Twitter reaches only 15 percent of the population."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous about which population is meant. Globally, Twitter/X has far fewer users than 15% of the world population (roughly mid-single-digit percent based on hundreds of millions of users versus ~8 billion people), while in the United States recent surveys show Twitter/X usage among adults is around the low-20s percent, not 15%.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the record. The major stimulus enacted under President Obama (the 2009 ARRA) totaled about $787 billion and consisted of tax cuts, transfers, infrastructure and other spending; only a portion went to public-sector hiring, and independent analyses do not show nearly $1 trillion spent solely on "make-work" government jobs. Characterizing a large share of the stimulus as nearly $1 trillion in make-work jobs is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: "California Democrat Maxine Waters charged on 3 counts."
rationale: There are no credible reports or public court filings indicating Rep. Maxine Waters has been criminally charged on three counts. Such an indictment would be major national news and widely documented; instead, Waters has faced political criticism and ethics complaints but not a three-count criminal charging.

claim: A photo of Pete Buttigieg in a military uniform without visible patches shows that "he is a fraud."
rationale: A single photo lacking visible patches does not prove someone is a 'fraud.' Military uniforms and insignia vary by uniform type and circumstance, and patches can be obscured, removed, or cropped out of images; furthermore, Pete Buttigieg's service in the U.S. Navy Reserve, including a documented 2014 deployment, is a matter of public record and reporting, so the photo alone is insufficient evidence to allege fraud.

claim: Says "the most dangerous time for children" is from "3 to 6 p.m., during which time juvenile crime rates triple"
rationale: The claim is unsupported and misleading. While some types of juvenile offending and child-victimization incidents often rise in the late-afternoon/early-evening after school in many places, there is no robust, generalizable evidence that juvenile crime rates universally 'triple' between 3 and 6 p.m., nor that this single window is the unequivocal 'most dangerous' time for children across contexts.

claim: "Across the country, $174 billion of the Recovery Act have been committed in its first 130 days."
rationale: Contemporary official Recovery Act tracking and Treasury statements for the early months of the program do not support a $174 billion 'committed' figure within the first 130 days; published updates from Recovery.gov reported lower totals and distinguished between funds enacted, allocated, obligated, and spent. The claim appears to conflate different categories or misstate the timeline, so it is not supported as written.

claim: Says Marco Rubio believes the earth is 9,000 years old and that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; says  Rand Paul believes the earth is 10,000 years old and God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans."
rationale: There is no reliable public record of Marco Rubio stating the Earth is 9,000 years old or that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction, nor of Rand Paul claiming the Earth is 10,000 years old or that God removed dinosaurs to "make space for humans." Both politicians have at times expressed religious views about creation or questioned aspects of evolutionary theory, but the specific ages and quotes in this claim are not supported by documented statements or reputable reporting.

claim: "The governor is trying to take credit for recent actions taken by these companies. The problem is that for all three companies, the decision to move or stay in New Jersey happened before Chris Christie became governor."
rationale: The claim asserts that all three corporate decisions to move or stay in New Jersey occurred before Chris Christie became governor (he was sworn in January 2010). Without specific company names and announcement dates this blanket statement cannot be verified and is unlikely to be correct, since many high-profile corporate location decisions involving New Jersey were announced after 2010 and credit attribution has been disputed. Therefore the categorical claim that all three decisions predated his governorship is probably false.

claim: A statewide poll showing 76 percent support and other surveys are a "strong indicator" of  broad public support in Milwaukee County for a $10.10 minimum wage
rationale: A statewide poll showing 76% support and unspecified other surveys do not by themselves constitute a strong indicator of broad public support in Milwaukee County. Statewide averages can mask regional and demographic differences, and county-level conclusions require either a Milwaukee County–representative sample or county-specific polling.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said, "When gays stayed hidden we had no mass shootings; we had no public nudity. Society was polite. Now anything and everything goes and I blame them."
rationale: No credible evidence or reliable reporting (video, transcript, or reputable news/fact-check organizations) supports that Senator Ted Cruz ever made this quoted statement. The wording appears to be a viral or satirical internet fabrication misattributed to him rather than a documented public remark. While Cruz has criticized aspects of LGBT advocacy, this specific quote is not corroborated by verifiable sources.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "collaborated with Marxist regimes in the Soviet Union, Nicaragua and Cuba."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bernie Sanders formally 'collaborated' with the Marxist regimes of the Soviet Union, Nicaragua, or Cuba. Sanders did make occasional fact-finding visits and had meetings with foreign officials decades ago, but those contacts are not documented as formal collaboration or operational support, and he has publicly criticized authoritarianism.

claim: Under the current procedure, if someone "on a terror watch list" tries to buy a gun, authorities are notified.
rationale: Being on a terrorist watchlist is not an automatic legal prohibitor for firearms and does not by itself trigger an automatic notification to authorities when someone attempts to buy a gun. The FBI NICS check can produce delays or referrals and law enforcement may be contacted in specific cases, but watchlist matches do not consistently or automatically generate a notification or denial.

claim: Says "$30 million gap" in stadium funding forced the Portland Beavers to leave.
rationale: Local reporting at the time and statements from team ownership indicated that failure to secure roughly a $30 million shortfall in public financing for a new ballpark was a key reason the Portland Beavers relocated. The club could not finalize a replacement facility after PGE Park was renovated for MLS, and the unresolved funding gap was widely cited as forcing the move.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will … force doctors to assist homosexuals in buying surrogate babies."
rationale: There is no record that President Barack Obama proposed or enacted any federal policy that would force doctors to help people (of any sexual orientation) 'buy surrogate babies.' Surrogacy and assisted-reproduction practices are governed largely by state law and private contracts, and federal authority to compel individual medical professionals to provide such services is limited. While the Obama administration supported nondiscrimination for LGBT people in health care, that is not the same as mandating doctors assist with commercial surrogacy.

claim: Women are "disproportionately impacted by voter ID laws — especially married women who change their names, or those whose IDs do not accurately reflect their gender."
rationale: Multiple studies and voting-rights analyses have found that voter ID laws can and do affect women at higher rates than men, particularly older women and those who have changed surnames after marriage because name mismatches between registration and ID can trigger additional hurdles. Transgender people whose IDs do not reflect their gender have also been repeatedly documented as facing increased barriers under strict ID rules. The degree of disproportion varies by jurisdiction and the specific design and implementation of the law.

claim: Says Barack Obama "endorsed a total ban on the manufacture, sale and possession of all handguns."
rationale: There is no credible record of Barack Obama explicitly endorsing a total ban on the manufacture, sale, and possession of all handguns. His public positions and proposals focused on measures like reinstating an assault-weapons ban, universal background checks, limits on high-capacity magazines, and other regulations—not an across-the-board handgun prohibition. Claims that he endorsed a total handgun ban are mischaracterizations or out-of-context paraphrases of his support for stricter gun-control measures.

claim: Says Chris Christie "vetoed equal pay for women 3 times. He only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Chris Christie vetoed an "equal pay for women" bill three separate times. Contemporary reporting and legislative records show he vetoed or opposed pay-equity measures at least once and faced criticism for his timing on related actions, but the claim of three vetoes and that he only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue is not supported by the public record.

claim: "White busses marked ‘Soros Riot Dance Squad’ spotted in Michigan: It’s official, the riots are staged."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that buses in Michigan were legitimately marked 'Soros Riot Dance Squad' or that riots were ‘officially’ staged. Similar images and captions have circulated previously and have been debunked as edited photos or misattributed publicity stunts; major fact‑checking organizations have found no verified instances of such labeling or proof of staged riots tied to George Soros.

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: There is no evidence that dues withheld by unions fund half of Democratic campaigns in Florida. Public campaign finance records and reporting show unions contribute to Democrats but typically represent a small share compared with individual donors, party committees, PACs, and other sources. The claim conflates terms and offers no timeframe or data supporting a 50% figure.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate elements with inaccuracies. It is true that several Nordic countries limited use of Moderna's mRNA vaccine (Spikevax) for younger people after rare myocarditis/pericarditis signals, but the exact measures, age cutoffs and timing differed by country and changed over time — Iceland was not uniformly 'pulled' in the blanket way implied, and policies were not identically 'for everyone under age 30' across Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark. The statement therefore overstates and generalizes the situation.

claim: "There have been zero reported instances of any child born alive after an abortion in Texas."
rationale: The claim that there have been zero reported instances is incorrect: rare cases of infants being born alive after attempted abortions have been documented in the United States, and reporting and news accounts include cases from Texas. While such events are uncommon, public records, medical literature, and media coverage contradict a blanket “zero” assertion.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: The statement is imprecise and depends on the year and the definition used (tax filers vs. households vs. tax units). IRS and policy-organization data show the share with zero federal income tax liability has fluctuated year to year and is not consistently between 40–50%; in some recent years it was lower (mid-30s) and in some years, after large refundable credits, it approached or exceeded 40%. Without a specified year and definition the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: The employer mandate "affects only 5 percent of businesses in this country."
rationale: This is misleading. The Affordable Care Act employer mandate applies to employers with 50+ full-time equivalent employees, and while a minority of business firms meet that size threshold by count, the exact share is not a simple, static '5 percent' and varies by definition and year. Larger firms represent a far bigger share of total employment, so the mandate affects many workers even if relatively few firms by count exceed 49 employees.

claim: Charlie Crist stopped "layoffs of some 20,000 school teachers during the global economic meltdown."
rationale: The claim overstates and simplifies complex events. During the 2008–09 fiscal crisis Florida school districts warned of as many as roughly 20,000 potential teacher job losses, and federal stimulus (ARRA) dollars plus state budget decisions helped avert many cuts. However, there is no clear evidence that Charlie Crist alone 'stopped' 20,000 layoffs; the figure and causal attribution are exaggerated.

claim: Quotes actor Will Smith as saying: "I’m not afraid to say that Trump and his supporters are ba…"
rationale: There is no reliable, verifiable record or reputable news reporting that Will Smith made the quoted statement; the snippet appears truncated and matches a common pattern of misattributed celebrity quotes. While Smith has occasionally commented on politics, this exact phrasing has not been substantiated.

claim: The Central Falls fire department is "one of the lowest, if not the lowest, paid fire departments in the state and entire region."
rationale: I cannot verify the assertion that Central Falls Fire Department is among the lowest‑paid in the state or region because there is no cited, up‑to‑date comparative salary data presented. Firefighter compensation varies by rank, union contract, overtime, and municipality, and without specific salary tables and a defined timeframe/region the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Austin Mayor Steve Adler’s transportation plans linked to Proposition 1 on the ballot remove "27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city," replacing "them with lanes dedicated to usage by bicycles" and buses.
rationale: This claim misstates and overgeneralizes Austin proposals. City and mayoral transportation proposals have included targeted lane reconfigurations and dedicated transit/bike lanes on specific corridors, but they did not call for wholesale removal of '27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city' and replacing them citywide; the cited mileage and scope are exaggerated or arise from counting lane-miles or bi‑directional segments rather than removal of entire corridors. Also, the ballot language tied to the relevant proposition focused on funding and specific projects, not an across-the-board elimination of vehicle lanes.

claim: "There was no violence on the Senate side, in terms of the chamber."
rationale: For the well-documented January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol, rioters breached and entered the Senate chamber, occupied the dais, damaged property, and there were physical confrontations with law enforcement. Video, photographs, congressional statements, and official investigations document violence and assaults occurring in and around the Senate chamber.

claim: A man arrested by Lubbock, Texas, police for a gun threat said "his accomplices will be going to different Wal-Mart stores and shooting."
rationale: I cannot verify that specific quoted threat from available reliable reporting; the claim asserts a precise statement attributed to a Lubbock arrestee but I find no corroborated public record or reputable news source that documents that exact quote. Without independent confirmation of the arrest report or police statement containing that wording, the claim should be treated as unverified and therefore judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says President Donald Trump this week will sign an executive order creating term limits for Congress.
rationale: A U.S. president cannot unilaterally create term limits for members of Congress by signing an executive order. Term limits for Congress would require a change to the Constitution (or a law enacted under existing constitutional authority and, in practice, a constitutional amendment/legal challenge), and executive orders only govern the executive branch, not alter constitutional qualifications for legislative offices.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: I find no credible contemporaneous news reports, transcripts, or recordings showing Ted Cruz uttered that sentence defending Josh Duggar by saying Duggar’s actions were "far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other." The wording is inflammatory and no major outlets or Cruz's known public statements from the time attribute that quote to him, suggesting it is a misattribution or fabrication.

claim: An estimated 56 million Americans don't have bank accounts.
rationale: Authoritative surveys (FDIC) report far fewer completely unbanked households — about 5% of U.S. households (roughly 7 million households) — and the number of individuals without any bank account is much lower than 56 million. Even combining unbanked and underbanked populations yields totals in the tens of millions but not as high as 56 million, so the claim overstates the unbanked population or confuses measures.

claim: Says Alex Sink "supported higher sales taxes."
rationale: There is no clear, uncontested record that Alex Sink publicly endorsed a general increase in sales taxes; during the 2010 Florida gubernatorial campaign opponents ran ads claiming she supported tax hikes, but Sink publicly framed her positions as opposing broad sales tax increases and favoring targeted revenue measures. The statement is an oversimplification and appears to reflect attack-ad rhetoric rather than a documented explicit endorsement of higher sales taxes by Sink.

claim: Says Joe Biden was asleep and snoring during a TV interview.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden fell asleep and was audibly snoring during any legitimate televised interview; viral clips making that claim have been shown to be edited or taken out of context. Major news organizations and fact-checkers have not verified an authentic instance of him sleeping and snoring on-air.

claim: "I deployed the Texas National Guard" to the Texas-Mexico border. "And the policy worked; apprehensions at the border declined 74 percent."
rationale: The governor did deploy the Texas National Guard to the Texas–Mexico border, but the asserted 74% decline in 'apprehensions' is misleading and inaccurate as stated. Official Border Patrol data and multiple fact-checks show no nationwide 74% drop; the 74% figure appears to come from a narrowly chosen timeframe or specific sector, not an overall, sustained decline attributable solely to the deployment.

claim: Obamacare premiums "have gone up 160 percent in West Virginia in 4 yrs."
rationale: The claim is misleading: it appears to cherry-pick an unsubsidized plan and time window without clarifying which premium (benchmark, average, or before/after subsidies) is being measured. Official analyses and fact-checkers found that while some list prices in West Virginia rose substantially for particular plans or ages, typical benchmark or average premiums and most consumers' net premiums after tax credits did not uniformly increase by 160% over a four-year span. Therefore the blanket statement is inaccurate as presented.

claim: "I negotiated open borders to let fleeing refugees into safety from Kosovo."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific personal action but provides no identity, date, or evidence. Historical records of the 1998–99 Kosovo crisis show neighboring countries (notably Albania and North Macedonia) and international organizations facilitated refugee crossings, but there is no way to verify that an unspecified individual personally negotiated 'open borders.' Without corroborating evidence attributing such a role, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: A "majority in every state favors path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants."
rationale: While national polls consistently show a majority of Americans favor a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, state-level support varies and there is no evidence that a majority in every single state supports it. More conservative states routinely show lower levels of support that can fall below 50% depending on question wording and timing.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: The U.S. national average retail gasoline price did not reach $5.49 per gallon during the Obama–Biden administration (2009–2017); national averages in that period were generally well below $5 and typically in the $2–4 range depending on year. While some local stations or high-tax states occasionally had higher pump prices, $5.49 is not an accurate characterization of gas prices 'during the Obama-Biden administration.'

claim: Video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after he was stuck in an Australian airport.
rationale: Independent fact-checking and contemporaneous news coverage found the circulated video is misattributed or edited; the clip does not show Nadal and Federer laughing at Djokovic in an Australian airport and instead comes from unrelated footage. There is no credible evidence that the two players were filmed mocking Djokovic while he was detained at an Australian border facility.

claim: "New Jersey's governor cut $1.6 billion from public education while handing out $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks, more than the entire previous decade."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not corroborated as written: it does not identify which governor or the exact time period, and publicly available budget analyses show education aid changes and corporate tax incentives have varied by year and by accounting method. While New Jersey governors have both reduced some school aid and approved sizable business tax incentives, independent records do not support the specific claim that a single governor cut exactly $1.6 billion from public education while granting $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks exceeding the entire previous decade without more context.

claim: Georgia has recovered more than $60 million that was lost to Medicaid fraud
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source and I cannot verify a documented statewide total exceeding $60 million from Medicaid fraud up to my knowledge cutoff. While Georgia has secured notable individual settlements and periodic recoveries related to Medicaid fraud, there is no confirmed, aggregate figure of more than $60 million that I can corroborate without additional context or an authoritative source.

claim: The Freedom to Vote Act "automatically registers ineligible voters."
rationale: The Freedom to Vote Act's automatic voter registration provisions applied to eligible citizens and included attestation and verification safeguards rather than a blanket registration of anyone. The bill and common automatic registration systems require proof or self-attestation of eligibility and allow states to exclude noncitizens, so the claim that it "automatically registers ineligible voters" is inaccurate.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda "will cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion"
rationale: There is no credible, widely accepted economic analysis showing Hillary Clinton’s stated energy agenda would impose over $5 trillion in costs on the U.S. economy. Estimates of energy and climate policies depend heavily on which specific measures, timeframe, and accounting (gross vs. net, private vs. social costs) are included, and independent nonpartisan bodies (CBO, DOE analyses and mainstream think tanks) did not produce a $5 trillion figure tied to Clinton’s platform. The claim appears to be an exaggerated or out-of-context political attack rather than a supported fact.

claim: "Many Nevadans relied on Uber for work, but after accepting $70,000 from taxi companies, Catherine Cortez Masto went after Uber ... (driving) them out of town."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate context with unsupported assertions. It is true that Nevada regulators and some elected officials (and taxi interests) clashed with Uber over background-check rules and that taxi-related entities made campaign contributions, but there is no substantiated evidence that Catherine Cortez Masto personally accepted exactly $70,000 from taxi companies and then orchestrated actions to "drive Uber out of town" as a direct quid pro quo. The statement therefore overstates and misrepresents the available facts.

claim: "You may not have stayed in a hotel in the past year, but illegals arriving since Biden’s inauguration, they get to stay free of charge."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes: while some migrants and unaccompanied children have been temporarily housed in hotels or motels at government or NGO expense during surges since Biden's inauguration, this is not a universal or permanent policy that applies to all people who entered illegally. Housing decisions vary by time, location, case status, and agency, and many migrants are processed, detained, or placed in other facilities rather than kept in hotels free of charge.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: Official labor statistics do not support a 59% unemployment rate for African-American youths; BLS series for Black teens or for ages 16–24 have historically been much lower (typically in the teens and at most around the low 30s during severe downturns). A 59% figure is inconsistent with standard unemployment measures and likely arises from a misreading or a different metric (such as percent not in school and not working) or a narrowly defined subgroup.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "himself has granted waivers allowing into the United States refugees who provided material support to terrorists."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Obama personally granted waivers allowing refugees who had clearly provided material support to terrorists into the United States. While the Obama administration did use statutory waiver authorities to admit some refugees with prior associations or suspected ties (often for humanitarian reasons or because the connections were ambiguous or under duress), waivers are issued by executive branch agencies under delegated authority, and fact-checkers found the claim of Obama himself admitting material-support perpetrators to be unsubstantiated.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: The statement is false as an absolute claim: Keystone XL was intended to transport Canadian crude into the United States, terminating at Gulf Coast facilities where U.S. refineries could process the oil. Although some oil arriving at the Gulf Coast can be exported depending on market conditions, a substantial portion would be available to U.S. refineries and domestic markets rather than "not even" serving America.

claim: "Health care premiums up 90 percent in New Hampshire."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks a timeframe or specific market; there is no evidence that overall health-care premiums in New Hampshire rose 90% statewide. Premium changes vary by year, insurer, and plan type, and publicly available rate filings and summaries for New Hampshire do not show a uniform 90% increase across the market. Isolated large increases for particular plans or age groups can occur, but they do not justify a blanket 90% statement for the state's premiums.

claim: "$1.8 billion Of Soros’ money just intercepted – he could officially go to prison for years"
rationale: There are no credible reports or official actions showing $1.8 billion of George Soros's funds were seized or that he faces imminent prison time. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated social-media assertion; seizing that scale of assets would require public legal filings and wide news coverage, which do not exist. The suggestion that he 'could officially go to prison for years' is speculative and unsupported by any disclosed charges or prosecutions.

claim: "Two-thirds of our economy is a consumer economy."
rationale: As commonly used, this refers to the United States, where personal consumption expenditures typically account for roughly two-thirds of GDP (commonly in the mid-60s to high-60s percent range). The exact share varies year to year, but describing the economy as "two-thirds consumer" is a reasonable rounded statement.

claim: Says Tennessee has some of the lowest beer excise tax rates in the country.
rationale: State-by-state comparisons of beer excise taxes routinely list Tennessee among the lower-rate states. While exact rankings shift over time, Tennessee's per-volume excise tax is notably below the national average and thus can reasonably be described as "some of the lowest."

claim: Says there are thousands of registered voters over 110 years old in North Carolina, including one who is 219 years old.
rationale: There are not thousands of verified supercentenarians in any U.S. state and no documented human has lived to 219 years (the verified maximum is 122). Claims of many voters over 110 and a 219-year-old almost certainly arise from data-entry errors, duplicate records, or incorrect birthdates in voter rolls rather than actual living people of those ages.

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: The statement as an absolute is false. Under New York law the NYC mayor controls the city Department of Education under mayoral control statutes and normally has authority to operate and open city schools, though the state education commissioner and the governor have statutory and emergency powers to order closures or limit reopening on health and safety grounds. Therefore it is not correct to say categorically that the mayor "can't open" the schools under the law, except in specific circumstances where state action overrides local control.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The claim asserts a blanket absence of news coverage for a recent raid but gives no specific date, location, or incident details, making it unverifiable as stated. In practice, significant law-enforcement raids or seizures near the Arizona border are typically reported by local outlets, official press releases, and often picked up by regional or national media, so the absolute claim of 'no news coverage' is unlikely to be true without corroborating specifics.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted for regime change with respect to Libya."
rationale: There was no congressional vote that explicitly authorized U.S. 'regime change' in Libya, and Bernie Sanders did not cast a vote authorizing a regime‑change military action. The 2011 Libya campaign was undertaken under a UN Security Council resolution and executive action; Sanders has publicly criticized the intervention and did not support an AUMF-like authorization for regime change. Claiming he "voted for regime change" mischaracterizes the available votes and his record.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: It is true that some buyers, including retirees, lost sizable deposits when certain Trump-branded condo projects failed or were never completed, but there is no clear evidence that Donald Trump personally 'pocketed' those funds and simply walked away. Deposits are typically held and controlled by the project developer or held in escrow, and many disputes involved the development companies, lenders, or subsequent bankruptcies; some purchasers pursued litigation and recoveries against developers or affiliated entities. The blanket assertion that Trump personally took the deposits is not supported by available public facts and court records.

claim: "Corrupt political bosses. Money laundering. Fraud. It’s just another day at the office for Vin Gopal."
rationale: The statement accuses Vin Gopal of routine criminality (corruption, money laundering, fraud) but there are no public records of convictions or credible, substantiated charges establishing that pattern as of mid‑2024. Without documented indictments, convictions, or reliable evidence, the claim is an unproven allegation and thus false. The language appears to be political rhetoric rather than a factual summary of proven crimes.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
rationale: The claim is incorrect because Beto O’Rourke was not uniquely the only U.S. Senate candidate to call for President Trump’s impeachment; multiple other Senate candidates and public figures publicly supported impeachment at various points during 2017–2019. The assertion omits timeframe and scope, and contemporary news coverage records several Senate contenders and challengers who urged impeachment or supported impeachment inquiries.

claim: Says the Obama administration plans to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties.
rationale: This is false. The Obama administration did not pursue a plan to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties; the most relevant agreement, the 2013 Arms Trade Treaty, addresses international state-to-state transfers and illicit flows, not domestic civilian ownership. U.S. treaties require Senate ratification, and Obama's gun-policy actions focused on domestic legislative and executive measures (background checks, regulations), not an international ban on private firearms.

claim: "New Jersey has the largest transit system in the entire country."
rationale: As stated this is false: the largest transit agency in the U.S. by ridership and system size is the New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA). New Jersey Transit is a large statewide system and is often described as the nation's largest statewide public transportation system, but it is not the largest overall transit system in the country.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: I find no clear legislative record that Rep. Patrick Rose cast a roll-call vote specifically to 'explore a state income tax.' This phrasing appears to be a campaign attack that conflates or overstates routine votes on studies, budget processes, or unrelated measures rather than a direct vote to create or study a state income tax.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: The Obama administration relied on the 2001 AUMF (and related authorities) as a legal basis for strikes against the Islamic State, while President Obama had publicly called for repeal or replacement of the 2001 AUMF as outdated. Administration and DOJ legal analyses invoked the 2001 AUMF for operations against ISIS even though Obama had urged Congress to repeal it.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: The "272" number originates from partisan tallies that aggregate a wide range of votes — including procedural votes, amendments, and bills that did not directly raise taxes — and independent fact-checkers found the methodology misleading. Major fact-checks have concluded the claim misrepresents how many distinct votes to increase taxes Nelson actually cast, so the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: Protest vandalism in Richmond "all started two weeks ago when Mayor Stoney’s police gassed - tear gassed - a peaceful crowd of protesters, moms and children, at 7:30 p.m. sharp."
rationale: The claim ties all subsequent vandalism to a single, precisely timed incident (a 7:30 p.m. tear-gassing of a peaceful crowd by ‘Mayor Stoney’s police’). Contemporary reporting and official statements from the Richmond protests show clashes and crowd-control actions occurred over multiple nights and do not support a single, verifiable 7:30 p.m. teargassing of only ‘moms and children’ that alone caused all vandalism. The available evidence describes a more complex sequence of events with disputed use of chemical agents and no clear, sole causal moment as claimed.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: This is false: no NFL franchise is based in Richmond and there is no record of a city named Richmond building a $14 million stadium for an NFL team. Modern NFL team valuations are in the billions and their stadium projects typically cost hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars, so a $14M city-built stadium would not correspond to a 'second richest' NFL team.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: The claim provides no speaker, location, timeframe, or corroborating evidence, so it is not verifiable. Personal attendance claims require records or witnesses to confirm; absent such evidence the statement must be treated as unproven and therefore classified as false in this fact-check.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: Both parts of the claim are false based on available public records and reporting: President Joe Biden has not resigned and continued to serve in office, and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi has not been detained. There have been no official announcements or credible media reports supporting either claim.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. Kurt Schrader voted for a measure that cut Medicare by $500 billion. Schrader, a Democratic representative, opposed major Republican health-care repeal bills that would have reduced federal Medicaid/insurance spending and has not been recorded voting to enact a $500 billion Medicare cut; the claim appears to misattribute or conflate different budget proposals and estimates.

claim: Says Joe Biden canceled the Keystone pipeline because Warren Buffett "donated $58 million" to his campaign.
rationale: There is no evidence that Warren Buffett donated $58 million to Joe Biden’s campaign, and Biden’s revocation of the Keystone XL permit was a stated climate-policy action taken on his first day in office. The claim conflates an unverified, large donation with causation for a policy decision without supporting campaign finance records or credible reporting.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning a country's central bank can severely disrupt financial transactions, oil revenues, imports and trigger sharp recession and inflation, but it does not inevitably or instantly 'shut down' an entire economy. Iran has in the past endured heavy central-bank-related sanctions and while its economy contracted and suffered major hardship, economic activity continued through alternative payment channels, barter, third‑country intermediaries and domestic adjustments.

claim: "We cut taxes for 95 percent of working families."
rationale: The claim is misleading because whether 95% of working families received a tax cut depends on the specific law, year, and how "working families" are defined. Independent analyses of major recent tax changes (for example the U.S. 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) show the share of households benefiting varies by year and income and often falls well short of a durable 95% once temporary provisions and timeframes are accounted for. Without a clear timeframe or jurisdiction, the blanket statement is not supportable.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: Interpreting the claim as referring to absolute Black population, Delaware (total population ~1 million, Black population roughly ~20–25% or ~200–300k) is far smaller than the top states (e.g., Texas, Florida, Georgia, New York, California, North Carolina, Illinois, Maryland) which have millions of Black residents, so it is not eighth in absolute numbers. If the claim meant share (percentage) rather than absolute numbers, Delaware’s Black share is relatively high but still not clearly eighth highest among states. Without a clear metric and date the statement is misleading or incorrect.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: The claim asserts 600-plus police and fire pensions “Downstate” are on the cusp of insolvency; that is not supported by available public summaries. While Illinois (commonly the referent for “Downstate”) does have on the order of 600–650 local police and fire pension funds overall and some are severely underfunded, statewide reports do not show that 600+ distinct downstate funds are all imminently insolvent. The statement appears to conflate the total count of local funds with the number actually at imminent risk and is therefore likely an exaggeration without a specific contemporaneous audit.

claim: "The State of Texas is funding … women’s health services at historically high levels; they just increased their level another $50 million for the next two years."
rationale: I cannot verify that Texas is currently funding women’s health services at historically high levels and has just added a specific $50 million increase for the next two years. Texas has enacted various maternal and family-planning appropriations in recent budgets, but the claim bundles a broad, qualitative statement (“historically high levels”) with a precise dollar increase that is not corroborated by readily available budget summaries as of mid‑2024. Without a cited bill, appropriation line item, or official budget document confirming a new $50 million increase, the statement is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: The claim asserts there are "probably plenty" of presidential choices who do not believe in God; in many countries (notably the United States) openly non‑religious or atheist major‑party presidential candidates have historically been rare. Publicly available records of high‑profile presidential contenders show relatively few who identify as nonbelievers, so the blanket statement overgeneralizes and is not supported.

claim: "This idea that it's the pandemic of the unvaccinated, it's just a total lie."
rationale: Calling the idea that COVID-19 is 'a pandemic of the unvaccinated' a 'total lie' is inaccurate. Vaccination substantially lowers risk of infection, symptomatic disease, hospitalization, and death, and epidemiological data from multiple countries have shown unvaccinated people accounted for a disproportionate share of severe cases and deaths. Although vaccinated people can experience breakthrough infections and contribute to transmission—especially with waning immunity and immune-evading variants—the overall burden of severe illness has been concentrated among the unvaccinated.

claim: Says his budget provides "the highest state funding level in history" for education.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unverified as presented because it does not identify which state's budget, which fiscal year, or whether totals are nominal or inflation-adjusted. Claims of 'highest funding in history' are frequently true only in nominal dollars but not when adjusted for inflation or measured per pupil, and can exclude federal contributions. Without those specifics and supporting budget data, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "The total (state) payroll has gone down. The total amount of the number of workers in the state has gone down. I like the fact that the bulk of that is just by retirements."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it names no specific state or time period and provides no supporting data. State payroll totals and headcounts fluctuate year-to-year and can rise or fall for many reasons (hiring freezes, layoffs, retirements, privatization), so asserting a net decline and that the bulk is due to retirements requires specific payroll and HR records. Without those figures, the broad unchecked statement cannot be treated as fact.

claim: A letter from BP to the Minerals Management Service "actually recommends improvements and specific recommendations around safety regulations should they choose to change them."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific BP letter to the Minerals Management Service explicitly 'recommends improvements and specific recommendations around safety regulations.' No single, verifiable public letter matching that exact characterization is widely documented; reporting about BP–MMS correspondence after Deepwater Horizon describes communications and critiques of MMS but does not universally show BP issuing detailed regulatory recommendations. Without the cited letter, the statement cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: The Aug 3, 2019 El Paso Walmart mass shooting killed 22 people, and El Paso's population is roughly in the high 600,000s to ~700,000. The city has historically had very low homicide totals (single-digit years have occurred) and a roughly low-teens to high-teens 10-year annual average; the one-day death toll from that shooting did exceed the cited ~18-per-year average. Thus the quoted comparison is accurate in intent and scale.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation is a charity where President and Secretary Clinton and their daughter, they take no salary, they get no money from it, they take no personal benefit from it."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While Hillary and Bill Clinton historically did not take regular salaries from the Clinton Foundation at times, Chelsea Clinton has been a paid employee of the foundation, and reporting and tax filings show the foundation paid for travel, staff and other expenses that provided personal benefits to the Clintons. Thus it is incorrect to say none of them ever received money or any personal benefit.

claim: "Border agents discover body of 6-year-old girl: 'She was raped By 30 men'."
rationale: This specific sensational claim has circulated widely online but was not corroborated by any credible news outlet or official agency and has been repeatedly debunked by independent fact‑checkers. The posts often reuse misattributed images and lack verifiable details (date, location, law‑enforcement confirmation), which is inconsistent with how a crime of this scale would be documented and reported.

claim: Says images show migrants on trains and buses heading toward the United States, not walking.
rationale: The statement is too general and unsupported: while some photos and videos do show migrants on buses or trains, many widely circulated images are from different times and places (local transport, internal relocations, or non-U.S.-bound contexts) or lack provenance. Without verifiable metadata tying the images to migrants specifically 'heading toward the United States,' the claim is misleading.

claim: "There's nothing in the voting instructions that we've been getting in the last several elections that lets you know" about the limitations of the master lever.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no recent voting instructions explain master-lever limitations; that is unlikely to be true. In many jurisdictions voter instructions, sample ballots, and poll worker guidance explicitly describe straight‑party or master‑lever voting and note common exceptions (nonpartisan races, cross‑endorsed candidates, or contests that do not follow the party lever).

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated: public reports and summaries of Portland composting pilots I am aware of either cite different participant counts, different durations, or different satisfaction percentages. Because the precise combination of '2,000 households', a 'year‑long' pilot, and an '87% satisfied' result is not corroborated by accessible summaries, the claim is not supported as presented.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who 'he' is or provide evidence of any public statements. Without a named governor, timeframe, or supporting records of statements or budget data, I cannot confirm that the person 'takes credit' for reining in spending.

claim: "Under Gov. Kasich, Ohio wages have increased by $10.3 billion."
rationale: The statement is a precise aggregate dollar claim but lacks a clear source or timeframe; public labor statistics do show wage growth in Ohio during John Kasich's 2011–2019 governorship, but I cannot verify the exact $10.3 billion figure from authoritative labor data. Without specification (annual vs. cumulative, nominal vs. inflation‑adjusted, private vs. total wages) the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that Jim Renacci was charged or convicted of criminal tax evasion; allegations of unpaid taxes surfaced as partisan attacks during campaigns but were not substantiated by criminal proceedings. Calling him a "deadbeat citizen" is a pejorative opinion and not a verified factual statement about criminal tax fraud or proven failure to pay taxes.

claim: "I have spent virtually every weekend since Memorial Day in the Panhandle."
rationale: This is a first-person statement about private movements and timing that cannot be independently verified from the claim alone. Without travel records, corroborating receipts, photos with timestamps, or other external evidence, it is not possible to confirm the assertion that the speaker spent 'virtually every weekend' in the Panhandle since Memorial Day.

claim: Blue Cross headquarters has "a $30,000 granite table."
rationale: There is no reliable, verifiable evidence that any Blue Cross headquarters purchased a granite table specifically costing $30,000. Fact-checking reporting on similar social-media claims found no purchase records or credible sourcing to substantiate that exact price and noted confusion among different Blue Cross entities and furnishings.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated because it provides no jurisdiction, source, or official fiscal analyses. Whether a measure "will cost a fortune" versus "cost less" depends on detailed fiscal notes, implementation specifics, and agency estimates; without those I cannot confirm the contrast between Measures 3-386 and 3-388.

claim: A photo shows "the Lincoln Memorial. His head damaged and defaced."
rationale: There are no credible reports or mainstream news accounts of the Lincoln Memorial statue in Washington, D.C. having its head damaged or defaced; such a high-profile act would have been widely documented. Viral images claiming this have repeatedly been shown to be edited or to depict other statues/replicas or decontextualized photos rather than the actual Lincoln Memorial.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: There is no evidence that House cafeterias are owned by or 'part of Koch Industries.' Congressional dining services are operated under House administrative offices and purchase supplies from commercial vendors. While there have been periodic disputes about use of polystyrene cups or procurement choices under Republican leadership, the claim that Republicans required the use of 'Styrofoam cups' that are part of Koch Industries is incorrect and conflates procurement choices with corporate ownership.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The blanket claim that "we could have saved ourselves the cost" of the Powell Butte reservoir is unsubstantiated without a specific, evaluated alternative. Decisions to build large water infrastructure are normally driven by capacity, seismic resiliency, regulatory and water-quality needs and are supported by planning and cost–benefit studies; absent evidence those needs could be met cheaper, the assertion is speculative.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: State- and program-level analyses by the Social Security Administration and Census Bureau’s poverty measures show that Social Security keeps well over one million Floridians above the poverty line. Because Florida has a large population of beneficiaries (retirees and disabled), the number lifted out of poverty by Social Security in that state is commonly reported as roughly 1.0–1.2 million people.

claim: Says Travis County, home to Austin, is the most liberal county in the United States.
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported as an absolute fact: "most liberal" is undefined, and by common measures (presidential vote share, Democratic registration) multiple U.S. counties -- for example San Francisco County and several New York City boroughs/Manhattan -- show stronger Democratic/lefter voting patterns than Travis County. While Travis County is solidly and reliably Democratic and more liberal than many counties, calling it the single most liberal county in the nation is inaccurate.

claim: "Common welfare programs give income of $43,330 or $20.83 an hour."
rationale: The claim is incorrect or misleading because common means‑tested U.S. welfare programs do not provide a standard cash income of $43,330/year (about $20.83/hour full time). Programs like SNAP and TANF typically provide monthly food or small cash benefits measured in the hundreds to low thousands, Medicaid provides health coverage not cash, and unemployment or other supports vary by state but are not universally that high.

claim: "Science says that being single will kill you faster than obesity."
rationale: This statement overgeneralizes and misrepresents scientific findings. While high-quality meta-analyses have found that poor social relationships, loneliness, or social isolation are associated with increased mortality risk comparable to some major risk factors, equating that to ‘being single’ is inaccurate, and evidence does not support a universal claim that being single kills you faster than obesity. The relative risk depends on how ‘single’ is defined, the degree of social isolation, obesity severity, and other health and demographic factors.

claim: Video shows Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots for a group of people "days before testing positive" for COVID-19.
rationale: The video that circulated showing Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots was taken well before the pandemic and was not filmed days before she reported a positive COVID-19 test. Independent fact-checkers traced the clip to an earlier event and found the timing claim misrepresents when the footage was recorded.

claim: "Probably one out of every two households in Oklahoma has a gun."
rationale: Multiple state-level surveys and national polls typically estimate Oklahoma household gun ownership near but below 50% (commonly in the mid-40% range), so the blanket statement that "one out of every two households" have a gun is likely an overstatement. Survey estimates vary by year and method, so the precise share is uncertain but not reliably as high as 50% in most published data.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: The claim misstates both the source and the metric: Lancet publications and the original phase‑3 trial reports show high relative vaccine efficacy (about 94–95% for the mRNA vaccines and lower but substantial protection for AstraZeneca and J&J), not the ~1% figures quoted. The ~1% numbers resemble absolute risk reductions or misinterpreted incidence rates, which are different from the relative risk reduction commonly reported as 'efficacy.'

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the official Wisconsin Republican Party account posted that explicit, insulting International Women’s Day message; major news outlets and social-media fact-checkers did not report such a tweet. The phrasing and tone are consistent with doctored or parody images that circulate to smear political actors rather than with verified party communications.

claim: "It's just outrageous that under President Bush, the National Institutes of Health have been basically decreased in funding."
rationale: If referring to President George W. Bush, NIH appropriations did not simply fall across his term: nominal NIH funding rose in the early 2000s (continuing the late‑1990s/early‑2000s boost) and then largely plateaued. However, when adjusted for inflation/purchasing power, NIH funding declined in parts of his presidency, so describing funding as having been "basically decreased" without qualification is misleading.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no U.S. Supreme Court opinion that contains or announces the quoted blanket statement that public schools "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law." Supreme Court jurisprudence under the Establishment Clause bars school-sponsored prayer or proselytizing (e.g., Engel v. Vitale, Abington v. Schempp) but expressly allows neutral, academic instruction about religions. The claim misstates and overgeneralizes the Court's holdings.

claim: Obamacare has led to fewer health insurance options for millions of Americans.
rationale: After implementation of the Affordable Care Act, many insurers withdrew from particular local markets and marketplace plan choices consolidated, leaving only one or a small number of carriers in large numbers of counties and reducing options for millions of people who shop on the individual marketplaces. However, the effect varied by state and year and some Americans gained coverage options through expanded Medicaid or new exchange offerings, so the impact is context-dependent.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: Queen Elizabeth II died on 8 September 2022 and was 96 years old at the time (born 21 April 1926), so the statement that she died at 95 is incorrect. The widely reported official announcements and obituaries list her age as 96.

claim: "Parents and teachers are already worrying about what they call the ‘Trump Effect.’ They report that bullying and harassment are on the rise in our schools, especially targeting students of color, Muslims and immigrants."
rationale: Multiple contemporary news reports, teacher surveys and civil-rights organizations documented that parents and teachers expressed concern about a so-called 'Trump Effect' and reported increases in bullying and harassment in schools, particularly toward students of color, Muslims, and immigrants. These complaints were widely reported during and after the 2016 campaign and early administration, citing specific incidents and survey data from educators and advocacy groups.

claim: "Nearly 60% of all student loan debt is held by the rich and upper-middle class," so forgiveness would give the wealthy a "financial windfall" but not really help low-income people.
rationale: The numeric part is a misleading simplification: analyses of Federal Reserve and think‑tank data show a large share of outstanding student loan dollars is held by higher‑income households (roughly the top 40% by income hold on the order of ~50–60% of dollars), but labeling that group uniformly as the “rich and upper‑middle class” is vague and inaccurate. Moreover, while dollar‑value benefits from broad forgiveness would skew toward higher‑income borrowers, meaningful relief would also accrue to lower‑income and distressed borrowers and reduce racial and regional disparities, so the claim that forgiveness would only give the wealthy a windfall and “not really help low‑income people” overstates the case.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks a timeframe or specific metric. Texas has reported record-high statewide four-year adjusted cohort rates in some recent years, but not every graduation metric or subgroup is at an all-time high and pandemic-era fluctuations complicate a blanket statement that 'graduation rates are at all-time highs.'

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: The statement is incorrect because Supreme Court justices have been confirmed in presidential election years within the last 80 years. For example, Anthony Kennedy was confirmed by the Senate in February 1988, which was a presidential election year. Therefore it is false to claim there has not been a nomination and confirmation in an election year for more than 80 years.

claim: "Of those 850,000 (new Texas) jobs, most were public-sector jobs and minimum-wage jobs."
rationale: Available labor-force data and typical employment composition make this claim unlikely: most job growth in Texas has come from private-sector industries (e.g., professional services, construction, leisure and hospitality), while government jobs comprise a relatively small share of total employment and workers paid exactly the minimum wage are a minority. Therefore it is unsupported to say that a majority of 850,000 new Texas jobs were both public-sector and minimum-wage positions.

claim: "Our last budget committed the highest level of need-based financial aid in state history."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not specify which state or which budget is meant. Determining whether a budget is the 'highest level' of need-based aid requires comparing specific line-item appropriations across prior budgets, adjusting for inflation, and clarifying whether one-time or recurring funding are included, none of which are provided here.

claim: "Women still earn about 77 cents for every dollar a man earns for working the same job."
rationale: The oft-cited “77 cents” statistic compares median earnings of all full-time working women to all full-time working men, not pay for the exact same job with the same qualifications and hours. When researchers control for job, occupation, hours, experience, and education the gap shrinks substantially (often to only a few cents on the dollar), though a smaller unexplained residual gap remains.

claim: Says Military Times reported that a study found "60% of sailors who had been fully vaccinated with 2-shot series vaccines are now at risk for heart disease."
rationale: There is no credible Military Times report or peer‑reviewed study showing that 60% of sailors fully vaccinated with two‑dose COVID vaccines are ‘‘now at risk for heart disease.’’ Established surveillance and published studies report rare cases of myocarditis after mRNA vaccines but not anywhere near a 60% risk, so this claim appears to be a misrepresentation or exaggeration of data.

claim: Photo shows R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021.
rationale: R. Kelly was convicted in federal court in September 2021 and remained in custody; there are no credible reports or official records showing he was released that year. Media and fact-check organizations repeatedly debunked circulating images claiming to show his 2021 release as miscaptioned or depicting other people.

claim: "The video doesn't show the broader picture of the firing that was going on at American troops."
rationale: The claim is unverified as presented because no specific video, time, location, or source is identified. Without the original unedited footage, metadata, or independent corroboration, one cannot determine whether the recording omits broader context of firing at American troops, so the assertion cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says photos show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and news reports found that images circulated claiming to show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Schumer, Warren, Pelosi and Clinton were misattributed or unrelated; there is no credible evidence linking the whistleblower to those photos. The whistleblower’s identity was protected at the time, and image provenance checks did not support the claim.

claim: "In West Virginia alone, overdoses have increased by 50% during the #COVID-19 pandemic."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as written because it gives no clear timeframe or metric (fatal overdoses, nonfatal overdoses, ED visits) and statewide data sources (CDC provisional overdose death data and West Virginia health reports) show increases during the pandemic but not a uniform 50% rise across the whole pandemic period. Some months or specific categories did experience sharp spikes approaching that magnitude, but the overall documented statewide increase is lower and varies by source and period.

claim: "MSNBC actually said on air ‘I hope enough people die from coronavirus that it harms Trump’s re-election.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any MSNBC anchor or guest said on air the quoted line. Media fact-checkers and available transcripts/videos do not corroborate the claim; the circulating clip appears to be misattributed or taken out of context rather than a verbatim on-air statement expressing hope for deaths.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is false. Prosecutions of former leaders are not unique to the so-called 'Third World' — developed democracies have also prosecuted or indicted ex-leaders (e.g., Jacques Chirac in France, Silvio Berlusconi in Italy, Park Geun-hye in South Korea, and multiple indictments of Donald Trump in the United States). Accountability practices vary by country and era, so such prosecutions are not exclusive or inherently habitual only in developing countries.

claim: "American coronavirus vaccine killed five Ukrainians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting from Ukrainian health authorities, international public-health agencies, or reliable news outlets confirming that an 'American coronavirus vaccine' killed five Ukrainians. While COVID-19 vaccines have extremely rare serious adverse events, deaths temporally associated with vaccination are investigated and causation is not assumed; this specific claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Due to U.S. Senate rules, Democrats need "more than a majority ... to codify Roe vs. Wade."
rationale: Under current Senate practice a filibuster can block most legislation, and invoking cloture to end debate normally requires 60 votes, so a bare Democratic majority (51 with the vice president) would typically need more than a simple majority to pass a law codifying Roe v. Wade. There are procedural exceptions (e.g., changing the filibuster rule by majority vote or using reconciliation for budget-related bills), but for ordinary substantive legislation the 60-vote threshold applies.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The statement lacks a specified state, time period, and data source; rankings of states by percentage of deaths in nursing homes have varied over time and by dataset. Without identifying which state and which dataset/timeframe the speaker meant, the claim cannot be substantiated and is therefore treated as false. If a specific state and source were provided the claim could be verified.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a '1776' flag was flown over the White House in January 2021. Contemporary news coverage and independent fact-checkers found 1776 flags among protesters and at the U.S. Capitol or nearby streets, but no verified photos, official statements, or reliable reporting showed such a flag flown over the White House itself; circulated images were miscaptioned or from other locations.

claim: The U.S. Justice Department "conservatively estimated that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives."
rationale: The U.S. Department of Justice did not itself issue a conservative estimate of 1.5 million defensive gun uses per year. That figure traces to academic survey estimates (notably Gary Kleck's work) and has been widely disputed; DOJ/Bureau of Justice Statistics has not endorsed 1.5 million as a DOJ estimate. Independent reviews have found large uncertainty and methodological problems with high-end estimates.

claim: Say Apple’s Tim Cook "will not do business with Indiana."
rationale: There is no credible record of Tim Cook saying Apple "will not do business with Indiana." He did publicly criticize Indiana's 2015 RFRA and oppose discrimination, but that criticism did not include a stated blanket refusal to do business with the state, and Apple continues commercial operations there. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or misquote of his remarks.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Historical congressional records and authoritative tallies show that since 1789 thousands of measures proposing constitutional amendments have been introduced in Congress, and the commonly cited total is roughly 11,000 (or slightly more). The claim is referring to proposals introduced, not the far smaller number actually ratified as amendments.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: Iowa is no longer determinative in the sense that its winner does not automatically become the Republican nominee — recent cycles (e.g., 2016, 2012, 2008) show Iowa winners or losers did not always secure the nomination. However, the caucus still matters as an early test that can generate momentum, media attention, fundraising, and winnow the field, so it is incorrect to say it "in no way determines" the nominee.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence that any authorized U.S. military tribunals began on January 20, 2021. That date was the presidential inauguration, and mainstream news, official government releases, and court records show no initiation of nationwide or mass military trials as claimed; the assertion appears to stem from conspiracy rumors.

claim: "The deficit was on track to top $1 trillion the year I took office."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it does not identify which president or which year 'I took office' refers to, so it cannot be verified as written. Historical data show that when Barack Obama took office in 2009 the deficit did exceed $1 trillion that fiscal year, but when Donald Trump took office in 2017 the deficit was about $665–700 billion and was not on track to top $1 trillion that year. Therefore the blanket statement as presented is misleading.

claim: U.S. Rep. Scott Rigell "wants gun owners in a federal registration system."
rationale: Scott Rigell, a Republican who served in the U.S. House from 2011–2017, is not known to have advocated placing law‑abiding gun owners into a federal registration system; his public record aligns with pro‑Second Amendment positions and opposition to broad gun‑owner registries. No reliable evidence or widely reported statement indicates he sought a federal gun‑owner registry, so the claim appears to be a mischaracterization or misattribution.

claim: Said President Barack Obama "said he was going to stop (signature strikes)."
rationale: There is no clear record of President Obama explicitly saying he would categoricaly "stop" signature strikes. He did announce tighter standards and more oversight for targeted killings (notably in his 2013 National Defense University speech and subsequent policy reviews), which curtailed some practices, but did not plainly promise to end all signature strikes in every theater. Reports and administration statements described limits and greater scrutiny rather than an absolute cessation.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The statement as written claims Japan abandoned its vaccine rollout, which is inaccurate. Japan implemented and continued a national COVID-19 vaccination campaign beginning in 2021 rather than dropping rollout entirely.

claim: Says Sen. Tim Kaine "approves of and even applauds his son's participation in a known terrorist organization, #Antifa."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Senator Tim Kaine said he "approves of and even applauds" a child's participation in Antifa. Antifa is a decentralized movement not designated as a U.S. federal terrorist organization, and Kaine has not publicly praised violent extremism; the claim appears to be a fabricated or misleading attribution.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the U.S. economy before Trump was recovering from the 2008–09 recession with several years of GDP growth, falling unemployment, and rising stock markets, so it was not experiencing "years of economic decay" that simply needed reversing. While the Trump administration did enact policy changes (notably the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and deregulatory actions), their effects were mixed—short-term growth gains but larger deficits and distributional impacts—and the 2020 pandemic caused a sharp economic downturn, so it is inaccurate to claim definitively that economic decay is "over" solely because Trump "reversed" prior policies.

claim: Says Romney and Ryan "both backed proposals that would outlaw abortions even in cases of rape or incest."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly stated during the 2012 campaign that he supported exceptions for rape and incest, while Paul Ryan has a long anti‑abortion voting record and backed very restrictive measures. The claim that both 'backed proposals that would outlaw abortions even in cases of rape or incest' overstates Romney's position (he endorsed exceptions) even if some proposals Ryan supported lacked such exceptions.

claim: "CNN-NPR photojournalist Jade Sacker was embedded with antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a CNN or NPR photojournalist named Jade Sacker was embedded with an 'antifa leader' at the U.S. Capitol attack. Major outlets and independent fact-checkers found the social-media claims misidentify people and presented no proof of a journalist named Jade Sacker working for CNN or NPR in that capacity. Additionally, 'antifa' is a decentralized movement without formal leaders, making the specific claim implausible.

claim: Says that under President Donald Trump, "not only have we not gone after al-Qaida ... our president is supporting al-Qaida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Trump deliberately supported al-Qaida as U.S. policy; his administration continued counterterrorism actions (strikes, sanctions, designations) against al-Qaida affiliates. Critics argue some Trump policies—such as the 2019 Syria withdrawal and support for certain rebel groups—may have indirectly benefited extremist actors, but that is not the same as actively supporting al-Qaida.

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The statement is incorrect because poor forest management is one of several contributing factors but not the sole cause of California's large, deadly fires. Major drivers include climate change (warmer, drier conditions and more extreme drought), expanding development into the wildland-urban interface, ignition sources such as utility equipment and human activity, and extreme wind events; historic fire suppression has also altered fuel loads but does not fully explain recent trends.

claim: "Joe Biden wants to end school choice."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad characterization. President Biden has opposed federal funding for private-school voucher programs and emphasized strengthening public schools, but he has not called for abolishing all forms of school choice—he and his administration have supported accountable public charter schools and options like open enrollment in many places.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous news reporting that Hillary Clinton left the country when any Mueller indictment was announced. Mueller's indictments were widely reported and involved other individuals; Clinton was not charged and no verified sources show a coordinated departure tied to an indictment announcement.

claim: This is the 911 call placed by the migrants trapped in the truck found in San Antonio, Texas.
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence tying a specific publicly circulated audio clip to a 911 call from the migrants in the San Antonio truck; major news outlets and local authorities did not release or confirm such a call as originating from that incident. Without provenance, timestamps, or official confirmation, claiming the clip is 'the 911 call' is unverified and likely misleading.
