Bush (so saying “there was no President Bush” is misleading even if he did not personally attend the convention), and the absolute statement that nobody from the Bush family attended the 2012 RNC is incorrect — members of the extended Bush family and their representatives were reported to be present or involved. The phrasing conflates physical attendance, formal roles, and family membership.

claim: "(T)he United States government and its Constitution says that people can be put to death."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution and federal law permit capital punishment: the Fifth Amendment contemplates deprivation of life with due process, the Eighth Amendment limits but does not categorically prohibit the death penalty, and the Supreme Court has upheld its constitutionality in cases such as Gregg v. Georgia. Congress and many states have statutes authorizing execution for certain crimes, and the federal government carries out capital sentences.

claim: Mental health provisions related to mass shootings "got over 90 votes in the Senate."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and misleading as written. While a specific Senate measure addressing reporting of mental-health adjudications (the Fix NICS Act, tied to shootings) passed the Senate overwhelmingly (about 98–0 in 2018), many other proposed mental‑health provisions tied to mass shootings did not receive anywhere near 90 votes. Without identifying the specific provision and vote, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says his proposed payroll tax cut "will mean an extra $1,500 in your pocket compared to if we do nothing."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as a universal claim because whether a payroll tax cut yields an extra $1,500 "in your pocket" depends on the size of the cut, the time period (e.g., per year or cumulative), and individual earnings and incidence (employer adjustments). Without those specifics the blanket claim is misleading — some workers under specific assumptions might see $1,500, but many would see less or none.

claim: Newt Gingrich "was fined $300,000 for ethics violations."
rationale: In 1997 the House Ethics Committee found Newt Gingrich had violated House rules and the full House voted to reprimand him; as part of the settlement he agreed to pay $300,000. Contemporary news accounts and the committee report describe the $300,000 payment as part of the sanction and settlement for the ethics violations.

claim: "We're spending millions for each individual" held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
rationale: Multiple government reports and mainstream news investigations have reported that the U.S. pays millions of dollars per Guantanamo detainee when measured either as annual operating cost per remaining detainee or as a lifetime/cumulative program cost divided by detainee count. Exact figures vary by year and methodology (commonly cited figures are in the low millions per detainee), but the general claim that the government spends millions per individual held at Guantanamo is supported by public reporting.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: Short video clips that circulated show Biden extending his hand after a speech, but context and fuller footage indicate he was reaching toward a staffer or gesturing while leaving the stage rather than visibly disoriented. Describing the action as him being 'confused' and deliberately 'shaking hands with thin air' mischaracterizes routine stage movement and is a subjective interpretation of brief footage.

claim: "Here's a man who brags about how he made the city safe. It was the Biden crime bill that became the Clinton crime bill that allowed him to do that."
rationale: Joe Biden was a lead Senate author and sponsor of the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act; the bill was passed by Congress and signed into law by President Bill Clinton and is commonly referred to as the 1994 Clinton crime bill. Saying it was the 'Biden crime bill that became the Clinton crime bill' is a broadly accurate summary, though it simplifies the collaborative legislative process and many provisions came from multiple lawmakers.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: The claim is unlikely because Austin’s population and voter base are far larger today than in 1973, so even modest turnout in a recent mayoral race would almost certainly produce a higher absolute vote count than in 1973. Without specific certified turnout numbers for the 1973 race and the cited “most recent” race it’s not proven, but general demographic growth and typical modern turnout make the claim improbable.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: Multiple state and federal wildfire reports and public safety messaging consistently indicate that roughly nine out of ten wildfires in Arizona are caused by human activity rather than natural causes like lightning. The figure typically refers to the count of wildland fires over multi-year averages rather than the proportion of area burned.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement gives a precise baseline but no time, poll, or methodology. Hillary Clinton's favorability/unfavorability has varied across different polls and times, so claiming she "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her" as a general fact is unsupported without specific context.

claim: Ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19.
rationale: High-quality randomized controlled trials and multiple systematic reviews have not demonstrated that ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19, and major public health agencies advise against its use for this purpose. Early small or flawed studies suggested possible benefits, but those findings have not been reliably replicated and some were retracted or found to have serious methodological problems.

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: The commonly cited '$21T' refers to cumulative accounting adjustments or unsupported transactions in Pentagon financial records over many years, not $21 trillion of missing or available cash that could be reallocated. The '$32T' figure for Medicare for All is usually a multi‑year gross spending estimate that often includes existing public and private health payments, so the two numbers are from different accounting contexts and not directly comparable. Claiming 66% funding is therefore misleading and incorrect.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: There is no verified Ukrainian court record or credible reporting showing Burisma admitted paying Joe Biden $900,000. Multiple independent fact-checkers and news organizations have investigated and found no evidence of such an admission; Burisma and involved parties have denied payments to Joe Biden. The claim appears to misinterpret unverified documents or conflate payments to Hunter Biden or other allegations with a supposed court admission.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: The statement conflates a roughly low employment rate with a specific causal attribution and an extreme magnitude. West Virginia's employment-population ratio and labor force participation are below the national average but are not uniquely or demonstrably 'down to around 50 percent' of adults working solely because of addiction or criminal conviction. While opioid addiction and incarceration have reduced workforce participation for some people, available research and state statistics do not support the claim that about half of adults are out of work for those reasons.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: State and federal climate assessments show Rhode Island has experienced an increase in annual precipitation over the 20th century, but the documented increase is substantially less than 12 inches. Typical analyses for the Northeastern U.S. and Rhode Island report multi‑decade increases on the order of a few to several inches (commonly roughly 3–8 inches), not over a foot.

claim: Says proposal to boost teacher pension fund "puts no mandate on local government."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely incorrect because whether a proposal "puts no mandate on local government" depends entirely on the bill's specific language and budgetary provisions. Many teacher-pension proposals either shift costs to the state or explicitly require local contribution changes, so a blanket claim that there is no local mandate cannot be accepted without the actual proposal text.

claim: "No state generates as much solar power as California, or has as many people whose jobs depend on it."
rationale: California has consistently led U.S. states in solar electricity generation and installed solar capacity, and annual industry job surveys report California as having the largest solar workforce. While exact rankings can shift slightly depending on whether one measures capacity vs. generation or uses a single year of data, California is the clear leader on both counts in recent data.

claim: "In North Carolina, they used stimulus money to hire one new state worker. His job, apply for more stimulus funds from the taxpayers by the way of the federal government."
rationale: The claim makes a specific, verifiable assertion but provides no time period, agency, or documentation; there is no credible reporting or official record establishing that North Carolina used stimulus funds to hire exactly one new state worker whose sole job was to apply for more federal stimulus money. States commonly funded grant-administration or program-management positions with federal or recovery funds to implement relief programs, but that is different from the claim's implication of a single hire created purely to seek more taxpayer funds. The statement appears to be a misleading simplification rather than an accurate factual account.

claim: According to a national survey, transit "ridership" among people age 16 to 34 increased 40 percent between 2001 and 2009.
rationale: I could not locate a reputable national survey that reported a 40% increase in transit ridership for 16–34 year‑olds between 2001 and 2009. U.S. national data sources (e.g., American Community Survey, National Household Travel Survey) and transit industry summaries show some increases in young adult transit use in that period but not a clear, nationwide 40% jump, and the claim lacks a cited source.

claim: "Military arrests Adam Schiff."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records that the U.S. military has arrested Representative Adam Schiff. U.S. military forces generally do not make domestic arrests of civilians except under extraordinary, well-publicized conditions (e.g., declared martial law), none of which have occurred in this case. The claim appears to be baseless or a rumor.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Multiple years of national polling show that a clear minority of self-identified Republicans say they favor the Affordable Care Act; Republican support is typically far below 74% and more often in the 20–40% range depending on question wording. A 74% figure would be inconsistent with mainstream poll results unless the question referenced a specific ACA provision (e.g., protections for people with preexisting conditions) or was misattributed.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over foreclosure case against Christine Blasey Ford’s parents, which fueled motivation for sexual assault accusation.
rationale: There is no evidence that Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over a foreclosure case involving Christine Blasey Ford’s parents; reputable fact-checkers and available court records found no such connection. The additional claim that such a nonexistent court action 'fueled motivation' for Ford's allegation is speculative and unsupported by any corroborated evidence.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: While it is true that many Michigan counties used the same voting vendor, the Antrim County anomaly was traced to a reporting/configuration and human-error issue in that county’s tabulation process, not a widespread software that secretly 'switched' votes. State and independent audits, hand recounts, and official reviews found no evidence of thousands of votes being fraudulently shifted statewide, and the initial 6,000-vote reporting error in Antrim was corrected and explained.

claim: "We enacted the biggest tax cuts and reforms in American history."
rationale: This is misleading. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a significant tax change, especially for corporate rates, but it is not clearly the biggest in U.S. history by standard measures. Earlier changes—most notably Reagan-era legislation in 1981 and the major 1986 Tax Reform—were larger either as a share of GDP or in structural impact, and independent analyses show the claim depends on which metric and timeframe you use.

claim: There are cities and counties in Georgia that don’t have websites, and where elected officials don’t have email addresses.
rationale: Small and rural municipalities frequently lack the resources to maintain dedicated websites, and it is common for some elected officials in such places not to have official government email addresses. Statewide surveys and reporting on the municipal 'digital divide' have documented counties and towns with minimal or no online presence and contact info.

claim: "80% of the American people support our Dreamers. Over 70% think they should have a path to citizenship, and that's Democrats, Republicans, independents."
rationale: Large, reputable polls consistently show broad overall public support for Dreamers and for providing a pathway to legal status or citizenship (often in the 70–80% range). However, the claim overstates the bipartisan uniformity: while Democrats and independents typically show very high support, Republican support in many polls is lower and often under 70%, so the statement that 'over 70%' applies to Democrats, Republicans, and independents is inaccurate as phrased.

claim: Says New Jersey Rep. Leonard Lance voted repeatedly "to let insurance companies charge more to people aged 50 and over."
rationale: The claim is vague and asserts repeated votes without identifying specific bills. While some Republican health proposals (e.g., the 2017 AHCA) would have allowed insurers to charge older adults substantially more, I cannot confirm from general knowledge that Rep. Leonard Lance repeatedly cast votes specifically to raise age-based premiums; his roll-call record on particular health bills would be needed to verify the assertion.

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable news reporting that Jennifer Aniston ever said or announced forming an organization called 'celebrities for Trump.' Aniston has not publicly endorsed Donald Trump or led any pro‑Trump celebrity campaign, and such a statement would have been widely reported if genuine.

claim: "I took over the school district when it had a $1 billion structural deficit and left them with $1 billion in cash and 70,000 more students than they have today."
rationale: The statement makes three specific, extraordinary numeric claims but provides no district or timeframe to verify them. Independent verification would require audited budget documents and enrollment records; based on typical U.S. district finances and enrollment reporting, holding $1 billion in cash or swinging enrollment by 70,000 students would be highly unusual and would be widely documented. Without supporting evidence, the claim is not substantiated.

claim: Sarah Palin endorsed a Wasilla policy that charged sexual assault victims for their "rape kits."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and municipal records show there was no Wasilla city policy enacted by Sarah Palin that required sexual assault victims to pay for forensic 'rape kits.' Charges for exams were tied to hospital billing practices and gaps in state reimbursement, not a city ordinance or an explicit Palin-endorsed policy, and there is no evidence she created or formally endorsed such a rule.

claim: " ‘Obamacare’ puts the federal government between you and your doctor."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) expanded insurance access, regulated insurers, created marketplaces, and expanded Medicaid, but it did not create a federal body that sits between most patients and their doctors or replace clinical decision‑making. The law primarily changes insurance rules and financing; care decisions are generally made by clinicians and insurers, not by a new federal gatekeeper.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "took away $1.6 billion from schools and handed it off as over $2 billion in tax breaks to the rich."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading: while Governor Scott Walker's budgets included reductions in certain K–12 aid lines and he signed multi-year tax cuts, independent analyses show the totals depend on the time period and accounting methods and do not cleanly amount to 'taking $1.6 billion from schools' and 'handing over $2 billion to the rich' as a single, documented transaction. Many budget changes reallocated funding, changed aid formulas, and spread tax cuts across income groups; fact-checkers have found such round-number claims overstate or misattribute the amounts.

claim: "More Texans have jobs today than ever before in the history of our state."
rationale: The claim as phrased is unverified and ambiguous because it doesn’t specify the date or the exact metric (employed residents vs. payroll jobs). While Texas has frequently set new records for total jobs in recent years due to population growth and post‑pandemic recovery, confirming that 'more Texans have jobs today than ever before' requires current BLS/Texas Workforce Commission data and a clear definition of 'jobs.' Without that specific, up‑to‑date evidence the assertion cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: "60 percent of all Americans do not want to see Planned Parenthood defunded."
rationale: The assertion of a precise 60% figure is not verifiable without a specific poll, date, and question wording; public-opinion surveys about defunding Planned Parenthood have produced varying results and no consistent, timeless 60% consensus. Because results depend heavily on timing and how the question is asked, the blanket claim that 60 percent of all Americans do not want defunding is unsupported as stated.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: Voting for short-term spending bills that do not include new protections for DACA recipients is not the same as voting to deport Dreamers. Continuing resolutions typically extend existing funding and policy; they do not by themselves order deportations, which are carried out by executive agencies under existing immigration law. Unless a specific bill included explicit language rescinding DACA or authorizing deportations, the blanket claim mischaracterizes the effect of such votes.

claim: "What the Arizona law does is make a state crime out of something that already is... a federal crime."
rationale: Arizona's 2010 immigration law (SB 1070) created state misdemeanor offenses that largely duplicated existing federal immigration crimes (for example, failure to carry alien registration documents and statutes against transporting/harboring undocumented immigrants). The U.S. Supreme Court later struck down several provisions as preempted but recognized the overlap, so the claim that the law made state crimes out of conduct already criminalized at the federal level is accurate.

claim: "Teenage births cost Texas taxpayers $1.1 billion in health care, foster care and lost tax revenue in 2010 alone."
rationale: I cannot verify an authoritative source that Texas taxpayers specifically paid $1.1 billion in 2010 for health care, foster care and lost tax revenue due to teenage births. Similar figures have been produced by advocacy groups using modeled estimates for various years, but the exact $1.1 billion claim for 2010 is not confirmed by independent government data and likely depends on methodological assumptions.

claim: Says Hunter Biden "died of a crack overdose."
rationale: The claim is false. As of the last reliable reporting, Hunter Biden was alive and there were no credible reports that he died of a crack overdose. While he has publicly struggled with substance abuse in the past, major news outlets and official sources did not report his death; the assertion appears to be a fabricated rumor.

claim: "Of all cities in the United States with more than 100,000 people, Providence is the 183rd safest."
rationale: This specific numeric claim cannot be confirmed without a cited source and year; there is no single authoritative list that universally ranks U.S. cities by safety. Rankings of "safest" cities vary widely depending on the dataset, crime measures (violent vs. property), and year, so an unsupported precise rank (183rd) is not verifiable and should be treated as false.

claim: "In Washington, Congressman Joe Heck supports privatizing (Social Security), turning our savings over to Wall Street and risking it on the stock market."
rationale: Public reporting and campaign materials show Joe Heck called for Social Security reform and at times supported options like personal/individual accounts for younger workers, but there is not clear authoritative evidence he endorsed wholesale privatization that would convert the entire program into stock‑market investments. Opponents frequently characterized his reform positions as 'privatization,' which is an exaggeration of his recorded statements and proposals.

claim: Says TriMet spends "$10.3 million in police contracts" a year for 56 transit police who must respond to non-transit calls
rationale: The dollar figure and officer count are plausible — TriMet has recently reported policing-related expenditures in the low tens of millions and maintained roughly 50–60 commissioned transit officers — but the assertion that those 56 transit police are required to respond to non‑transit calls is misleading. TriMet officers can and do assist other agencies under mutual aid or by virtue of their sworn status, but they are not universally obligated by a single contract to answer all non‑transit calls.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: In 1973 the U.S. Department of Justice sued Trump Management, Inc. (and Donald and Fred Trump) alleging the company refused to rent to African-Americans and violated the federal Fair Housing Act; the case was resolved with a 1975 consent decree. The suit was a formal federal charge of discriminatory housing practices under federal law.

claim: "After filing a lawsuit in Rhode Island, we reached an agreement with state agencies that resulted in more voters being registered in the first full month after our lawsuit than in the entire previous two-year reporting period."
rationale: The claim is highly specific and asserts an extraordinary change in voter-registration totals tied to a single lawsuit and subsequent agreement, but I find no corroborating public records or contemporaneous reporting supporting that a single month exceeded the prior two years' total. Without official state voter-registration reports or court/settlement documents showing those exact figures, the assertion cannot be verified and is implausible as stated.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Kim Jong Un directly called President Biden those English-language insults in a public speech. North Korean leaders give speeches in Korean via state media, and viral videos that show Kim using colloquial English insults have previously been shown to be dubbed, edited, or AI-manipulated. The claim therefore appears to be a misrepresentation of the video's provenance or language.

claim: China recovered from COVID-19 "without a vaccine."
rationale: China did not recover from COVID-19 without vaccines: the country developed and widely deployed domestic vaccines (e.g., Sinovac, Sinopharm, CanSino) and ran mass vaccination campaigns in 2021–2022. While China initially contained outbreaks in 2020 using strict non-pharmaceutical interventions, its later management and reopening occurred after substantial vaccine rollout, so the blanket claim is false.

claim: "They were going to build the wall a while ago, not so long ago, like in '06. And they couldn't get environmental impact statements."
rationale: It is true that plans to build border fencing date to about 2006 (Secure Fence Act), but the claim that "they couldn't get environmental impact statements" is misleading. In practice DHS sometimes faced legal challenges over environmental reviews, yet the 2005 Real ID Act explicitly gave the agency authority to waive environmental laws and NEPA reviews to expedite fence construction, so EISs were not uniformly unobtainable.

claim: Scientists are "questioning the original idea that man-made global warming is what is causing the climate to change. … (It is) more and more being put into question."
rationale: The overwhelming majority of climate scientists and major scientific organizations conclude that recent global warming is primarily caused by human activities (greenhouse gas emissions). While researchers continue to refine details like climate sensitivity and regional impacts, the core conclusion is widely supported and is not 'more and more being put into question.'

claim: "Today, the United States has, sadly, one of the lowest voter turnouts of any major country on earth."
rationale: The United States typically has lower voter turnout than most other large, established democracies (especially in non-presidential midterms) and ranks near the bottom among major OECD countries when using comparable measures. While it is not the absolute lowest in the world, it is accurate to say the U.S. is one of the lower-turnout major countries.

claim: Says a new report shows the "devastating tax hikes (in the health care law) will have on middle-class Kentuckians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a new report shows broad, 'devastating' tax hikes on middle-class Kentuckians from the federal health-care law. Analyses of the law's tax provisions show most new taxes target higher earners, insurers, employers, or specific industries (e.g., medical devices), and independent budget offices did not find widespread middle-class tax increases of the magnitude described.

claim: The Obama administration "went to court to keep one of these five in jail at Guantanamo just three years ago because he was such a huge risk."
rationale: The claim asserts the Obama administration went to court to keep one of “these five” in Guantanamo three years earlier, but there is no clear public record of the Obama DOJ filing a court action to retain one of the well-known “Taliban Five” in custody after their 2014 transfer. The Obama administration negotiated transfers and occasionally sought detention or prosecution for certain detainees, but the specific assertion (a court action three years earlier to keep one of five jailed) is not supported without more context.

claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: The quoted sentence is not a factual excerpt from the 1992 Democratic Party platform. The 1992 Democratic platform discussed immigration and reform but did not contain language asserting that undocumented immigrants as a group were coming, committing felonies, being sent back, and immediately reentering in the precise accusatory terms quoted. The claim appears to be a paraphrase or mischaracterization rather than a direct platform provision.

claim: America’s federal business tax rate is the highest "in the world."
rationale: The U.S. federal statutory corporate tax rate was cut to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (effective 2018), and even when combined with state corporate taxes the U.S. rate is generally in the mid-20s percent range. Many countries have equal or higher combined statutory corporate tax burdens, so the U.S. federal rate is not the highest in the world. Historically (pre-2018) the U.S. federal rate of 35% was among the higher rates internationally but still not uniquely the highest in every comparison.

claim: "Sen. Mark Begich cast the deciding vote in favor of President Obama’s authority to issue executive amnesty to illegal aliens."
rationale: No Senate vote gave President Obama authority to carry out an "executive amnesty"; deferred-action programs (DACA/DAPA) were implemented by executive action, not by a specific Senate authorization. Sen. Mark Begich did vote for the 2013 bipartisan Senate immigration bill (S.744), but that bill was comprehensive reform and did not delegate unilateral executive amnesty power to the president, and it was not the decisive vehicle for Obama's later executive actions.

claim: "We've seen the increase of alcohol use for underage kids even though alcohol has been illegal ... for kids under 21."
rationale: National surveillance data do not show a broad increase in underage alcohol use; rather, long‑term trends from major U.S. surveys show declines in past‑month drinking and binge drinking among adolescents since the 1990s and 2000s despite the legal drinking age of 21. While there can be short‑term or local fluctuations, the overall prevalence among youth has fallen.

claim: "The estimated savings of this (debt ceiling) deal only pay for half of the cost of extending all of the Bush-era tax cuts for another decade."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it does not identify which specific debt‑ceiling deal or which scoring source is meant. In commonly cited US cases, the cost of extending the full set of Bush‑era tax cuts for ten years was measured in multiple trillions of dollars, while negotiated debt‑ceiling “savings” or cuts were typically much smaller and would not reliably equal exactly half of that cost. Without a precise deal and official score, the blanket claim that the deal’s savings cover half the extension’s cost is misleading and unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters; major fact-checkers and campaign finance records do not show such a transfer. The $20 million figure is likely a conflation with fundraising by independent groups, local bail funds, or other organizations, not a direct campaign donation.

claim: "Biden confirms agenda to microchip the masses"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official statement that President Biden has "confirmed" any policy to microchip the general population. The claim echoes long-standing conspiracy theories (e.g., about vaccine microchips or mass tracking) that have been repeatedly debunked by reputable fact-checkers and lack any supporting official policy documents or announcements.

claim: President Barack Obama "has doubled the size of government since he took office."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: common measures of government size did not double during President Obama's tenure. Federal civilian employment stayed roughly flat (around 2.7–2.9 million), and annual federal outlays increased but did not double; independent fact-checkers and government budget/employment data do not support a doubling.

claim: The Benghazi probe is "the longest-running congressional investigation ever."
rationale: The Benghazi investigations (various congressional inquiries from 2012–2016, including the House Select Committee from 2014–2016) were lengthy but not the longest in U.S. congressional history. Other congressional probes and standing investigations (for example, the long-running activities of committees like the House Un-American Activities Committee and multi-decade oversight efforts) have spanned longer periods or involved more continuous inquiry. Fact-checkers have repeatedly rejected the claim that Benghazi was the longest-running congressional investigation ever.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Faso "voted for an age tax on seniors."
rationale: The phrase "age tax" is a partisan slogan, not the name of a specific law, and there is no clear, established statute called an "age tax" that Rep. John Faso voted for. While Faso did vote for GOP tax legislation during his tenure, the claim as stated is vague and misleading because it asserts he "voted for an age tax on seniors" without specifying a bill or provision shown to be an explicit age-based tax increase on seniors.

claim: "The U.S. Constitution owes its notion of democracy to the Iroquois Tribes."
rationale: While some Founding-era Americans (notably Benjamin Franklin and other colonial leaders) admired the Iroquois Confederacy and cited it as an example of inter-tribal federation, mainstream historical scholarship finds little evidence that the U.S. Constitution directly borrowed its structure or core democratic doctrines from the Iroquois. The Constitution’s ideas primarily reflect Enlightenment political theory, British legal traditions, and colonial self-government debates rather than a specific institutional transplant from the Iroquois. Claiming the Constitution 'owes' its notion of democracy to the Iroquois therefore overstates the degree of influence.

claim: "We have doubled our (oil) imports from Russia in the last year."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as written because it gives no defined subject or exact 12‑month period, and there is no evidence that major purchasers broadly doubled their Russian oil imports in the last year. Public trade data and reporting since 2022 show many large buyers (notably the US and EU) reduced or only modestly changed imports following sanctions and market shifts, rather than doubling them. While a few smaller buyers may have increased purchases, the blanket claim is not substantiated.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Boulder, Colorado, shooting was a "false flag" operation; law enforcement investigations and mainstream reporting identify an individual shooter with no substantiation of a staged event. Likewise, the claim that most other shootings are "false flags" is a broad conspiracy assertion unsupported by investigative findings or documented proof.

claim: "Tommy Thompson created the first school choice program in the nation, giving thousands of Milwaukee students the choice of where they go to school – no matter where they live or how much money their parents make."
rationale: Tommy Thompson did sign the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program in 1990, which is widely credited as the first modern state-funded school voucher program in the U.S. However, the program was limited to Milwaukee residents and initially targeted low-income families; it was not universally open to students regardless of where they live or how much their parents earn.

claim: As a Member of Congress, Chris Murphy "was raking in $1 million in salary."
rationale: U.S. Members of Congress receive a statutory annual salary (about $174,000 for rank-and-file representatives in recent years), with leadership pay higher but well below $1 million. There is no evidence Chris Murphy earned a $1 million salary while serving; at most members may report outside income or assets separate from official congressional pay.

claim: "Under my administration, 7 million Americans have come off of food stamps, and 10 million people have been lifted off of welfare."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported by available data: while SNAP (food stamp) enrollment did fall by a few million in the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, independent counts do not clearly show a 7 million drop attributable to a single administration, and 'welfare' (typically measured by TANF) has a much smaller caseload that did not decline by 10 million during that period. The statement mixes ambiguous definitions and likely overstates or misattributes longer-term declines that predate the administration.

claim: Wisconsin was embroiled in a "constitutional crisis" brought on by the Democratic senators fleeing the state for Illinois to block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill.
rationale: In February 2011 fourteen Democratic Wisconsin state senators left the state (traveling to Illinois and elsewhere) to deny the Senate a quorum and block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill; the action produced a prolonged governmental standoff with legal fights and recalls that many observers and media outlets described as a constitutional crisis. The underlying events and their direct link to the attempt to block the bill are well documented.

claim: Quotes Anthony Fauci as writing, "I reject the notion that it’s ‘just a virus’ and we’ll all get it eventually. What a careless, lazy, heartless stance."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Anthony Fauci writing that exact sentence; the phrasing circulates on social media and appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution of his frequent criticisms of 'herd immunity' approaches. While Fauci publicly rejected laissez-faire 'let it rip' approaches to COVID-19, reputable sources do not show him authoring that specific quoted line.

claim: "Supreme Court issues its first bench warrant ever."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: the Supreme Court (in the U.S. context) has long exercised contempt powers and has issued orders for arrest/bench warrants in its history rather than this being a first-ever action. Reports saying it was the "first" typically misinterpret a narrow procedural novelty or confuse lower-court practice with Supreme Court history.

claim: Says Thai police found bodies of children with their organs removed.
rationale: The claim is a vague, sensational allegation that lacks verifiable details (date, location, victims) and there are no corroborating reports from reputable Thai law-enforcement statements or mainstream news outlets. Similar stories of children killed with organs removed frequently circulate as unverified social media hoaxes and have not been substantiated by officials in Thailand.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The absolute claim that Proposition 2 “does not cost state taxpayers any money” cannot be verified without the specific year and the official fiscal analysis. Texas ballot measures are routinely accompanied by fiscal notes from the Legislative Budget Board (LBB) and some measures that appear cost-free can create direct or indirect costs when implemented. Unless the LBB or another official analysis explicitly states zero fiscal impact, the blanket statement is unreliable.

claim: "Before this law was passed, Americans were told they could keep their current health care plans. After it became law, the administration issued regulations stating nearly half of Americans would lose their current plan."
rationale: The statement mixes two different facts to create a misleading impression. President Obama did repeatedly say people could keep their plans, but the administration’s analysis that cited “nearly half” referred to plans in the individual insurance market (a subset of coverage), not nearly half of all Americans, and the administration later issued temporary renewals and other relief. Thus the claim as phrased is false because it incorrectly portrays the scope of the administration’s estimate.

claim: Originally "almost all models predicted" Dorian would hit Alabama.
rationale: Contemporary National Hurricane Center model guidance and post-event analyses showed that only a minority of model tracks ever took Dorian into Alabama; most model runs and the official forecast kept the storm off the Alabama coast or aimed it elsewhere. NOAA and multiple independent fact-checkers concluded the claim that 'almost all models predicted' an Alabama hit was incorrect.

claim: Says the "South African Government is now seizing land from white farmers" and alleges a "large scale killing of farmers" in the country.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the South African government is conducting a widescale, state-led seizure of white-owned farms; the country has an ongoing land-reform debate and limited, legally contested measures (including discussions of expropriation without compensation), but not mass forcible confiscation. Similarly, while murders and attacks on farmers do occur, independent crime statistics and multiple fact-checks show these incidents do not constitute a large-scale, targeted campaign against white farmers comparable to claims of wholesale killing.

claim: Says McCain "supported George Bush's policies 95 percent of the time."
rationale: The 95% figure is misleading and not supported by objective analyses of McCain's Senate voting record versus Bush administration positions. Independent fact-checkers and vote-comparison analyses produced much lower alignment figures (typically in the roughly 70–85% range) and found the 95% number came from selective counting and campaign spin.

claim: In nine Democratic debates, "We've not had one question about a woman's right to make her own decisions about reproductive health care, not one question."
rationale: This is incorrect — Democratic primary debates in 2019–2020 included multiple questions about reproductive rights, abortion access, and related issues. Moderators and reporters asked candidates about abortion, Planned Parenthood, and contraception across several debates, so the claim that there were no such questions in nine debates is not supported by debate records and media coverage.

claim: Medicaid "is contributing to 70 percent of our budget deficit right now. It’s the one that is in our lap because of Obamacare."
rationale: Medicaid federal outlays are large but nowhere near 70% of the federal budget deficit. Recent federal Medicaid spending has been on the order of a few hundred billion dollars annually while federal deficits are in the hundreds of billions to over a trillion, so Medicaid is a minority contributor; moreover, CBO and other analyses found the Affordable Care Act did not create a Medicaid-driven 70% share of the deficit and its net impact on the federal deficit was modest.

claim: Says Jeb Bush -- not Charlie Crist -- signed legislation that let Duke Energy collect money for nuclear projects.
rationale: In 2006 Governor Jeb Bush signed Florida legislation allowing utilities to recover pre‑construction and related costs for new nuclear projects. The law applied to in‑state utilities such as Progress Energy (which later merged with Duke Energy), and Charlie Crist was not governor until 2007, so he did not sign that bill.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported as a general claim; typical national unemployment rates even in high-unemployment countries are well below 42% on standard (official) measures. While some countries' broader or alternative unemployment measures or specific subgroups (for example youth unemployment or discouraged-worker-adjusted rates) can exceed 40%, without a country, time period, and definition this assertion is misleading and likely incorrect as a general fact.

claim: The Dow Jones Industrial Average "jumped 1000 points in last 5 weeks, Record fastest 1000 point move in history."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the Dow has produced 1,000‑point moves much faster than five weeks (including single‑day and intraday moves during high volatility, notably in March 2020). Saying a 1,000‑point rise in five weeks is the "record fastest" is incorrect without a specific date or metric, since historical fastest 1,000‑point moves occurred within days or a single session.

claim: In Milwaukee, "murder is up an astonishing 57 percent."
rationale: The statement is presented without any timeframe or data source and therefore cannot be verified as a general fact. Milwaukee has seen large year-to-year swings in homicides in some periods, so a 57% increase could be true for a specific short interval (e.g., a particular month or year-over-year span) but is misleading as a standalone claim.

claim: "The CBO, the Congressional Budget Office has said that Obamacare will kill 800,000 jobs."
rationale: The CBO did not state that the Affordable Care Act would 'kill 800,000 jobs.' CBO analyses discussed modest reductions in labor supply (fewer hours worked or lower labor-force participation) and reported effects in terms of hours or full-time-equivalent workers; commentators have sometimes misinterpreted or rounded those estimates into a claim about 'job losses.' The agency framed the effect as behavioral responses to subsidies and insurance availability, not as literal job deaths.

claim: Says in 2000, Fox News broke the story of George W. Bush’s drunk driving arrest. "Who broke it? Fox News."
rationale: This is false. The reporting about George W. Bush’s 1970s-era drunk driving/arrest records in 2000 was carried by major newspapers and local outlets (e.g., New York-area and Maine papers) and was not first “broken” by Fox News; Fox was not the originator of that revelation. Saying “Who broke it? Fox News” misattributes the initial reporting.

claim: Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s and other companies support rioting.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coca‑Cola or Ben & Jerry's have publicly endorsed or encouraged rioting. Both companies have issued statements supporting racial justice and peaceful protest and have made donations to advocacy groups, but public records and corporate communications do not show official support for violent riots. Broad claims that these firms "support rioting" are a misleading conflation of support for social justice causes with endorsement of violence.

claim: Health care premiums for consumers have doubled since 2001.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and lacks specification; while health insurance premiums have risen substantially since 2001, the amount of increase depends on the measure used (employer‑sponsored vs individual market, single vs family). Some series have not exactly doubled while others have grown more than twofold, so the absolute statement is misleading without context.

claim: The Trans-Pacific Partnership "knocks out 18,000 tariffs that other countries place on American products and goods."
rationale: The TPP negotiators and U.S. Trade Representative estimated the pact would eliminate tariffs on roughly 18,000 tariff lines that partner countries apply to U.S. exports. The statement accurately reflects that estimate, though it simplifies the detail that many cuts were phased in over time and some exclusions or sensitive items remained.

claim: Says Democratic Party created Planned Parenthood
rationale: Planned Parenthood traces to birth-control activist Margaret Sanger and the American Birth Control League (founded 1921) and was organized as Planned Parenthood Federation of America in 1942 by activists and physicians, not by the Democratic Party. While many Democrats have supported and funded Planned Parenthood over the years, the Democratic Party as an institution did not create it.

claim: Twitter removed this tweet from Donald Trump: "My blood IS the vaccine!!!!!"
rationale: There is no record in Donald Trump's official Twitter archive or contemporaneous credible news reports of him tweeting "My blood IS the vaccine!!!!!"; the phrase circulated as a doctored screenshot and was debunked by fact-checkers. While Twitter did remove and later suspend Trump's account for other posts, this specific tweet appears fabricated rather than removed by the platform.

claim: "Romney signed government-mandated health care with taxpayer-funded abortions."
rationale: Romney signed Massachusetts' 2006 health reform which created an individual mandate and a Connector marketplace, but the law did not authorize taxpayer-funded elective abortions. The statute and subsequent implementation required that abortion coverage be paid for with separate private premiums and prevented the use of federal subsidies for elective abortion; critics conflated the availability of abortion coverage in some plans with direct taxpayer funding.

claim: Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker’s estimate of a $3.6 billion state budget deficit is "manufactured" and a "bogus figure."
rationale: Walker’s $3.6 billion shortfall figure corresponded to the projected budget gap for the relevant biennium and was broadly in line with nonpartisan Legislative Fiscal Bureau analyses and official revenue forecasts; critics disputed accounting choices and one-time fixes but did not demonstrate the number was simply manufactured or completely bogus. Statements calling it 'manufactured' overstate the case given available independent fiscal estimates.

claim: "Today, it is more difficult to enlist in the U.S. military than it is to enroll in college."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and misleading. Military enlistment requires specific age, medical, moral, and aptitude (ASVAB) standards that disqualify many applicants, but college admission standards vary widely and many institutions—particularly community colleges—have open enrollment and accept most applicants; therefore there is no general truth that enlisting is harder than enrolling in college.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included provisions that reduced projected Medicare spending by roughly $400–$500 billion over the first decade after enactment, a finding reflected in CBO and administration analyses. Those were cuts to projected payments (especially to Medicare Advantage plans and providers) and measures to reduce waste, not across-the-board benefit cuts for current beneficiaries.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified from the information provided — whether a majority of contributions came from private individuals averaging $125 and excluded PACs/groups requires campaign finance records. Many campaigns receive a mix of small-dollar individual donations and contributions from PACs or organizations, so the claim is unprovable as stated without evidence. In the absence of supporting disclosure filings, I treat the assertion as false.

claim: "Too many" tattoos "on visible body parts" keep some applicants out of the military.
rationale: U.S. military branches maintain rules limiting the number, placement, size, and content of visible tattoos, and applicants whose tattoos exceed those limits can be denied enlistment or required to obtain a waiver. While policies have been relaxed in recent years, visible tattoos that violate branch standards still prevent some applicants from joining.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson said he wants to "do away with Medicare."
rationale: Tommy Thompson did not literally say he wanted to “do away with Medicare.” His public record and campaign statements indicate he called Medicare as structured unsustainable and supported major reforms — including increased use of private plans or a premium-support-style approach for future beneficiaries — which critics paraphrased as ending or doing away with Medicare. The claim is a misleading characterization rather than an accurate literal quote.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about an unspecified city and thus is unverifiable as written. More importantly, it is implausible: municipal histories commonly include cases where sitting aldermen or council members have defeated incumbent mayors, so a blanket 'never' is unlikely to be true without strong, city-specific evidence.

claim: "(Mexican immigrants) are more law-abiding than U.S. citizens and that is a statistic."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and U.S. government data have found that immigrants, including Mexican immigrants, tend to have lower crime and incarceration rates than native‑born U.S. citizens. While exact numbers vary by study, time period, crime type, and location, the overall statistical evidence supports the claim that Mexican immigrants are, on average, more law‑abiding than U.S. natives.

claim: Says Denmark’s suicide rate has been about twice as high as the United States’ over the past five decades.
rationale: This claim is not supported by long-term data: Denmark had higher suicide rates than the U.S. in parts of the mid‑20th century, but Danish rates declined substantially over the last decades while U.S. rates rose at times. Over the past 50 years there is no consistent pattern showing Denmark’s rate was roughly double the U.S. rate throughout that entire period.

claim: "Under Pat McCrory, (North Carolina) has fallen to 41st in teacher pay."
rationale: During Pat McCrory’s governorship (2013–2017), multiple reports based on National Education Association data showed North Carolina’s average teacher salary ranking slipping to about 41st in the nation by the mid-2010s. Media and education analyses at the time cited that drop in state teacher pay rankings during his term.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The statement is a broad unsupported generalization: without specifying the storm type, location, and time period, one cannot assert a 10–15 year recurrence. Snowstorm frequency varies widely by region and climate drivers, and determining a return period requires multi‑decadal observational records and statistical analysis.

claim: Women are paid 77 cents for every $1 men get for the same work.
rationale: The "77 cents" figure is an unadjusted comparison of median annual earnings for women versus men overall, not a measure of pay for the same job with identical hours, experience, and qualifications. When researchers control for occupation, hours worked, education and experience the gap narrows substantially, though a smaller unexplained difference often remains.

claim: "Rosalyn Dance voted against President Obama’s Medicaid expansion."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: Rosalyn Dance, a Democratic member of the Virginia legislature, did not cast a vote against the state’s decision to adopt Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act. The Medicaid expansion in Virginia was enacted with Democratic support and Dance voted with her party to approve expansion at the state level.

claim: Obama came into office "with a $1.3 trillion deficit before I had passed any law. ... We came in with $8 trillion worth of debt over the next decade."
rationale: When Obama took office the fiscal year 2009 deficit was about $1.3–1.4 trillion (most estimates and CBO figures put FY2009 near $1.3T) before his administration’s laws took effect. CBO baseline projections at the time also showed roughly $7–8 trillion in cumulative deficits over the coming decade under then-current policies, so the quoted figures match contemporaneous official estimates (though "debt" is a looser term here than "projected deficits").

claim: "Every day over 450,000 Americans sit in jail not because they've been convicted of anything, but because they are too poor to pay bail & don't have high powered attorneys."
rationale: The claim correctly echoes recent estimates that roughly 450,000–470,000 people are held in jails pretrial on a given day, but it overstates the cause. Not all of those people are detained solely because they are too poor to pay bail or lack strong attorneys; many are held because bail was denied, for immigration or probation holds, or other court orders.

claim: On Donald Trump’s plan to cut federal funding to sanctuary cities, "because of a decision by the Supreme Court, no president's in a position to cut off funding across the board. It has to be very specific to the matter at hand."
rationale: Supreme Court precedent constrains a president’s ability to unilaterally cut off appropriated federal funds and requires spending conditions to be clearly authorized and related to the program’s purpose. Cases such as Train v. City of New York (1975) (president cannot frustrate Congress’s appropriations) and South Dakota v. Dole (1987) (conditions on spending must be unambiguous and related) support the statement that withholding must be specific rather than an across-the-board cutoff.

claim: The Democratic health care plan is a "government takeover of nearly 20 percent of our economy."
rationale: Calling a Democratic health care plan a "government takeover of nearly 20 percent of our economy" is rhetorical and misleading. U.S. health care spending is roughly 17–18% of GDP, but the Affordable Care Act and similar Democratic proposals expanded government financing and regulation rather than nationalizing or transferring ownership of that portion of the economy; private insurers, employers, and providers remained central.

claim: Says Ron Johnson justifies his support of trade agreements by saying the U.S. has the Trade Adjustment Assistance program for displaced workers, but then he "voted to eliminate it."
rationale: There is no clear, documented record that Sen. Ron Johnson justified support for trade agreements by citing Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) and then cast a specific vote that eliminated the TAA program. While Republicans including some senators have backed reducing or restricting TAA funding or reauthorizations, elimination would require explicit legislation and a recorded repeal vote, which is not clearly attributable to Johnson. Without a specific cited vote or bill, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "In the past two years in Congress, I’ve written more bills, passed more amendments on the floor of the House and enacted more of my bills into law than any other member of the House."
rationale: The claim is an absolute superlative that cannot be substantiated without specific, auditable data for the stated two-year window and definitions (e.g., authored vs. sponsored bills). Public congressional records routinely show variation among members in bills introduced, amendments adopted on the floor, and bills enacted, and leadership or committee chairs typically account for many of the top counts. Because the statement lacks precise timeframe and measurable criteria and is unlikely to be uniquely true, it is assessed as false.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: As a general rule members of Congress must be physically present to participate in floor debates and to cast votes; the Constitution and each chamber’s rules require a quorum and in-person voting. There was a temporary exception when the House adopted proxy voting during the COVID-19 pandemic, but that was a limited, time-bound rule change and is not the standing practice for either chamber.

claim: Says a Bureau of Labor Statistics report attributed a sharp increase in work-related fatalities to "increasing numbers of employees and drivers could not read or understand warning signs in English."
rationale: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' fatality reports (CFOI) provide counts and categorizations of work-related deaths but do not issue broad causal claims blaming a sharp rise on employees or drivers who "could not read or understand warning signs in English." That phrasing appears to be a misattribution; while language barriers are recognized by OSHA/NIOSH as a workplace safety risk factor, BLS reports do not contain that specific attribution.

claim: Says Rick Scott cut education by over a billion dollars, meaning thousands of teachers "lost their jobs" and "class sizes went up."
rationale: The claim mixes several contested points. Florida did see major K–12 budget reductions around 2011 during Rick Scott's early term (figures near $1 billion are often cited depending on how cuts are counted), but the exact $1+ billion figure, the attribution solely to Scott (vs. the legislature), and the assertion that thousands of teachers statewide 'lost their jobs' and class sizes rose as a direct, statewide consequence are not conclusively supported. Districts made staffing cuts in some places and class-size impacts varied, so the blanket causal statement overstates and oversimplifies the facts.

claim: "Any Republican that has led for two months and led every state has won the GOP nomination."
rationale: The statement asserts a universal rule tying short-term polling leads to nomination, which is false. Polling leads (even sustained ones or leads across states) do not guarantee delegate wins or nomination — primary elections, caucuses, campaign events, fundraising, and scandals can change outcomes. Historical GOP cycles show multiple long-time frontrunners who ultimately lost the nomination, so the logical universal claim fails.

claim: The federal government only ordered BP to pay "to do one of those six segments" of sand barriers for Louisiana.
rationale: The statement is misleading. During the Deepwater Horizon response the federal government ordered BP to fund emergency coastal-protection work and BP agreed to pay for multiple sand-barrier/berm projects that Louisiana sought, not a federal order limited to paying for only one of six segments. Details and scope changed over time in negotiations and approvals, but it is not accurate to say the feds only ordered payment for a single segment.

claim: "We've made other countries rich while the wealth ... of our country has dissipated over the horizon."
rationale: The statement is a vague rhetorical claim rather than a specific factual assertion and is not supported as written. While globalization and trade have helped some foreign economies grow and have coincided with manufacturing job losses and rising inequality in the U.S., U.S. GDP, corporate profits, and aggregate national wealth have generally increased over recent decades rather than having "dissipated over the horizon." Therefore the blanket claim is misleading and unsupported without precise timeframe, metrics, or causal evidence.

claim: Says "every school will be negatively impacted" if Education Stability Fund is not tapped.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that cannot be true in general. Whether schools would be negatively impacted by not tapping an "Education Stability Fund" depends on the fund's size, the jurisdiction, other revenue sources (local property taxes, federal aid), and budgetary choices, so it is unlikely every single school would be affected the same way.

claim: Ilhan Omar called for "violence" against President Trump over Middle East dispute.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Ilhan Omar explicitly called for physical violence against President Trump over a Middle East dispute. Public records and fact-checking reports show she has used rhetoric about political resistance or 'fighting' policies, but not calls to commit violence against the president.

claim: Novak Djokovic is the first professional athlete to be banned from a major sporting event for "not taking drugs."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Novak Djokovic was not banned for "not taking drugs." His high-profile removal from the 2022 Australian Open involved a visa cancellation related to COVID-19 vaccination/entry rules, not a sporting ban for refusing medication. Moreover, the statement that he was the first professional athlete ever to be barred for such a reason is false—there is a long history of athletes being excluded or sanctioned for various medical and drug-related issues, and other competitors faced COVID-related entry restrictions before or contemporaneously with Djokovic.

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: While the U.S. Chamber of Commerce has repeatedly warned that proposed carbon regulations would cost jobs and raise household energy bills, there is no clear record that the Chamber itself officially stated the exact figures '244,000 jobs a year' and '$1,200 a year' as a single definitive claim. Impact numbers the Chamber cites vary by study, rule, and time frame, so the precise paired figures in this claim do not match verifiable Chamber statements in my knowledge.

claim: "Thousands of folks are opening West Virginia E-ZPass accounts."
rationale: The claim is unverified and vague—no specific timeframe, source, or corroborating data is provided. As of my knowledge cutoff I am not aware of authoritative reports confirming that "thousands" have opened West Virginia E‑ZPass accounts; such a statement requires a cited public statistic or news report to be treated as factual.

claim: "Bill O’Reilly in critical condition after being attacked by ‘tolerant’ liberals."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or confirmations from major outlets that Bill O’Reilly was attacked and placed in critical condition; the phrasing and partisan framing match common social-media hoaxes. Such a serious event would have been widely reported, and the absence of corroboration indicates the claim is false or fabricated.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: There is no reliable documentation of Carly Fiorina saying the exact line "I would have done them all faster" after laying off about 30,000 HP employees. While Fiorina did oversee roughly 30,000 job cuts and has been quoted discussing restructuring, the specific phrasing appears to be a viral misattribution or paraphrase rather than a verifiable direct quote.

claim: The United States gives $8 million a day to Israel and gives that country a blank check.
rationale: The headline "$8 million a day" is a rough, non‑standard arithmetic that depends on which grants and time period are counted; under the 2016 U.S.–Israel Memorandum of Understanding the baseline military assistance is about $3.8 billion per year (roughly $10–11 million per day), so $8M/day is an imprecise simplification. The phrase "blank check" is rhetorical and inaccurate as a factual claim: U.S. aid is provided under multi‑year agreements, laws and congressional appropriations and is subject to oversight and some conditions, not literally unlimited or unconditional funding.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The statement is overbroad and likely incorrect as written because it gives no timeframe or geography; globally the oil and gas sector still employs more people than the solar industry. In some places (notably the United States) solar employment has grown rapidly and in certain years and employment categories solar jobs have been comparable to or exceeded some oil-and-gas subsectors, but that does not validate the blanket claim 'we now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil.'

claim: Says Clint Eastwood is dead.
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim that Clint Eastwood is dead. As of my last reliable update in June 2024, Clint Eastwood (born 1930) was reported alive, and celebrity death hoaxes are common. Without access to real-time sources beyond my cutoff, I cannot verify any change since then.

claim: Elderly people were "beat up by a BLM hate group" for being white.
rationale: The assertion that elderly people were "beat up by a BLM hate group" for being white is not supported by credible evidence. Major news outlets and independent fact-checkers have not corroborated any verified, organized Black Lives Matter group carrying out racially motivated assaults on elderly people; viral videos making similar claims have often been misattributed or lacked context. Additionally, Black Lives Matter is a decentralized movement and is not officially designated as a hate group by mainstream authorities, so isolated incidents (if any) do not substantiate the broad claim.

claim: "It was under Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton that changed the rules of engagement that probably cost (Capt. Humayun Khan’s) life."
rationale: Captain Humayun Khan was killed in 2004 in Iraq, during the George W. Bush administration, five years before Barack Obama became president and while Hillary Clinton was a senator, not a member of the Obama administration. Therefore any rules of engagement changed under Obama or while Clinton was Secretary of State (2009–2013) could not have 'probably cost' his life. The claim is chronologically inconsistent with known facts about Khan's death.

claim: "Workers in the United States are making less than they were almost 20 years ago, and yet they are working harder."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad statement that depends heavily on how you measure pay and effort. Inflation‑adjusted median wages for many U.S. workers were largely stagnant in the 2000s–2010s but have risen in recent years for some groups, so it is not uniformly true that workers are making less than ~20 years ago; at the same time productivity has grown faster than typical wages, and many measures show increased workloads or longer hours for some workers. Because the statement lacks a clear timeframe, pay metric (nominal vs real, median vs mean, total compensation), and definition of “working harder,” it cannot be accepted as universally true.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that Schwarzenegger ever slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself after being turned away from a hotel. Biographical accounts note he struggled early in the U.S. (sleeping in cars or modest housing) and that statues of him were erected much later, but these facts are from different times and have not been linked in trustworthy sources to the anecdote claimed.

claim: The largest number of gamblers are "from the poorest segments of the population."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and unsupported: while problem gambling prevalence is often higher among lower-income groups, overall gambling participation and the largest absolute numbers of gamblers vary by country, type of gambling, and population distribution. In many settings middle-income groups make up a larger share of total gamblers simply because they are a larger segment of the population. Without specifying location, measure (participation vs problem gambling) or time period, the blanket statement is not accurate.

claim: Says state Rep. Jim Keffer, a GOP lieutenant to House Speaker Joe Straus, "did mail pieces for Democrat Mark Strama to help him defeat" a Republican.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public record that Texas Republican state Rep. Jim Keffer produced or mailed campaign pieces on behalf of Democrat Mark Strama; such a cross-party action would have been notable in Texas political coverage and is not documented. Keffer has been identified with GOP leadership, so the claim lacks supporting evidence and appears to be a conflation or error.

claim: "Californians are overwhelmingly against this concept of the illegal sanctuary state."
rationale: The claim is unsupported because it makes a broad assertion without specifying which proposal, timing, or data source, and available public-opinion polling in California generally shows mixed to pro-immigrant or pro-‘sanctuary’ sentiments rather than an overwhelming opposition. Whether Californians oppose or support sanctuary policies depends strongly on question wording and context, so the blanket statement that they are "overwhelmingly against" is inaccurate.

claim: "Voted the ‘best specialty plate in America’"
rationale: The assertion provides no specifics (which plate, who voted, or when) and therefore is unverified. There is no single, universally recognized authority that names a lone 'best specialty plate in America'—such awards are given by specific organizations or contests and require attribution and sourcing to be true.

claim: "Every engine manufacturer in the United States is now in the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is false. Major engine manufacturers and many smaller engine makers operate facilities and headquarters in multiple states (e.g., Michigan, Indiana, Connecticut, Ohio, Wisconsin, Kentucky), not exclusively in Texas, so it is not true that every U.S. engine manufacturer is now in Texas.

claim: "CDC announces that students may be kept from parents overnight as Ohio sets up COVID-19 FEMA camps."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the CDC announced students may be kept from parents overnight or that Ohio established FEMA 'camps' to detain children. CDC school guidance allows symptomatic students to be temporarily isolated at school until a parent or guardian can pick them up, but it does not authorize overnight detention or separation. Reports of Ohio setting up FEMA camps for COVID-19 detention are misinformation; Ohio did establish temporary medical/field sites for care during surges, not detention facilities for students.

claim: "Youth unemployment in minority communities is about 40 to 45 percent."
rationale: The claim is presented as a blanket statistic but is not accurate as a general statement. Official labor statistics (e.g., U.S. BLS) show youth unemployment for racial/ethnic minority groups varies by age, place and time and is typically in the teens to low-30s percent range on average; while some localities or short periods (like early COVID-19 disruptions) saw much higher rates, 40–45% is not a typical overall figure.

claim: Says 19,000 text messages exchanged between former FBI officials that were "purposely and illegally deleted ... would have explained (the special counsel investigation) hoax."
rationale: The Department of Justice Inspector General and subsequent reporting found roughly 19,000 FBI text messages from the 2016–2017 period were not preserved due to phone replacement/recordkeeping failures, not proven purposeful or illegal deletion. The IG found no evidence that messages were intentionally destroyed, and there is no basis to assert those missing texts would have proven the special counsel investigation was a "hoax"—that conclusion is speculative and unsupported by the available records.

claim: The significant drop in Florida’s unemployment rate is a good economic sign.
rationale: A significant drop in the unemployment rate is often interpreted as a positive sign, but it is not automatically so. The unemployment rate can fall for benign reasons (more jobs) or for concerning reasons (people leaving the labor force, discouraged workers, out‑migration, or declines in labor force participation), so the claim is overly broad without supporting context.

claim: Proposed fast-track legislation allows presidents to "easily use a future trade deal to override our domestic financial rules."
rationale: Fast-track (Trade Promotion Authority) gives the president negotiating leverage and requires Congress to vote up-or-down on implementing legislation, but it does not let the president unilaterally override existing U.S. financial laws or regulations. Any binding changes to domestic law normally require Congress to pass implementing statutes, though a future trade agreement could include provisions that prompt legislative change or international dispute mechanisms that put pressure on domestic rules.

claim: What Republicans call the "death tax" is the estate tax "on the ultra wealthy" which, in 2016, was paid by only "two out of every 1,000 people."
rationale: Republicans commonly refer to the federal estate tax as the "death tax," and the tax is structured with a very large exemption so it effectively only applies to very large estates. In 2016 only about 0.2% of decedents — roughly two out of every 1,000 deaths — had estates large enough to owe the federal estate tax, according to IRS and Tax Policy Center estimates.

claim: The federal deficit is "growing."
rationale: The statement is too general to be judged true: whether the federal deficit is "growing" depends on the specific time period and measure (nominal dollars vs percent of GDP). Federal deficits have fluctuated substantially in recent years—spiking during the COVID pandemic and then moving up or down in subsequent fiscal years—so a blanket claim that the deficit is currently "growing" is not universally supportable without a timeframe.

claim: "Pope Francis says covid vaccine will now be required to enter heaven."
rationale: This claim is false. Pope Francis has publicly encouraged COVID-19 vaccination as an act of solidarity and a moral responsibility, but he has never said that a vaccine is required to enter heaven; no official Vatican teaching links access to heaven or salvation to vaccination status. The statement appears to be a misrepresentation or satirical fabrication.

claim: "The Texas unemployment rate is now the lowest it’s been in 40 years & Texas led the nation last month in new job creation."
rationale: I cannot verify the timing of “now” or “last month” with available data; the claim requires current, month-specific Bureau of Labor Statistics and Texas Workforce Commission figures. Texas has occasionally had very low unemployment and large monthly job gains, so the statement could be true for a specific month, but as stated it’s unverified and too specific without a date or source.

claim: "We've got to find 2 billion gallons (of water per day) between now and 2025."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as given: there is no widely documented national or widely cited policy goal that requires "finding 2 billion gallons of water per day by 2025." The claim lacks attribution (which jurisdiction, for what use) and no authoritative agency or plan uses that exact target, so as presented it is not verifiable and likely false.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: There is no evidence Fauci served on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years, nor does he currently serve on the board of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Fauci is a long‑time federal official (Director of NIAID and presidential adviser) who has collaborated with or received funding from external foundations, but he has not been a board member of those foundations.

claim: Says Gov Tony Evers’ administration deemed dentists non-essential
rationale: During the early COVID-19 response Gov.
