Tony Evers' administration issued guidance to postpone non‑urgent or elective dental procedures to conserve PPE and limit virus spread, but it did not categorically label all dentists as 'non‑essential.' Emergency and urgent dental care remained permitted, so the claim that the administration deemed dentists non‑essential is misleading.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: There is no credible record of the CDC director making a blanket statement that 75% of COVID deaths occurred in people with at least four comorbidities. CDC data do show that most COVID-19 deaths list one or more underlying conditions, but the specific claim about '75%' and 'at least four' comorbidities appears to be a misquote or misinterpretation of cause-of-death reporting.

claim: Says with "Gov. Chris Christie and bipartisan reformers" New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years."
rationale: The claim is vague and not verifiable as stated because it provides no specific time period or job-growth metric. New Jersey employment gains fluctuated during Chris Christie’s tenure and while there were periods of strong hiring, BLS state data do not support a clear, unqualified claim that New Jersey experienced "the most job growth in 11 years" attributable to Christie and bipartisan reformers without specifying the exact interval and measure.

claim: "We have more coal reserves in the United States than they have oil reserves in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: U.S. recoverable coal reserves (on the order of a few hundred billion short tons) contain substantially more energy than Saudi Arabia's proven oil reserves (around 260–270 billion barrels) when converted to an energy-equivalent basis. Using standard energy-content conversions (coal BTU per ton vs BTU per barrel of oil) yields a coal energy total several times larger than Saudi oil reserves.

claim: "If the Republicans were the majority, (Rep. Barton) would have actually the gavel and the chairmanship."
rationale: The claim states as a certainty that Rep. Barton would hold the gavel and chairmanship if Republicans were the majority, but whether any individual becomes a committee chair depends on specific factors (which Barton, which committee, seniority and the majority party’s internal selections). Often the ranking minority member becomes chair when control flips, but it is not automatic and requires the majority party to elect them. Without identifying the committee and timeframe, the asserted certainty is unsupported.

claim: "At the time that (Medicare Part D) was passed (it) was actually less popular than the Affordable Care Act, according to the polls."
rationale: Contemporaneous national polls around the March 2010 passage of the Affordable Care Act generally showed low approval and more opposition than support. Polling around the 2003 passage of Medicare Part D showed mixed-to-moderately favorable views (especially among seniors) rather than systematically lower popularity than the ACA at its passage. Therefore the claim that Part D was actually less popular than the ACA at the times they were passed is not supported by the overall polling picture.

claim: "A DWI costs $17,000."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute single-dollar cost but DWI (DUI) expenses vary widely by jurisdiction and case details. Typical estimates for a first offense including fines, attorney fees, towing, ignition interlock, and long-term insurance increases often fall in the range of several thousand to tens of thousands, so $17,000 can be a plausible example but is not a universally true fixed cost.

claim: "Half the workforce in the country may have just been idled" by coronavirus.
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsupported exaggeration. Even at the COVID-19 peak many countries saw sharp increases in unemployment and temporary layoffs, but nowhere was half of a national workforce documented as idled; official labor statistics (e.g., peak unemployment rates and counts of unemployed or furloughed workers) are far below 50% of the workforce. The claim also fails to define 'the country', the time frame, or what 'idled' means (unemployed, furloughed, unable to work), further weakening it.

claim: The projected revenue from the Mayweather/Pacquiao fight is "larger than the annual GDP of 29 different countries."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented. Reported projected revenues for the Mayweather–Pacquiao fight varied (commonly cited in the ~$600–$700 million range), and while many very small countries have GDPs under that level, whether the fight exceeded the annual GDP of exactly 29 countries depends on which revenue estimate and which year's GDP data are used; there is no clear authoritative source confirming the precise count of 29.

claim: "If Trump had just put his father’s money in a mutual fund ... he’d have $8 billion."
rationale: This is not accurate — plausible estimates of the amounts Fred Trump transferred to Donald and historical mutual-fund (S&P 500‑type) returns would not compound to $8 billion. A $1 million windfall invested in the 1970s would grow to tens or low hundreds of millions today, and even the reported cumulative family transfers (hundreds of millions over decades) are unlikely to reach $8 billion under normal market returns without additional large contributions or implausibly high sustained returns.

claim: Israel's per capita income "is greater than probably three-fourths of the rest of the world."
rationale: Israel is a high‑income OECD country whose per‑capita income consistently ranks well above the global median, placing it within the top quartile of countries by standard measures (GDP per capita or GNI per capita). Given the large number of low‑ and middle‑income countries worldwide, Israel’s per‑person income is higher than roughly three‑quarters of other countries in typical international datasets.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The claim is overly absolute and incorrect: over the past two decades France has at times disagreed with U.S. policy but has also repeatedly supported and cooperated with the United States on major foreign-policy actions. Examples include French participation in NATO operations in Afghanistan, leading a coalition role in the 2011 Libya intervention alongside U.S. goals, and close counterterrorism and sanctions coordination on Russia and other issues. Occasional policy disagreements do not mean the French have not 'stood by' the U.S. at all in the last 20 years.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentage but provides no timeframe or source, so it cannot be verified as stated. While the private sector often accounts for the majority of net job growth in Virginia, the exact share varies by period and data source and is not reliably known to be exactly 90% without specifying the dates and source.

claim: "Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have changed their positions (on the Iraq war withdrawal) to follow Chris Dodd."
rationale: This claim is not supported by the historical record: Barack Obama consistently opposed the 2003 Iraq invasion and campaigned on a phased withdrawal, so he did not “change” his position to follow Chris Dodd. Hillary Clinton did shift from her 2002 vote for the war to supporting a withdrawal timetable during the 2007–08 campaign, but that shift was widely attributed to political pressure, public opinion, and the dynamics of the Democratic primary rather than evidence that she and Obama followed Dodd specifically. There is no clear evidence that both altered their stances in deference to Dodd.

claim: Ninety-six percent of failing schools are spending above $8,400, the average annual per student expenditure, and 26 percent spend considerably more than that.
rationale: I could not find any authoritative source that supports the precise figures given. While national per‑pupil spending has been around $8,000–$12,000 depending on year, definitions of “failing schools” vary by state and no comprehensive study shows 96% of such schools spend above the national average or that 26% spend “considerably more.” The claim likely misstates or cherry‑picks data without context.

claim: "The United States ended slavery around the world, and maybe we should get some credit for that, too."
rationale: The United States did not end slavery around the world. The U.S. abolished slavery domestically via the Civil War and the 13th Amendment (1865), but abolition in other countries was driven earlier or independently—most notably Britain’s 19th-century abolition and global suppression of the slave trade—and many nations abolished slavery on their own timelines. While the U.S. later supported international human-rights norms, the claim that the U.S. ended global slavery is an overstatement.

claim: Gov. Kitzhaber oversaw creation of the Oregon driver card law "behind closed doors without allowing any input from citizens who represent the public interest."
rationale: The Oregon driver card was created through legislation and administrative processes involving the state legislature, DMV, and advocacy groups, not solely by Governor Kitzhaber in secret. The bill was debated and passed through the normal legislative process with public hearings and stakeholder involvement before being signed by the governor.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it "can't build a factory in a non-union state."
rationale: The NLRB did not tell Boeing it categorically "can't build a factory in a non-union state." The NLRB filed a complaint alleging Boeing committed unfair labor practices in moving work to non-union South Carolina and sought remedial relief, but it did not issue a blanket prohibition on building in non-union states and courts later constrained the NLRB's remedies.

claim: The Internal Revenue Service spent $60,000 on a "Star Trek" training video.
rationale: This claim is a misleading simplification. Fact-checkers and procurement records show the material in question was a short, tongue-in-cheek training/parody produced by a contractor and not an official 'Star Trek' production licensed from the franchise, and the commonly cited $60,000 number was mischaracterized (it reflected contract or aggregated costs rather than a single licensed 'Star Trek' video purchase). There is no evidence the IRS bought an official Star Trek training video for $60,000.

claim: "Trump just gave a $12 billion bailout to farmers hurt by his failed tariffs. This will cost every household in the U.S. $95 … Trump is borrowing the money from China since his tax cuts blew a trillion dollar hole in the deficit."
rationale: It is true the Trump administration announced about $12 billion in 2018 aid to farmers hurt by tariffs, but the statement that it "will cost every household $95" is a simplistic per-household division and misleading because federal spending is covered from the general budget and debt rather than a direct household charge. The claim that "Trump is borrowing the money from China" is inaccurate in its literal sense: the Treasury issues debt to a broad market of buyers and while China holds a large stock of U.S. Treasuries, it does not directly fund specific programs; likewise, tax cuts did increase projected deficits but the phrasing "blew a trillion dollar hole" is imprecise.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Critical Race Theory as an advanced legal and academic framework has been adopted wholesale into every K–12 school in Virginia. K–12 curricula sometimes include lessons on race, history, and systemic racism, but that is not the same as formal CRT instruction and curricula vary by district. High-profile state-level debates and policies in Virginia have also focused on restricting rather than uniformly implementing CRT in public schools.

claim: "Of our 98,000 teachers who are K-12, over 53,000 of those teachers today are over 50 years old."
rationale: The claim provides a precise count and percentage (53,000 of 98,000 ≈ 54%) but gives no named jurisdiction or source, so it cannot be verified as stated. National and many state-level K–12 workforce reports (e.g., NCES and state education reports) generally show a smaller share of teachers aged 50+ than 54%, so the blanket claim is unsupported without additional context or evidence.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Bruce Starr directly 'voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment' as an incontrovertible fact. While Starr has voted on bills affecting unemployment policy, attributing a precise number of people removed from benefits to a single vote is a specific causal claim that requires official estimates and context (which are not provided).

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: Declassified CIA files and contemporary reporting show that after Eartha Kitt’s January 1968 anti‑Vietnam remark at a White House luncheon, Lady Bird Johnson and the White House requested background information, and intelligence agencies (including the CIA and FBI) collected material on Kitt. The requests from the First Lady’s office prompted official attention that contributed to Kitt being investigated and effectively blacklisted in the aftermath.

claim: Says Cracker Barrel’s name has racist origins and its logo depicts a whip.
rationale: This claim is false. The restaurant was named for the 'cracker barrel' found in old country stores and company history and branding point to that folk-cultural image rather than an explicitly racist origin; the etymology of the word 'cracker' is complex and contested but not definitively tied to a racist 'whip' origin in this brand's naming. The Cracker Barrel logo shows an older man seated by a barrel and a rocking chair, not a whip.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: The statement is a broad, future-facing assertion with no specifics or evidence. While some governments perform targeted interception under legal authority or have run surveillance programs, there is no credible proof that any government is imminently planning to universally 'infiltrate' all personal text messages. The claim therefore is unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: "After years of 5.5 percent average tuition increases, we now have a two-year tuition freeze for the first time in the history of the UW System."
rationale: The claim combines an unspecified "5.5 percent average" increase and a sweeping historical claim that a current two-year freeze is the first in UW System history; both parts are unsupported as stated. The UW System has existed for decades and has had periods of freezes, rollbacks, or very small increases at various times, and the 5.5% figure lacks a defined timeframe, so the blanket assertion is misleading or false.

claim: "Obamacare … means that for up to 20 million Americans, they will lose the insurance they currently have, the insurance that they like and they want to keep."
rationale: The claim overstates the impact. While millions of people (mainly in the individual and some small-group markets) received cancellation notices because some plans did not meet ACA standards, mainstream estimates from HHS, the CBO and independent analysts put the number affected in the low millions rather than as high as 20 million. The statement therefore exaggerates and generalizes beyond the best available estimates.

claim: "Under the Obama plan . . . all the health care in this country is eventually going to be run by the government."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act (the 'Obama plan') did not convert the U.S. health-care system into government-run care; it preserved private insurance, created regulated marketplaces, subsidies, and expanded Medicaid in many states. No provision in the law mandated a government takeover or a universal government-run system, and a federal 'public option' was not included in the final law.

claim: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not spoken or appeared publicly for several weeks.
rationale: The claim gives no date range and is unverifiable as presented; prominent public figures like Dr. Anthony Fauci typically have intermittent media appearances, interviews, and public statements. Without a specific timeframe it is not accurate to assert he "has not spoken or appeared publicly for several weeks."

claim: Says Gov. Chris Christie’s "poll ratings have been going up."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated because no timeframe or poll source is given. Chris Christie’s approval and poll numbers have fluctuated over time (periods of rises and declines), so a blanket statement that his "poll ratings have been going up" cannot be confirmed without a specific poll series and dates.

claim: "The health care price tag for childhood obesity in Georgia is $2.4 billion annually and rising."
rationale: I could not find an authoritative public-health estimate confirming that childhood obesity in Georgia currently generates $2.4 billion in annual health-care costs. Published cost studies of obesity often report different numbers, measure lifetime or adult obesity costs, or give national totals, so the specific claim appears unverified or conflates categories.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: The claim frames a 50/50 public-private split as clearly 'much better' than most other U.S. arena deals, but public shares for arena financing vary widely and many recent projects have had public shares at or below 50%. Some projects have required larger public subsidies, but many others relied on comparable or greater private contributions, so 50/50 is not demonstrably 'much better than most' without a specified sample or timeframe.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: Governor Roy Cooper has vetoed multiple budget bills and some legislation that included teacher pay provisions, but it is not true that he vetoed every single teacher pay raise the legislature ever passed. Over his tenure there have been teacher pay increases enacted by different means (including negotiated budgets, overrides, or bills that became law) rather than a universal pattern of him vetoing every raise.

claim: "We spent $3-million of your money to study the DNA of bears."
rationale: The claim is unverified and too vague to be treated as fact: it does not identify who “we” refers to, the timeframe, or the specific program that allegedly spent $3 million. Without a named agency, appropriation, or budget line, there is no reliable evidence to confirm that exactly $3 million of taxpayer money was spent specifically 'to study the DNA of bears.' Such funding for wildlife genetics research does occur, but the blanket statement is unsupported as presented.

claim: "Atlanta just lost 75% of its police force"
rationale: There are no credible reports that Atlanta lost 75% of its police force. While the Atlanta Police Department has experienced resignations, retirements, and localized staffing shortages at various times, those losses have been far smaller than three-quarters of the force and would have been widely documented if true.

claim: "Victory! Republicans by 2 to 1 vote to endorse Mark Neumann on first ballot at GOP convention."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that Republicans endorsed Mark Neumann by a 2-to-1 vote on the first ballot at a GOP convention. The assertion lacks a date, state, or source and does not match readily recalled, verifiable reports from known Mark Neumann endorsement events in my knowledge base.

claim: "An 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronts a Russian soldier telling him to go back to his country."
rationale: I cannot find reliable, verifiable evidence tying a documented incident to the specific claim that an 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronted a Russian soldier telling him to 'go back to his country.' While short, emotional clips circulated from the war have shown children confronting soldiers, many of those items were unverified or misattributed and ages/contexts are often uncertain. Without a specific source, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Ten percent of violent deaths in the U.S. each year are due to strangulation."
rationale: Available U.S. mortality and crime data show that deaths from strangulation/suffocation are a small minority of violent deaths. Firearms and suicides make up the largest shares of violent and injury deaths, and homicide-by-strangulation comprises far less than 10% of homicides. Therefore the claim that 10% of violent deaths are due to strangulation is not supported.

claim: Says Quaden Bayles committed suicide.
rationale: There are no credible reports that Quaden Bayles committed suicide. After his 2020 viral bullying story, claims of his death circulated as hoaxes and were debunked by mainstream outlets and family statements; a suicide would have been widely reported by reputable news organizations.

claim: "National Guard doctors find hospitals empty of COVID patients."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some National Guard medical teams reported seeing few or no COVID patients at particular facilities or at certain times, other Guard units and civilian hospitals—especially in COVID hotspots—were treating large numbers of COVID patients. Nationwide reporting and official data show substantial local variation rather than a uniform absence of COVID patients in hospitals.

claim: Says "if current trends continue, by 2040, one out of three Texas workers will not have a high school diploma."
rationale: Historical and projected educational-attainment trends show the share of adults without a high school diploma has been declining, and high school graduation rates in Texas have improved; current data show far fewer than 33% of Texas workers lack a diploma. No mainstream demographic or labor projection predicts that one in three Texas workers will lack a high school diploma by 2040 if current trends continue.

claim: Says when Rhode Island Lottery was proposed, "state residents were enticed to vote for it with the promise that the money would be used for education."
rationale: When the Rhode Island Lottery was put to voters (approved by referendum in 1974), proponents campaigned that proceeds would support public education, and that promise was a central argument used to win voter approval. This messaging mirrors the common pattern in other states' lotteries at the time.

claim: The typical anglerfish is seven feet long.
rationale: Most anglerfish species, especially the deep‑sea ones people typically think of, are quite small (often only a few inches to about a foot for females), and males are tiny parasites. While some related bottom‑dwelling species called monkfish/goosefish can reach several feet, a typical anglerfish is not seven feet long.

claim: Says "New Jersey’s $1 billion horse racing industry … employs 13,000 individuals and ensures the preservation of 176,000 acres of horse farmland."
rationale: The three specific figures read like an industry promotional claim and are not corroborated by independent state agricultural or labor data. 176,000 acres devoted to horse farmland in New Jersey and 13,000 employees appear implausible given the state's scale and typical agricultural statistics; the $1 billion figure may reflect broader economic impact estimates rather than direct receipts. Without a clear independent source and definitions (direct vs. indirect jobs, what counts as ‘horse farmland’), the precise claim is not supported.

claim: Says Dick Cheney "supported gay marriage sooner" than Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Hillary Clinton publicly announced her support for same-sex marriage on June 11, 2013. Dick Cheney is known to have privately supported LGBTQ rights and his daughter’s marriage, but there is no clear public record showing Cheney endorsed same-sex marriage earlier than Clinton’s June 2013 public statement.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible record or major news reporting that Senator Lindsey Graham has threatened to formally change his party registration to Democrat as leverage to force Republicans to abandon Trump. Graham has at times criticized Trump or broken with him politically, but he has not publicly announced a conditional party switch of the sort described in the claim.

claim: Says the case of a Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings exposes a double standard in the case against Kentucky clerk Kim Davis.
rationale: The claim misstates well‑known comparisons around the Kim Davis case. Contemporary reporting and legal records describe public officials who refused to participate in issuing or performing same‑sex marriages after Obergefell, not a widely reported Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings to expose a double standard. There is no clear, documented instance matching the claim as stated.

claim: "I've either balanced every budget or we turned back a surplus."
rationale: The statement is unverified and unlikely as phrased because no recent major elected official is documented to have 'balanced every budget' or 'turned back a surplus' in every budget cycle. In the U.S. federal case, balanced budgets and surpluses are rare (notably only in the late 1990s), and most administrations experienced deficits; state and local budgets vary widely and are set with legislative involvement. Without specifying who 'I' is, the time period, and the jurisdiction, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "The unemployment rate among (the) non-college-educated is well into the double digits in America. It's 4 percent or 5 percent for people who have college degrees."
rationale: Recent BLS data and typical labor-market measures show that most groups without a college degree have unemployment rates in the single digits, not "well into the double digits"; only certain subgroups or brief recession periods (e.g., early COVID-19) saw >10%. Meanwhile, unemployment for workers with a bachelor’s degree has generally been lower, often in the ~2–5% range, so the 4–5% figure for college grads can be reasonable but the first part of the claim is inaccurate as a general statement.

claim: Ebola is "incredibly contagious," "very transmissible" and "easy to catch."
rationale: Ebola is not "incredibly contagious" in the sense of airborne viruses; it requires direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids of a symptomatic person, contaminated surfaces, or contaminated needles. Transmission is highest in close-contact settings (caregiving, unsafe funerals, or healthcare without PPE), so it is less transmissible than common airborne diseases like measles or influenza.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: Academic and government analyses consistently find that voter fraud in the U.S. and in Texas is extremely rare but not literally non‑existent. Texas has had documented and prosecuted instances of absentee ballot fraud, registration and voting irregularities, so the absolute statement that studies show it is non‑existent is incorrect.

claim: "The $5 billion website for Obamacare … never worked. Still doesn't work."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: HealthCare.gov did suffer major technical failures at its October 2013 launch, but engineers fixed many problems and the site was functioning for enrollments by early 2014. The commonly cited development cost for HealthCare.gov was about $1 billion (not $5 billion), though total federal/state IT and implementation spending related to the ACA was larger and varies by accounting. Saying it "never worked" and "still doesn't work" is false based on subsequent fixes and successful enrollments.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that Rep. Sean Duffy was specifically among seven 'Tea Party freshmen' who personally spent an average of $15,000 apiece on cars. Reports that made this claim appear to conflate campaign or official vehicle-related expenses, use small selective samples, or mischaracterize campaign finance entries rather than documented personal car purchases. Without clear campaign-finance or personal-asset records showing Duffy was part of such a seven-member group, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "When the national debt reaches $15 trillion, it means that U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio will reach 99.7 percent of our debt and this is $47,900 for every living American."
rationale: The per‑person figure (~$47,900) is roughly correct if you divide $15 trillion by a U.S. population around 313–314 million, but the statement that $15 trillion automatically implies a debt‑to‑GDP ratio of 99.7% is not generally true—it only holds if nominal GDP is about $15.05 trillion. Debt‑to‑GDP depends on the current GDP and population at that time, so the claim presented as an absolute fact is misleading.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: Texas automatic admission policies are based primarily on class rank (the top percentage rule) and do not universally mandate passing Algebra II statewide as a condition for automatic admission. While some institutions and certain admission tracks or programs emphasize Algebra II or require completion of more rigorous graduation plans (like the Distinguished Level of Achievement), there is no single statewide rule that all high school graduates must pass Algebra II to qualify for automatic admission to Texas public universities.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees, including the House Intelligence Committee, have longstanding authority under House rules to conduct investigations and to hold classified or confidential sessions behind closed doors. Many legal scholars and parliamentary interpretations have concluded that a formal floor vote is not strictly required to open an impeachment inquiry, though members of the minority disputed the process and sought a floor vote.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Nancy Pelosi was drunk and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Viral posts and clips making this claim have been debunked or shown to lack context; available footage and official records show no documented removal or disciplinary action matching that description.

claim: "...Over 30 years, federal spending on education has grown by 375 percent, but test scores remain flat."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the often-cited '375 percent' increase typically uses nominal federal education dollars over an unspecified 30-year span, and when adjusted for inflation and measured per pupil the increase is much smaller. In addition, national test data (NAEP) show long-term gains in reading and math across several decades, though progress has plateaued in some recent years and for some groups, so it is incorrect to say scores have been uniformly 'flat.'

claim: When President Donald Trump walked across Lafayette Square to a church, he held the Bible upside down.
rationale: Contemporaneous photos and video from multiple angles, as reviewed by major news organizations and fact-checkers, show President Trump holding a closed Bible with its cover oriented outward, not upside down. Independent analyses concluded the claim that he held it upside down is incorrect, though certain single-frame images caused initial confusion about orientation.

claim: "Pads and tampons (are) still taxed when Viagra and Rogaine are not."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. Sales tax treatment for menstrual products, prescription drugs like Viagra, and hair‑loss treatments like Rogaine varies by jurisdiction and by whether a product is prescription or OTC; in some places pads and tampons are still taxed but many jurisdictions have removed that tax, and Rogaine (OTC) may be taxed while prescription medicines are often exempt. Because tax rules differ widely, the blanket claim that pads/tampons are taxed while Viagra and Rogaine are not is inaccurate.

claim: "The nine-day deer hunt contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state of Wisconsin."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the nine-day firearm deer hunt by itself delivers more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state government. Published studies and surveys that produce figures in the billion-dollar range refer to total hunting-related economic activity or expenditures (often across all seasons and activities), not direct state revenues from a single nine-day season; direct license, fee and tax receipts attributable to the season are far smaller. The claim conflates broad economic impact with direct state revenue and misattributes the total to just the nine-day hunt.

claim: "Eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit" from Wisconsin's manufacturing and agriculture tax credit.
rationale: There is no verifiable public evidence that exactly eleven individuals each earning over $30 million received a $22 million Manufacturing and Agriculture tax credit in Wisconsin. The MAC is an entity-level credit claimed by businesses (including pass-throughs), and public reporting typically shows credits by business entities or aggregate recipients, not individual salaries; the claim appears to conflate entity credits with individual incomes and gives precise numbers without a cited source.

claim: "There are 63 million abortions a year in this country."
rationale: The claim is implausible: no single country reports anywhere near 63 million abortions in a year. Global estimates of annual induced abortions are on the order of tens of millions total, while major countries' national totals are far lower (for example, the United States reports under one million annually in recent years).

claim: "COVID ends next Wednesday."
rationale: There is no evidence or authoritative process that would cause COVID-19 to definitively 'end' on a specific upcoming Wednesday. Infectious diseases like SARS-CoV-2 do not cease globally on a fixed date, and public health agencies have not announced any such event.

claim: "Donald Trump is the first president in modern history (who) did not start a new war."
rationale: Several post‑World War II presidents did not initiate new major wars (for example Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter), so Trump is not the first in 'modern history' to avoid starting a new war. The claim also hinges on ambiguous terms—what counts as 'starting' a war and the period defined as 'modern history'—which many accounts treat differently.

claim: "I said two years ago that the Fannie and Freddie thing was a very serious problem and we had to work on it."
rationale: The statement claims the speaker warned "two years ago" that Fannie and Freddie were a very serious problem, but no speaker, date, or supporting citation is provided. Without a verifiable timestamped quote or record showing the speaker made that specific claim exactly two years prior, the assertion cannot be substantiated. In absence of concrete evidence, the claim is treated as false.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: The 2015 Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA) contained staggered, time-limited restrictions on specific activities and equipment, not a single blanket expiration in seven years. Even after particular limits lapse, Iran would still be bound by the Non‑Proliferation Treaty and IAEA safeguards, and the agreement extended its "breakout time" for obtaining enough fissile material. Therefore it is incorrect to say the deal simply expires in seven years and frees Iran to build nuclear weapons unilaterally.

claim: "Democrats oppose any effort to secure our border."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping absolute that is false: Democrats do not oppose every measure to secure the border. Many Democrats support border security investments such as increased personnel, surveillance technology, ports-of-entry improvements, and targeted enforcement, while opposing particular policies (for example, a large border wall or family-separation practices) or preferring different approaches and accompanying immigration reforms.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The claim presents a precise "minimum" of $900 million for Atlanta's infrastructure needs without specifying scope, timeframe, or source, and there is no single authoritative figure that matches that exact, context-free number. Estimates of infrastructure needs for Atlanta vary by agency and project and are typically reported as multi-year capital plans or ranges rather than a single undisputed minimum.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous because it gives no date; it is therefore not a reliable standing fact. While many U.S. Attorney posts were initially held by interim appointees when Obama took office, there are 93 U.S. Attorneys and Obama nominated and secured confirmation for many during his first year, so saying 'more than half remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama' as a general claim is inaccurate without a specific timeframe.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: Recent national analyses (Census American Community Survey and Kaiser Family Foundation summaries) show Missouri’s child uninsured rate around the national average and well below the handful of states that consistently rank highest (e.g., Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma). Missouri is not typically listed among the states with the very highest rates of uninsured children.

claim: The FEMA health care workers replacing the noncompliant nurses and doctors are NOT required to get vaccinated via the CDC."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The CDC issues public-health guidance but does not itself "require" vaccinations; however FEMA personnel are federal employees under DHS and during the COVID-19 response were generally subject to federal vaccine requirements and agency/occupational health policies. Deployed medical staff (including USPHS officers and many contractors) routinely must meet agency or occupational vaccination rules, so it is incorrect to state categorically that FEMA health care workers are not required to be vaccinated.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "has directed that tens of millions of City of Milwaukee tax dollars be used for the construction of a downtown trolley at the expense of: health and public safety; repair and replacement of public infrastructure; public education; and, job creation and economic development."
rationale: While Mayor Tom Barrett supported Milwaukee's downtown streetcar (The Hop), the project was financed through a mix of federal, state, and local sources rather than solely by the mayor directing 'tens of millions' of city tax dollars. City budgets and capital commitments require Common Council approval, and there is no clear evidence that the streetcar funding directly forced cuts to health and public safety, infrastructure repair, education, or job-creation budgets as claimed.

claim: Mercedes-Benz USA  moving its headquarters to Atlanta will create at least 800 jobs.
rationale: When Mercedes-Benz announced its move of Mercedes‑Benz USA headquarters to the Atlanta area, company and state officials publicly projected the relocation would result in about 800 new jobs. Multiple contemporary news reports and the company press release cited that figure as the expected job creation tied to the move. The statement reflects the official projection tied to the relocation.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: The claim cannot be substantiated as stated because it gives no specific years, subgroup definitions, or source for the data. Graduation rates are reported annually by district and by racial/ethnic subgroup, and without precise timeframes it is not possible to verify that Beloit's minority rate rose from below Milwaukee and Madison to above 80% during the superintendent's tenure. Absent cited, year-by-year data, the assertion is unproven.

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: Oregon Health Plan (the state's Medicaid program) operates with clinical eligibility rules, prior-authorization requirements, and a historical prioritized list of services that can limit or deny procedures even if they would otherwise be covered. In practice OHP has denied or delayed covered procedures when patients do not meet specific medical criteria or program conditions, which is commonly described as rationing under certain circumstances.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: New Jersey does rank highly on many common measures of school segregation (e.g., black-white dissimilarity, isolation/exposure indices) and is frequently cited in studies as among the more segregated states. However the phrase "by any measure" is overstated: rankings vary by metric, population subgroup, grade level, and year, and not every segregation index or study places New Jersey at the very top.

claim: "Biden concedes 6 million votes."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Joe Biden "conceded 6 million votes." Concession is a statement by a losing candidate; Biden won the 2020 presidential election and did not concede to that effect, and no credible reports say he relinquished or admitted losing 6 million votes. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or unsupported assertion.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The claim lacks a specified year or metric and does not match major compilations of state rankings for women in elected office (such as Rutgers CAWP), which typically place Georgia in the low 40s rather than 49th. Rankings also vary depending on whether the measure is state legislature representation, federal delegation, or combined offices, so a blanket '49th' rank is unlikely to be accurate without context.

claim: Newt Gingrich has been a proponent of selecting a president by popular vote instead of the Electoral College.
rationale: Newt Gingrich has generally defended the Electoral College and spoken against abolishing it or switching to a direct national popular vote. In public comments over many years he has framed the Electoral College as an element of federalism that protects smaller states and has criticized efforts to replace it with a pure popular vote.

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: This statement is an overgeneralization. AMBER Alerts are issued by law enforcement based on established criteria (confirmed abduction, imminent danger, and sufficient descriptive information) rather than the child's race; although there have been documented concerns about racial disparities in media attention and some alert use, there is no evidence that Milwaukee systematically issues alerts only for white children and not for Black children.

claim: "Coca-Cola has lost $4 bil in market value as people are boycotting Coke for their ‘try to be less White’ statement."
rationale: The claim links a $4 billion market-cap loss directly to a boycott over Coca‑Cola's leaked training remark about 'try to be less white.' Major fact‑checks and market reports found no evidence that a coordinated boycott caused a $4 billion loss; stock market capitalization fluctuates for many reasons and any small dip after the leak was temporary and not demonstrably caused by a boycott. The training video did contain the quoted phrase, but the asserted causal $4 billion loss is unsubstantiated.

claim: "There's not a major bill I know with Hillary's name on it."
rationale: There is no widely recognized major federal statute commonly known by Hillary Clinton's name. While Clinton sponsored and championed policy proposals (for example on health care, children's issues, and foreign policy) there is no landmark law that is popularly titled as a 'Hillary' bill in U.S. legislative history. The statement is accurate under the ordinary meaning of 'major bill with Hillary's name on it.'

claim: The United States "is the only major country that taxes its own exports."
rationale: This is false: the U.S. Constitution bars federal export taxes, and the U.S. does not impose a general federal tax on exported goods. By contrast many other major countries levy export duties or taxes on specific commodities (for example on certain agricultural products, minerals, or energy exports), so the U.S. is not uniquely taxing its exports.

claim: The president's health care proposals will cause "most Americans to have their premiums increased, not decreased, and hundreds of millions of people lose their current insurance coverage."
rationale: The claim is vague and implausible as stated: policy effects depend entirely on the specific proposal, and independent analyses (such as CBO and other nonpartisan models) produce widely differing estimates. Past credible projections of large coverage losses from major repeal plans have been in the tens of millions, not "hundreds of millions," and there is no consensus finding that "most Americans" would face higher premiums under a single, identifiable presidential proposal. Without naming the exact proposal and model assumptions, the sweeping numeric claim is unsupported.

claim: "The vast majority of our public school students are receiving less state support than their private voucher peers."
rationale: The claim is misleading: voucher programs typically enroll a small share of students and the per-student voucher amount in most jurisdictions is equal to or less than the average public per-pupil funding, not greater. Because most students remain in public schools and public per-pupil funding is generally higher than voucher payments, it is unlikely that a 'vast majority' of public students receive less state support than their private voucher peers.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated: public reporting on Georgia’s criminal sentencing reforms indicates the state has realized some savings and projected future savings, but there is no widely corroborated, stand-alone figure of exactly $20 million tied to 'changes in criminal sentencing' without a specified year or program. Different reports cite varying amounts (projections vs. realized savings) depending on the reform, time period, and whether costs avoided or budgetary savings are counted.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting or public record of an incident in which a babysitter on crystal meth ate a 3-month-old baby. An event this extreme would generate wide, corroborated media coverage, criminal charges, and forensic documentation, none of which are known. The claim reads like a sensational or viral rumor rather than a substantiated fact.

claim: An anonymous e-mail says that Hillary Clinton advocates communism.
rationale: Anonymous chain e‑mails and forwarded messages alleging that Hillary Clinton advocates communism have circulated widely, particularly around election cycles. The statement only asserts that an anonymous e‑mail makes that claim, which is consistent with known patterns of political misinformation and rumor e‑mails.

claim: "Sen. Obama's chair in New Hampshire is a lobbyist. He lobbies for the drug companies."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the person serving as Barack Obama's campaign chair in New Hampshire was a pharmaceutical industry lobbyist. Public reports and records about Obama's New Hampshire campaign leadership do not identify a named chair who lobbied for drug companies, and the claim appears to conflate or misidentify individuals.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: The claim greatly understates likely Texas combat fatalities: total U.S. military KIA in post‑9/11 wars numbers in the several thousands, and Texas—being the second largest state with large active-duty and reserve populations and many military installations—accounts for a substantially larger share than ~250. Multiple public tallies by state show populous military states typically have several hundred to over a thousand combat deaths, making 250 implausibly low for Texas since 9/11.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan did not "win championships in New York" or win the AFC twice. As New York Jets head coach he took the team to the AFC Championship Game twice (after the 2009–10 and 2010–11 seasons) but lost both games (to the Pittsburgh Steelers and Baltimore Ravens). He never won an AFC conference title or a Super Bowl as a head coach.

claim: Says the CBO said "it's not that people are getting pushed off a plan; it's that people will choose not to buy something they don't like or want."
rationale: There is no clear record of the Congressional Budget Office using that colloquial wording as a direct quote. CBO reports do quantify how many people would remain uninsured or not enroll under policy changes and sometimes distinguish between involuntary loss of coverage and voluntary non‑takeup, but the specific sentence appears to be a paraphrase by another speaker rather than a documented CBO statement.

claim: "The number of uninsured people in Massachusetts is about the same as it was when the mandates were passed in 2006."
rationale: Massachusetts' 2006 health reform (the individual mandate and related programs) produced a large, sustained drop in the number and share of uninsured residents. Current uninsured totals and rates are substantially lower than they were prior to the 2006 reforms, so the number is not "about the same."

claim: Photos show cemeteries and war memorials damaged during George Floyd demonstrations.
rationale: While some monuments and statues were vandalized or removed in the wake of the George Floyd protests, numerous viral photos purporting to show cemeteries or war memorials damaged during those demonstrations have been debunked or shown to be from other times and places. The broad claim that photos show such damage during the George Floyd demonstrations is therefore misleading.

claim: "President Trump marshalled the full resources of our federal government from the outset. He directed us to forge a seamless partnership with governors across America in both political parties."
rationale: The assertion that President Trump marshalled the full resources from the outset and created a seamless, bipartisan partnership with governors is inaccurate. Early federal pandemic response featured testing delays, PPE and ventilator shortages, restrained initial use of the Defense Production Act, and numerous public disputes and supply-competition between the federal government and governors of both parties.

claim: "Why should you get a break for racehorses and not get a break for child care?"
rationale: The question asserts a blanket contrast that racehorses receive a policy "break" while child care does not, which is misleading. Tax and policy treatment vary by jurisdiction and time—many places (including the U.S. federal system) offer child-care tax credits and employer-dependent care benefits, while racehorse owners may receive industry-specific deductions or incentives. Presenting the situation as a universal either/or is therefore inaccurate.

claim: The Biden administration inherited gains of "50,000 jobs a month. We're now finally back to 500,000 jobs a month. We inherited a country where 4,000 people a day were dying from Covid. That's now down 75%."
rationale: The claim mixes and misstates metrics. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show the U.S. was still millions of jobs below pre-pandemic levels when President Biden took office and monthly payroll changes around the transition varied widely (they were not a steady '50,000 jobs a month'); while some months in 2021 did approach or exceed 500,000 jobs, that was not a simple restoration to a single steady monthly pace. Similarly, daily COVID deaths did peak around the 3,000–4,000 range in January 2021 and later fell substantially, but saying they are uniformly 'down 75%' depends on which later date is chosen and oversimplifies the trajectory.

claim: "Whole of Italy goes into quarantine."
rationale: In early March 2020 the Italian government issued a decree extending lockdown measures to the entire country (announced March 9, effective shortly thereafter), imposing stay-at-home orders, travel restrictions, and closure of non-essential activities. Major news outlets and government statements described the measure as putting the whole of Italy into quarantine/lockdown.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Julia Roberts ever made this statement; such a provocative insult by a high-profile actress would have been widely reported by major news outlets and on her verified social accounts but no such coverage or primary source exists. The claim matches patterns of fabricated or satirical quotes that are frequently misattributed to celebrities.

claim: "Greg Casar passed paid sick leave."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading because it lacks context. Greg Casar sponsored and helped enact a paid sick leave ordinance while on the Austin City Council, but he has not enacted a federal paid sick leave law as a member of Congress; saying he 'passed paid sick leave' without specifying level of government implies a broader accomplishment than is accurate.

claim: To abide by Environmental Protection Agency rules when mining or drilling you have "to take caution not to disturb bodies of water barely bigger than a puddle."
rationale: This statement is an exaggeration. EPA/Clean Water Act rules can require permits for discharges or disturbance of certain small streams and wetlands that qualify as “waters of the United States,” but the agency does not categorically restrict activity around every tiny puddle; scope depends on connectivity, site conditions, and legal definitions which have been narrowed by court decisions and regulatory changes.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no verifiable record, transcript, video, or reliable news report showing Keanu Reeves gave a speech beginning with that line. The quotation appears online as an unauthenticated meme or misattribution and has not been corroborated by primary sources or reputable fact-checkers.

claim: President Barack Obama’s latest executive order "mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of ‘respiratory illness.’ "
rationale: There is no Obama executive order that broadly mandates apprehending and detaining Americans merely for showing signs of 'respiratory illness.' U.S. public health law does allow limited quarantine/isolation for specific communicable diseases under defined legal processes, but that is not equivalent to a blanket order authorizing detention for general respiratory symptoms.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no public record that Sen. Sherrod Brown made a binding promise that the very first COVID‑era stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. Brown publicly urged federal investment and said he would work to secure funding for the bridge, but the initial stimulus bills did not include a specific earmark for that project and funding decisions require broader congressional action.

claim: Under a public health care option, 120 million Americans will "lose what they now get from private companies and be forced onto the government-run rolls as businesses decide it is more cost-effective for them to drop coverage."
rationale: The specific claim that 120 million Americans would lose private coverage and be "forced" onto government rolls under a public option is unsupported and implausible. Nonpartisan analyses of typical public-option proposals (e.g., CBO and health-policy research groups) project much smaller shifts from private to public coverage, and a public option is generally voluntary rather than a mandate that would automatically force mass employer drop-off. Employers also face legal, financial, and competitive incentives that make wholesale abandonment of benefits unlikely.

claim: "Mass media destroyed! Blackout for mass arrests event!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or widespread reporting that mass media outlets were destroyed or that a coordinated 'blackout for mass arrests' took place. An event on that scale would be immediately and independently verifiable across many international news organizations and reporters, but no such corroboration exists. The message is vague, lacks specifics, and fits common misinformation patterns designed to provoke alarm.

claim: Says a picture he posted on Facebook of a man posing in front of five decapitated human heads is "one of the subhuman mongrels our president set free."
rationale: The claim provides no verifiable evidence linking the photo or the people pictured to individuals released by any president. Graphic images are frequently misattributed online, and without provenance, identification of the poster, or independent reporting tying the photo to released persons the assertion is unsupported. The dehumanizing caption is an allegation, not a documented fact.

claim: The Republican election platform "was actually written with the help of a former lobbyist for AIG and a former lobbyist for Exxon-Mobil."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated: party platforms are drafted by platform committees and while outside advisers or lobbyists sometimes influence policy, there is no clear, corroborated reporting that a Republican platform was 'actually written' by a former AIG lobbyist and a former ExxonMobil lobbyist. The statement is also ambiguous about which election cycle it refers to, and I could find no reliable evidence tying those specific former lobbyists to authoring a GOP platform.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: The statement 'Jeff Greene can buy anything' is an absolute, hyperbolic claim that is not supportable simply because he owns two mansions. While Greene is a very wealthy real estate investor and does own multiple high-value properties, no individual—regardless of wealth—can literally buy anything due to legal restrictions, unique or non-saleable items, and practical limits. Owning two mansions does not justify the universal claim.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton sold 20 percent of America’s uranium to Russia and then "the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation." Former FBI Director and special counsel Robert Mueller "delivered it."
rationale: The claim conflates and misstates several points. The 2010 Uranium One transaction involved a Russian company acquiring interests that represented about 20% of U.S. uranium production capacity, but the sale was approved through a multi-agency CFIUS process (not unilaterally by Hillary Clinton), there is no evidence the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation, and Robert Mueller had no role in 'delivering' any such funds.

claim: The ACLU didn't call for an investigation (of the Newark police department), they called for an immediate federal monitor.
rationale: The claim is presented categorically but lacks corroborating context or a specific ACLU statement; the ACLU commonly calls for Department of Justice civil‑rights investigations and in some cases federal monitoring. Without a cited press release showing they expressly refused an investigation and only sought an immediate federal monitor, the absolute wording is unsupported. It's therefore likely inaccurate as stated.

claim: Says "Cost of Mueller’s investigation: $3,200,000; Benghazi "investigation": $7,000,000; Trump’s golfing trips: $83,000,000; New debt from Republican tax bill: $1,500,000,000,000."
rationale: The claim mixes roughly accurate and incorrect figures and omits important context. The Special Counsel Mueller office's reported spending was about $32 million, not $3.2 million; the often-cited ~7 million for Benghazi refers to limited committee expenditures or narrow timeframes and undercounts wider congressional oversight costs; estimates of taxpayer costs for Trump's golf/travel vary by timeframe but commonly fall in the tens of millions (reports around $70–80M), and the Republican tax bill was projected to add roughly $1.5 trillion to deficits over 10 years (context: score and time period matters).

claim: Quotes Winston Churchill as saying "Diplomacy is the art of telling people to go to hell in such a way that they ask for directions."
rationale: The quip is widely attributed to Churchill in popular sources, but there is no reliable primary source or appearance in Churchill's collected speeches and writings to confirm he said it. Quotation researchers treat it as apocryphal or misattributed and note that similar lines circulated later and were credited to various authors.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: There is no authoritative, blanket recommendation from regulators or Bath & Body Works that their products must be avoided during pregnancy due to suspected damage to fertility or the unborn child. While some cosmetic ingredients (certain phthalates, some fragrance components) have been studied for possible endocrine or developmental effects in animal or limited human studies, evidence is mixed and risk depends on specific ingredients, concentrations, and exposure. Individual products vary and standard medical advice is to check ingredient lists and consult a healthcare provider about specific concerns.

claim: Old photograph shows a group of women in KKK attire holding a sign that reads "Women of the Democrat Party."
rationale: The specific viral image was doctored: the original historical photograph shows women in Ku Klux Klan robes holding a banner identifying the Klan, not a sign reading 'Women of the Democrat Party.' Fact-checkers and photographic archives have identified the altered text as a later edit used to mislead viewers. The claim that the old photo originally labeled them as 'Women of the Democrat Party' is therefore false.

claim: "In this country, we have a 25 percent dropout rate."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it fails to specify which country, which education level or cohort, the time period, or the exact definition of 'dropout rate'. Dropout rates vary widely across countries and by how the metric is measured, so an unqualified claim of 25% cannot be judged true.

claim: The coronavirus "was constructed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was purposefully constructed at the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Multiple genomic analyses find signatures consistent with natural evolution rather than engineered manipulation, and major scientific bodies and intelligence reviews have reported no direct proof of deliberate laboratory construction.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: Multiple contemporary fact-checks and news reports documented that several public‑employee unions circulated materials claiming Walker's 2011 budget‑repair bill would force workers to pay roughly 12–13% of their incomes for health insurance. Those 12–13% figures were based on misleading calculations (e.g., dividing average family premiums by average wages) and did not reflect how the bill actually structured employee premium contributions, so the specific percentage claim was false or exaggerated for many workers.

claim: "In Minnesota, well over 6,200 election-day registrations from 2008 proved fraudulent."
rationale: Investigations and contemporaneous reporting found no evidence that 'well over 6,200' election-day registrations in Minnesota in 2008 were proven fraudulent. State and local reviews determined that the vast majority of questioned registrations reflected clerical errors, duplicate entries, or later-validated registrations, with only a small number resulting in fraud findings or prosecutions.

claim: Says Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "didn't change his position" on a two-state solution.
rationale: Netanyahu has at times claimed continuity, but the public record shows he has made contradictory statements and policy shifts about a two-state solution (for example endorsing a demilitarized Palestinian state in his 2009 Bar-Ilan speech and later rejecting or qualifying that stance in subsequent years). Because his position has changed in rhetoric and practice, the blanket claim that he ‘didn't change his position’ is misleading.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama’s biological father. Contemporary records, Obama's birth certificate, his own memoirs, and genealogical research identify Barack Obama Sr. as his father; Davis was a friend and mentor to Obama’s maternal family but not reported or documented as his parent. The claim is a long-discredited conspiracy theory with no substantiating documentation.

claim: Says Joe Biden "will destroy your protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden plans to eliminate protections for people with pre-existing conditions; Biden campaigned on protecting and expanding those protections and his administration and DOJ have defended the Affordable Care Act. Public policy proposals from Biden and his party have focused on preserving or strengthening ACA rules rather than removing them. The absolute claim that he "will destroy" those protections is not supported by his stated positions or actions.

claim: Says when Republicans took over the state legislature in 2010, New Hampshire’s tax rate for employers was 50th in the nation, and unemployment had more than doubled under Democrats.
rationale: While Republicans did win control of New Hampshire’s legislature in the 2010 election and the state’s unemployment rose substantially during the 2008–2010 recession (roughly from the mid‑3% range to the mid‑6/7% range), the statement that New Hampshire’s “tax rate for employers was 50th in the nation” is unsupported and ambiguous. Public records do not uniformly rank New Hampshire as the absolute worst for a generic “employer tax rate” and the claim conflates different tax measures; attributing the unemployment rise solely to Democrats is misleading because the increase coincided with the national Great Recession.

claim: "Tell me what Madeleine Albright’s position was on the War on Iraq. I wouldn’t be surprised if she supported it."
rationale: Madeleine Albright publicly supported the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq. While she was no longer Secretary of State then, she endorsed removing Saddam Hussein and later acknowledged problems with postwar planning and consequences.

claim: Decriminalizing marijuana "will save the state anywhere from $4 (million) to $11 million dollars."
rationale: The statement is too specific and presented without context (which state, what time period, and which costs are included). Savings from decriminalizing marijuana vary widely by jurisdiction and depend on what budget items are counted (police, courts, corrections, treatment, etc.), so a blanket claim that it "will save the state anywhere from $4 million to $11 million" cannot be verified as universally true. Some states have reported annual savings in the low millions while others project different magnitudes or net costs when accounting for regulatory and public health expenditures.

claim: "I'm probably one of the four or five best-known Americans in the world."
rationale: This is an unverified, subjective self-assessment and cannot be treated as fact without objective evidence. Being 'one of the four or five best-known Americans in the world' requires clear metrics or global polling data, which are not provided, so the claim is not supportable.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: Contemporary reporting documents that Ed Gillespie worked as a lobbyist and that his firm represented some foreign clients, but I find no clear, corroborated evidence that his firm lobbied for exactly five foreign governments including a specific dictator who was then awaiting trial for war crimes. The statement appears to conflate or overstate press accounts of his lobbying clients and ties to controversial regimes.

claim: Says series of 11 photos are "from the 1918 flu pandemic."
rationale: There is no provided provenance or visual evidence to confirm those 11 photos are from the 1918 influenza pandemic, and many historic photos circulated online are routinely misattributed. Without original sources, metadata, or expert dating, the claim cannot be verified and is more likely to be incorrect than reliably true.

claim: Opposition to having a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in the "super minority."
rationale: The claim asserts that opposition to a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in a 'super minority,' but there is no clear, cited evidence that opposition is vanishingly small. Public opinion and political positions on an elected board have been mixed across different stakeholder groups (voters, unions, community groups) and have varied over time and by poll or vote, so labeling opposition as a 'super minority' is unsupported. Without a specific poll, vote, or definition of 'super minority,' the claim cannot be verified.

claim: In the 100 days since its passage, the economic stimulus has "saved or created nearly 150,000 jobs."
rationale: The assertion is not verifiable as a factual count: within the first 100 days after major U.S. stimulus legislation (e.g., the 2009 ARRA) official payroll data continued to show net job losses, and government claims about jobs 'saved or created' in short windows were model-based estimates rather than directly observed hires. Such headline figures typically come from projections or program estimates and cannot be treated as measured, attributable employment increases in that immediate timeframe.

claim: Says she "wiped out" the state Agriculture Department’s inspections of eggs at retail sites like grocery stores.
rationale: The claim as presented lacks any named person, state, time period, or supporting source, so it cannot be verified. Eliminating routine retail egg inspections by a state agriculture department would be a documented administrative action and is not substantiated here. Without specific attribution or evidence, the statement cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says CNN President Jeff Zucker ordered employees to downplay Bill Clinton’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and make it look like Epstein was "Trump’s partner in all of this."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that CNN president Jeff Zucker instructed employees to downplay Bill Clinton’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein or to frame Epstein primarily as associated with Donald Trump. Major outlets reported on Clinton’s relationship with Epstein, and no internal memos, corroborated whistleblower testimony, or documents have surfaced to substantiate this directive. The claim appears to be an unverified partisan allegation.

claim: "9,871,525 is the number of registered voters in AZ according to FB. AZ population is 7,270,000."
rationale: The claimed 9,871,525 registered voters in Arizona exceeds the state's total population figure given (7,270,000) and is inconsistent with official voter-registration counts. Arizona's population is around 7.2–7.3 million (2020-era estimates) and official registered-voter totals are roughly 4–4.5 million, so the 9.87 million figure is not credible.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 'internal government documents' have exposed an Obama-era presidential cover-up of an explosion that killed 29 miners. Official investigations (MSHA and DOJ) and mainstream reporting attribute the disaster to company safety failures and regulatory shortcomings, and prosecutions targeted the mining company and executives rather than showing an administration-level cover-up. Claims framing it as 'Obama’s deadliest cover-up' are not supported by the available documentary record or authoritative news reporting.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: While former DNI James Clapper publicly expressed his belief that there was no collusion, it is incorrect to say that "virtually everyone else" said the same. The Mueller report carefully stated it "did not establish" that the Trump campaign conspired with Russia, which is not an unequivocal declaration of "no collusion," and officials and experts offered differing characterizations of the findings. Many commentators and some officials emphasized evidence of contacts and coordination efforts even while noting lack of charges for a criminal conspiracy.

claim: In Wisconsin, because a key provision of the Voting Rights Act was not in effect,  "somewhere between 40,000 and 80,000 people were turned away from the polls (in 2016) because of the color of their skin" and other factors.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 40,000–80,000 people were turned away from Wisconsin polls in 2016 specifically “because of the color of their skin.” While Shelby County v. Holder (2013) ended preclearance and some states implemented restrictive voting rules afterward, available investigations and academic studies do not document tens of thousands of voters being denied ballots for race; the claim appears to conflate estimates of people lacking certain IDs or eligible-but-unregistered residents with confirmed instances of being turned away due to race.

claim: Says Chuck Todd said the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or transcript showing Chuck Todd explicitly said the Roy Moore story 'felt completely orchestrated.' Fact-checking of the circulating quote found it was a misattribution from social media rather than a verifiable on-air statement. The claim appears to be a paraphrase or fabrication rather than a documented quote.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: Contemporary budget records and independent fact-checks indicate that the county property tax levy was not held flat for eight consecutive budgets during that county executive's tenure; at least one annual budget showed an increase in the levy. Therefore the blanket claim that "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy" is not supported as stated.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: Renacci supported Republican budgets and legislation that proposed restructuring Medicare (for example, moving toward a premium-support or voucher-like system), but he did not cast votes that literally repealed or abolished the Medicare program. Characterizing those votes as having 'voted repeatedly to end Medicare' misstates the record and is misleading.

claim: Says Oregon ranks 43rd in education.
rationale: The claim gives no source or year and state education rankings vary substantially by publisher and year; Oregon is not uniformly ranked 43rd across common measures. Without a specified dataset the statement cannot be verified and is likely incorrect because reputable ranking systems place Oregon at different positions.

claim: Letting the Bush tax cuts expire would raise taxes on small businesses.
rationale: Generally true: the 2001/2003 Bush tax cuts lowered individual income and preferential capital gains/dividend rates, and most small businesses operate as pass-through entities taxed on owners' individual returns. If those cuts expire and individual rates revert upward, owners of pass-through small businesses would generally face higher federal tax bills. This does not automatically apply to small businesses organized as C corporations or to every income level or deduction situation.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: There is no reliable, corroborated reporting or law-enforcement confirmation that TikTok located Cassie Compton, who was reportedly missing since 2014. Viral social-media claims about finding missing people are common but require independent verification from police or reputable news outlets, which is not present here.

claim: Florida is "second in the nation in the uninsured."
rationale: The statement is presented without a year or whether it refers to the absolute number of uninsured people or the uninsured rate. Rankings of states by uninsured change over time and by metric; while Florida is often among the states with high uninsured counts because of its large population, it is not consistently second across sources and years.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: While many high-poverty counties are in Appalachia and are majority white, the very poorest U.S. counties are not exclusively Appalachian nor more than 90% white. County-level poverty data (by rate or median income) often show deepest poverty in places like Oglala Lakota County (South Dakota) and numerous Mississippi Delta counties that are majority Native American or Black. Thus the blanket claim overstates and mischaracterizes the geographic and racial makeup of the poorest counties.
