rationale: There is no clear evidence that the City of Cincinnati as a whole is already powered 100% by clean energy; most large U.S. cities that have announced ‘100%’ targets refer to future goals or to municipal operations only. While Cincinnati has climate targets and municipal renewable purchases, claiming it is already one of the largest U.S. cities running entirely on 100% clean energy overstates the current public record.

claim: Says Emma Gonzalez, a survivor of the Parkland school shooting, ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Emma González deliberately ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution. Video and contemporary fact-checking coverage show she tore a sheet of paper onstage, but investigators found the torn paper was not authenticated as the Constitution and critics’ claims were not substantiated. Major news outlets and fact-checkers treated the allegation as unsupported or misleading.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported as presented: credit ratings are issued by specific agencies (S&P, Moody's, Fitch) and the "highest possible" designation differs by agency and fund type. While STAR Ohio has historically carried high ratings, without a date and named rater the claim that it "just received the highest possible credit rating" cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "While states used to have regulatory power over fishing, federal law now regulates down to the tenth of the inch the minimum size of fish that anglers can keep."
rationale: The claim overstates federal reach and precision. In the U.S. states retain primary authority over inland and many nearshore recreational fisheries, while the federal government (via the Magnuson–Stevens Act and NOAA/ regional councils) regulates certain marine and interstate fisheries; federal rules do not universally set minimum recreational fish sizes to the tenth of an inch and most size limits are specified in whole inches or other measures. Management is often shared or varies by species and waterbody.

claim: "In ‘Resident Evil’ the Umbrella Corporation releases a virus that infects the people of Raccoon City. A biological research lab with the exact same logo as the Umbrella Corporation can be found in the city where the coronavirus outbreak originated."
rationale: The first part is accurate: Resident Evil’s Umbrella Corporation is a fictional company that releases the T-virus, causing the Raccoon City outbreak. The second part is false: there is no credible evidence that any real-world lab in Wuhan (the city tied to the initial COVID-19 outbreak) uses the Umbrella Corporation’s distinctive red-and-white umbrella logo, and the Wuhan Institute of Virology’s emblem is different from the fictional logo.

claim: "Since 2007 David Jolly has given almost $30,000 to keep Democrats in Congress!"
rationale: I could not verify the specific claim and there is no clear evidence that David Jolly has given nearly $30,000 specifically to ‘keep Democrats in Congress’ since 2007. Public campaign contribution records (FEC/OpenSecrets) are the authoritative sources and show Jolly is a Republican who may have made occasional bipartisan donations but not the large, targeted sum asserted. Without direct citation to FEC data, the claim appears unsupported.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Bill Nelson has not been a U.S. Senator since January 2019 (he was later confirmed as NASA Administrator in 2021), so he could not recently have joined Senate Democrats in passing a Senate budget; moreover, Congress frequently uses appropriations bills and continuing resolutions rather than a single Senate-passed "budget," and there is no verifiable single event matching the unspecified "750 days" statement. Without a clear reference date or definition of "passed a budget," the assertion is not supported.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi "made millions in coronavirus insider trading."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi personally engaged in insider trading related to coronavirus or that she 'made millions' from such activity. Public financial disclosures and multiple fact-checks and reporting found no proof of illegal insider trading by Pelosi; some trading by her spouse has been cited but was not shown to involve insider information or criminal charges.

claim: Says "we had to cut 13 billion dollars in state spending over two years."
rationale: The statement gives a specific dollar amount and timeframe but provides no identifying details (which state, which two years, or a source), so it cannot be verified as presented. State budget cuts vary widely and a $13 billion reduction could be true for some states or periods but is unsubstantiated without context or supporting data.

claim: "Cory Gardner is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions right now."
rationale: Cory Gardner is not currently a member of Congress and therefore is not formally sponsoring federal legislation right now. While as a senator (2015–2021) he supported and cosponsored some abortion restrictions, there is no evidence he is presently sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions.

claim: "Wife of Pfizer’s CEO dies after complications from the vaccine."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authoritative reporting that the spouse of Pfizer’s CEO died from COVID-19 vaccination complications. Major fact-checking organizations investigated similar social media claims about Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla’s wife and found them to be false or unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: While Bruce Poliquin did vote for Republican health-care bills (including the 2017 AHCA) that CBO said would reduce coverage nationally, there is no authoritative, widely accepted source showing his vote would specifically 'strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance.' State-level estimates of coverage losses vary by model and the exact 117,000 figure is not a clearly supported official estimate tied to his vote.

claim: The new health care law "will cut $500 billion from Medicare. That will hurt the quality of our care."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did include roughly $500 billion in Medicare savings over about a decade, but those were reductions in projected federal Medicare spending largely from lower payments to plans and providers, not direct cuts to beneficiaries' guaranteed benefits. Independent analysts (CBO, Medicare actuary, fact-checkers) found the law preserves Medicare benefits and eligibility, and there is no clear evidence that the savings will inherently 'hurt the quality' of care—effects on quality are uncertain and depend on implementation.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: Statewide violent-crime trends in Wisconsin are mixed and depend on the metric and timeframe. While some categories (notably homicides and shootings) and certain cities such as Milwaukee experienced increases in several years, statewide violent-crime rates have fluctuated over the 2010s and do not unambiguously show Wisconsin is overall less safe than in 2011 without specifying which measure and period is used.

claim: ABC News recently banned reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air.
rationale: There is no credible, widely reported evidence that ABC News has recently issued a network-wide ban on reporters wearing American flag lapel pins on air. While news organizations often discourage overt partisan symbols to preserve perceived neutrality, a specific recent prohibition by ABC has not been documented in major reporting or official statements.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: While Rep. Sean Casten has at times held RSVP-limited meetings or small closed briefings, public reporting indicates he generally held a mix of public town halls and virtual events rather than a widespread pattern of numerous 'invite-only' town halls. The claim overstates the frequency and treats occasional limited-capacity meetings as a pervasive practice.

claim: "We have that program where immigrants come here and they have to bring a million dollars in order to get a green card if they’re going to create jobs."
rationale: This refers to the U.S. EB-5 Immigrant Investor Program, under which foreign nationals can obtain conditional permanent residence by making a substantial investment and creating jobs. The program’s standard investment threshold has been about $1 million (with a lower threshold for targeted employment areas) and requires creation of generally 10 full-time U.S. jobs, though other regulatory conditions apply.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The statement asserts an exclusive claim but gives no name, timeframe, or definition of "balanced budgets" or "brought jobs," making it unverifiable as written. Public records and historical accounts show multiple Providence officials and mayoral administrations have managed balanced budgets and pursued job-creation efforts, so it is very unlikely that only one current candidate could uniquely claim both accomplishments.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and municipal financial statements around the time Angel Taveras took office (2011) show Providence's pension funded ratio was higher than 30% (commonly reported in the high 30s to low 40s) and the funded level fluctuated with market returns and valuation assumptions. Therefore the specific claim that it was "only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he took office" is not supported by the available figures and oversimplifies differing measurements.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: This is a speculative counterfactual with no evidentiary support. Ronald Reagan remained a leading and celebrated figure in the Republican Party throughout and after his presidency, and there is no record or plausible mechanism showing the GOP would have expelled him under an undefined "new litmus test."

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Donald Trump saying that exact sentence verbatim. The line appears to be a paraphrase combining themes Trump has often used (that opponents are targeting his supporters' guns, religion, and freedoms), but the precise wording shown is not documented in reputable transcripts or video records.

claim: "Special education categorical aid" from the state "hasn’t been raised in over a decade."
rationale: The statement lacks a specified state, and as a general claim it is unlikely: many states have adjusted or increased special education categorical aid within the past decade. State education funding is typically revisited in biennial/annual budgets and several states enacted increases or reforms to special education funding over the last ten years. Without a named state and supporting budget data, the blanket claim cannot be verified and is likely incorrect.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: The Republican Party's official platform documents use formal policy language and do not contain the crude phrase 'deport everybody and to hell with it.' While GOP platforms and many Republican officials have called for stricter immigration enforcement, border security, and removal of certain unauthorized immigrants, they do not state a blanket directive to deport all immigrants in that language.

claim: Says that Biden’s ban on new federal leases will kill 120,000 Texas jobs.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that a Biden 'ban' on new federal leases will (or did) definitively kill 120,000 Texas jobs. The administration implemented a temporary review/ pause on some new oil and gas leasing early in 2021, but independent fact-checks and employment data show that job-loss estimates of that magnitude are based on industry projections with broad assumptions and often apply nationally, not specifically to Texas. Moreover, most Texas oil activity occurs on private or state lands, reducing the direct statewide employment impact from changes to federal leasing.

claim: "The median income in America has dropped by 10 percent in the last four years."
rationale: Official U.S. income series do not show a roughly 10% decline in median income over the past four years; Census and BLS data show that median household income rose in the early part of the period and only small changes occurred afterward. The claim also fails to specify whether it means nominal or inflation‑adjusted (real) income or whether it refers to household or individual median, which would change the interpretation.

claim: Says the 2008 book "End of Days" predicted the current coronavirus outbreak.
rationale: Sylvia Browne's 2008 book 'End of Days' includes a passage saying that 'in around 2020 a severe pneumonia-like illness will spread throughout the globe' originating in Asia and resisting treatments, which is the claim being referenced. The wording does not explicitly name coronavirus or SARS-CoV-2 and is fairly vague about details, but the book does contain the quoted prediction.

claim: In the past decade in New York State "more than 30 current and former state officeholders have been convicted, sanctioned or accused of wrongdoing — more than any other state."
rationale: I cannot corroborate a verifiable count showing New York had more than 30 current or former state officeholders convicted, sanctioned, or accused in the past decade nor that this exceeds every other state. Such tallies depend heavily on definitions (convicted vs. accused vs. sanctioned), the exact ten-year window, and the source methodology, and no authoritative, comparable dataset supports the specific comparative claim.

claim: "This year, Eric Cantor has received more money from oil companies than any other member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is unlikely and not supported by general campaign‑finance reporting: analyses of oil and gas industry contributions typically show members from oil‑producing states or key energy committee members receiving the largest sums, and Eric Cantor has not been widely reported as the single top recipient. The statement also lacks a specified year and would require checking FEC/Center for Responsive Politics data to verify.

claim: The Washington D.C.-area "never has a recession."
rationale: The claim is demonstrably false: the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area has experienced economic downturns and job losses during national recessions (for example in the early 2000s, the 2008–2009 Great Recession, and the 2020 COVID downturn). While the region is often more resilient because of large federal employment and contracting, that cushioning does not mean it has 'never' had recessions or contractions in local employment and output.

claim: Wagon arriving at Detroit counting center after deadline "may have been a ballot box."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the wagon in question actually contained a ballot box; contemporary reporting and post-election reviews found the footage did not show ballots being illicitly added after a deadline. Official accounts and neutral fact-checkers concluded the item was not shown to be a sealed ballot container and that chain-of-custody and counting procedures were followed.

claim: "McDonald’s (makes) you all sign noncompete contracts that you cannot go across town to try to get a job at Burger King."
rationale: McDonald’s does not universally require all employees to sign noncompete agreements that bar them from taking jobs at competitors like Burger King. While some franchisees or higher‑level managers may be asked to sign restrictive covenants, such agreements are uncommon for rank‑and‑file crew members and are often limited in scope or unenforceable under state law.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and campaign-finance disclosures showed Rep. John Culberson charged purchases described as collectibles — including Civil War–era items and fossils — to his campaign account. Reporting documented the expenditures and drew criticism, though it did not necessarily mean he was criminally charged.

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The percentage of released Guantanamo detainees who have 'reengaged' in terrorism depends on how 'recidivism' is defined (confirmed vs. suspected) and has varied across Department of Defense reports; there is no stable, unambiguous figure of 'nearly 29%' that applies universally. Moreover, the measured rate has not shown a continuous, monotonic rise since releases began—published numbers have fluctuated and changed with methodology and new information.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated—no specific policy, law, or action is identified that shows Charlie Crist directly 'made it easier for Duke to take your money.' Without naming which 'Duke' (presumably Duke Energy), which time period, or which specific measure is meant, the assertion cannot be verified and is likely a rhetorical accusation rather than a documented fact.

claim: "We are currently using only around 20% of our testing capacity."
rationale: The statement is too specific to be true as presented because it gives a precise percentage without specifying what kind of testing, which jurisdiction, or what date. Testing capacity and utilization vary widely by test type and location and are reported by health agencies; a blanket claim of 'only around 20%' is unsupported without a cited data source. Absent verifiable, contextual data, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Says Stacey Evans "voted for (school) vouchers...in the beginning."
rationale: I find no reliable record or reporting showing Stacey Evans saying she “voted for…school vouchers in the beginning.” Public statements and campaign materials from Evans emphasize opposition to privatizing public education, and available voting records do not show a clear admission that she supported voucher legislation early in her career.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: While Wisconsin did provide about $80 million in state support toward the Bucks arena, the claim that new income-tax revenue from basketball events alone is “probably over $600 million over the life of the lease” is unsupported and highly disputed. Independent analyses and press reports show that projected tax gains were based on optimistic assumptions, broad economic multipliers, and long time horizons; neutral estimates and fiscal analysts found much smaller net state revenue impacts. The $600M figure appears to be a promotional projection rather than a reliably verified outcome.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate but context-dependent facts with misleading assertions. Trump did win West Virginia by a very large margin (roughly 42 points in 2016 and about 39 points in 2020), but saying his state has the single strongest percentage support of any state is not clearly true across elections or polls — several states gave him comparable or higher vote shares. Likewise, statewide approval has varied over time and is not reliably "close to 60%" in recent polling.

claim: Says he banned texting while driving in Austin.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because the referent “he” is unspecified. Traffic restrictions like a ban on texting while driving are enacted by a legislative body (city council or state legislature) or signed by an executive, not unilaterally 'banned' by an unnamed individual, so the statement as phrased is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: The claim is too broad and not supported by recent data. While Mexican net migration to the U.S. reversed in the late 2000s–2010s and the Mexican-born unauthorized population fell from its 2007 peak, overall undocumented flows have varied by year and origin country and recent periods have seen large inflows and encounters at the border. Therefore it is incorrect to state currently that there is a clear, ongoing net outflow of undocumented workers from the U.S. back to Mexico.

claim: "Sixteen [federal] programs exist to fight homelessness" and some of them are duplicative.
rationale: The claim is misleading: federal efforts to address homelessness span many more than 16 programs when one includes initiatives across HUD, VA, HHS, Education, Labor and other agencies. Counts vary by definition (programs directly dedicated to homelessness versus broader housing, health, and benefit programs that serve people experiencing homelessness), so a flat number of 16 is not supported by authoritative summaries. The related assertion that some programs overlap is plausible, but the broad numeric claim is inaccurate without a clear definition.

claim: "Without a shred of clinical data to support its decision, the Biden Administration has revoked the emergency use authorization for lifesaving monoclonal antibody treatments."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: U.S. regulators cited laboratory (in vitro) neutralization data showing markedly reduced activity of specific monoclonal antibodies against circulating SARS‑CoV‑2 variants (notably Omicron and its subvariants), together with surveillance of variant prevalence, when they withdrew or limited EUAs. In addition, those products had prior randomized clinical trial evidence of benefit against earlier variants, so the decision was not made “without a shred of clinical data.”

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it gives no specific date or event to check; attendance claims for public officials require a concrete time and identified summit to confirm. Without that context, I cannot confirm that Florida Governor Rick Scott skipped an education summit he hosted while attending a Tea Party convention the same week, so the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: The only budget Ted Cruz "ever voted for in his time in the Senate is a budget that cut defense spending by more than Barack Obama proposes we cut it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. Ted Cruz has participated in multiple budget-related Senate votes since 2013, and the assertion that the only budget he 'ever voted for' cut defense more than any proposal from President Obama ignores which specific budget and which Obama proposal are being compared; such comparisons depend on differing baselines and years. Public vote records and prior fact-checks show the statement conflates different measures and misstates Cruz's voting history.

claim: Trade deals are negotiated in "secret" and, unlike corporate interests, politicians never invite "the leaders of the AFL-CIO or steelworkers or the mine workers to come in and sit down in these meetings."
rationale: The claim is overly absolute. While many trade negotiation sessions and draft texts are handled confidentially, governments typically consult stakeholders and there are formal mechanisms (and historical examples) in which labor leaders and unions have been invited to briefings and advisory processes, so it is incorrect to say politicians 'never' invite AFL-CIO, steelworkers, or mine workers to meetings. That said, corporate actors often have greater and more frequent access.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: There is no clear, consistent record of Trump calling for outright abolition of the federal minimum wage. He has spoken about letting states set wages or offering flexibility and has criticized the federal minimum wage at times, but he did not campaign on or enact a policy to 'get rid' of the federal minimum wage.

claim: "There's going to be a slowdown and delays in flights" as a result of the sequester.
rationale: The statement is a broad predictive claim that cannot be asserted as universally true: whether a sequester causes flight slowdowns depends on which programs and agency budgets are cut and what mitigation steps are taken. In past U.S. sequestration episodes (e.g., 2013) cuts threatened FAA staffing and service contracts and could have produced delays, but many impacts were reduced or avoided through reallocation, contingency plans, or alternate funding, so the claim as stated is not categorically true.

claim: Says Josh Mandel bet against Ohio families
rationale: The phrase appears to be a political attack and is not a specific, verifiable factual claim showing that Josh Mandel personally placed trades or financial bets that targeted or profited from harm to Ohio families. Public reporting and Mandel's disclosures do not document any clear transaction that would unambiguously constitute 'betting against Ohio families,' so the assertion is unsubstantiated as stated. Without precise evidence (dates, transactions, instruments) the claim is misleading.

claim: "Speaker Rubio supported gun restrictions that included background checks and waiting periods."
rationale: This is false as stated. Marco Rubio has generally opposed broad universal background checks and mandatory waiting periods — he voted against the 2013 Manchin-Toomey expanded background-check amendment — and has framed his support around targeted measures (e.g., improving NICS reporting, school-safety steps) rather than blanket background checks and waiting periods. While he has backed some gun-related proposals, he has not broadly supported the kinds of restrictions described.

claim: "Zach Nunn took money from Adventureland’s CEO, then sponsored legislation to loosen amusement park safety rules. A child died. Zach Nunn put his big donor first, ahead of the safety of Iowa families."
rationale: The claim ties three assertions together (a donation from Adventureland’s CEO, sponsorship by Zach Nunn of legislation loosening amusement-park safety rules, and a child’s death caused by that sponsorship). Public campaign-finance and congressional sponsorship records do not show clear evidence that Nunn received a notable contribution from Adventureland’s CEO or that he sponsored federal legislation specifically to loosen amusement-park safety standards; likewise, there is no documented causal link between any bill he sponsored and a child's death. Without specific names, dates, or bill numbers this appears to be a misleading amalgam rather than a supported factual claim.

claim: "In campaigns in the past with Sen. McCain and President George W. Bush and others, they have tended to release tax records in April."
rationale: The claim implies a consistent pattern that McCain, George W. Bush and similar campaigns tended to release tax records in April; in fact timing has varied by year and campaign. While some politicians sometimes time releases around Tax Day, neither McCain nor George W. Bush showed a reliable, consistent practice of releasing returns specifically in April across their campaigns.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and ambiguous. By mid-2024 many countries already had more than 50% of their populations fully vaccinated and the U.S. had passed 50% earlier; claiming 'more than any other country' is incorrect because several countries (for example Portugal, Spain, Chile, Uruguay and some small states) reported higher full-vaccination shares. Without a date, a definition of 'fully vaccinated', or a clear geographic scope, the claim cannot be supported.

claim: "At my first ‘Let’s Get to Work Day’ … we sold out;" more than 240 dozen doughnuts by 8:30 a.m.
rationale: This is a specific, numeric claim about sales at a particular event that I cannot corroborate from independent records. Without vendor receipts, contemporaneous news reports, or other documentation confirming that more than 240 dozen doughnuts were sold by 8:30 a.m., the assertion is unverified and should be treated as false per the instruction to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: "Reagan took the deficit from $70 billion to $175 billion. Bush 41 took it to $300 billion. Clinton got it to zero. Bush 43 took it from zero to $1.2 trillion. Obama halved it to $600 billion. Trump’s got it back to a trillion."
rationale: The statement mixes and misattributes annual deficit figures and is inaccurate in key places. Clinton delivered multi-year budget surpluses in the late 1990s (not just “zero”), George W. Bush’s deficits did rise but did not reach $1.2 trillion during his term (the ~1.2–1.4 trillion peak occurred in FY2009 during the recession/early Obama period), and other numbers are approximate or rounded in misleading ways. While some broad directions are right (deficits rose under Reagan and fell under Clinton, Obama reduced large deficits, Trump’s pre-COVID deficit approached ~$1 trillion), the specific sequence and magnitudes as stated are false.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: The claim implies Governor Evers did not send help until after people were killed in Kenosha. In fact, Evers authorized deployment of Wisconsin National Guard members and state resources during the unrest period (he ordered Guard assistance in the days around Aug 24–25, 2020), so help had been mobilized before or contemporaneously with the shootings even if troops were not yet fully on-scene. The statement is therefore misleading about the timing and makes an absolute causal claim that is not supported.

claim: A government analysis shows under a proposed transportation tax, "metro Atlanta will create or support an additional 200,000 new jobs, including jobs that are maintained year over year."
rationale: There is no verifiable government analysis that unequivocally shows metro Atlanta would gain 200,000 additional jobs that are maintained year over year under a proposed transportation tax. Government and regional studies sometimes report large job 'creation or support' totals for transportation investments, but those figures typically combine temporary construction, indirect and induced jobs rather than 200,000 net permanent jobs; without a named study the claim is unsubstantiated or misleading.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: The statement overstates and mischaracterizes the payments. Scott Walker did return or forgo portions of his Milwaukee County Executive pay while in office, but public records and contemporary news reports indicate the total amount and timeframe cited are inaccurate or presented without needed context, so the specific claim of "over $370,000 since being elected in 2002" is misleading.

claim: Says Rob Portman "said the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that Rob Portman used the exact phrase "the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio." Portman has criticized aspects of federal auto-industry interventions at times, but the specific quoted wording and attribution are not documented in reliable public records. Without a clear source, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "700 jobs (were) lost because Allen Boyd" voted for the health care bill.
rationale: There is no credible evidence tying a specific, quantifiable loss of “700 jobs” directly to Representative Allen Boyd’s individual vote on a health-care bill. Economic effects of major legislation are diffuse, mediated by many actors and factors, and cannot reliably be attributed to a single member’s vote; claims that assign an exact job-loss number to one vote are typical political spin and lack substantiating analysis.

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: The claim that North Carolina hospital beds are 'typically 85% full across the state' is misleading. Hospital occupancy fluctuates by season, region, and during public-health surges; typical statewide averages pre-COVID and in non-surge periods have generally been lower (often in the 60–75% range), although some hospitals or periods have exceeded 85%.

claim: "Congressman Duffy has long record of voting against VA backlog fixes."
rationale: The statement overstates the case: public roll-call records for Congressman Sean Duffy show a mixed voting record on veterans’ issues—he supported several high-profile VA reform measures aimed at addressing wait-times and access while opposing some specific proposals. There is not clear evidence of a consistent, long-term pattern of voting against efforts to fix the VA backlog.

claim: When Sara Gideon "knew the truth about" sexual allegations against a state lawmaker, "she could have called for an immediate investigation, but didn’t…Gideon knew for months, using her power to cover up."
rationale: The claim alleges Gideon knowingly learned the truth of sexual allegations and deliberately used her authority to cover them up for months. Public reporting and official records from her time as Maine House Speaker do not provide evidence that she intentionally suppressed or obstructed investigations; complaints were handled through House ethics processes and there is no credible documentation that she orchestrated a months‑long coverup.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: Contemporaneous reports and the official passenger manifest for the January 26, 2020 helicopter crash list nine people aboard and do not include Rick Fox. Rick Fox is a former NBA player but was not on the helicopter with Kobe Bryant and his daughter.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no reliable record that David Axelrod formally joined Jason Carter's campaign as his campaign advisor. Contemporary reporting on the 2014 Georgia governor race does not list Axelrod as an official campaign advisor; at most Axelrod provided informal support or made limited appearances for Democratic causes, but did not serve in a formal advisory role to Carter.

claim: Says Keene, N.H., requested a "military-grade armored personnel truck," citing their annual Pumpkin Festival as "a possible target" for terrorists.
rationale: There is no reliable public record that Keene, N.H. formally requested a “military‑grade armored personnel truck” specifically citing its Pumpkin Festival as a potential terrorist target. While many small U.S. police departments sought surplus armored equipment after high‑profile attacks, reporting on Keene does not substantiate this precise claim or the cited phrasing about the festival as a terrorist target.

claim: "I'm pro-life. He's not."
rationale: The claim asserts opposing positions on abortion for two unspecified people but provides no identities or supporting evidence. Without knowing who 'I' and 'he' are and without corroborating public statements, voting records, or policy positions, the assertion cannot be verified. Therefore it should be treated as false/unsubstantiated in this context.

claim: "U.S. teenagers have now fallen behind their counterparts in Ireland, Poland and even Vietnam in math and science."
rationale: Recent international assessments (notably OECD PISA results in the most recent major cycles) show U.S. students scoring below their peers in Vietnam and Poland in math and often in science, and Ireland also outperformed the U.S. on those measures. Thus the statement that U.S. teenagers have fallen behind counterparts in those countries is supported by available PISA comparisons.

claim: Says Roy Moore "has advocated getting the federal government out of health care altogether, which means doing away with Medicaid, which means doing away with Medicare."
rationale: Roy Moore has publicly opposed the Affordable Care Act and promoted reducing the federal role in health care and returning authority to states, but there is no clear evidence he explicitly called for doing away with Medicare. Fact-checks and his public statements focus on repealing Obamacare and changing Medicaid, not an outright elimination of Medicare for seniors.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by aggregate industry data: insurance profits have varied widely since 2001 with major downturns (e.g., 2008 financial crisis, large catastrophe years) and no consistent fivefold increase across the sector. While some individual insurers or shareholder returns may have risen substantially, there is no clear evidence that total industry profits universally soared by more than 400% since 2001.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim is overly categorical. Empirical criminology research shows CCTV can reduce some property crimes and deter offenders in particular settings, but its deterrent effect is variable and depends on factors like camera visibility, active monitoring, signage, prosecution likelihood, and offender motivations; it does not "certainly" prevent robberies.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it does not specify which geographic 'region' or which metric defines 'worst drought.' While 2011 was indeed among the most severe drought years in some places (for example parts of the United States such as Texas), that does not make it the worst year ever recorded in every region. Without region-specific hydrometeorological records, the blanket claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: The omnibus bill "does not designate a single dollar for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The statement is misleading and depends on which omnibus bill and year are meant. Federal omnibus appropriations normally fund programs (Medicaid, community health centers, etc.) rather than naming specific organizations, and those program dollars can and do reimburse or flow to Planned Parenthood affiliates; some bills also include explicit riders restricting funds to Planned Parenthood. Claiming the omnibus “does not designate a single dollar” to Planned Parenthood as a blanket fact is therefore false or at best incomplete without specifying the bill and provisions.

claim: President Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid support Rick Perry’s "decision to give in-state tuition to illegal immigrants."
rationale: While Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid have generally supported measures like the DREAM Act or policies expanding in-state tuition eligibility for undocumented students, there is no clear evidence they specifically endorsed or publicly supported Governor Rick Perry’s particular decision or timing on Texas in-state tuition. Perry signed a Texas law in 2001 allowing certain undocumented students to get in-state tuition but later shifted his public position, and the three federal leaders did not issue explicit, documented endorsements of Perry’s action.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public court record that former President Barack Obama was ordered to pay $400 million in restitution. A judgment of that size against a former U.S. president would have been widely reported by major news outlets and legal databases, but no such reports exist. The claim appears to be fabricated or a misattribution.

claim: Texas and Florida have a "balanced budget" while California is "in debt $54 billion and New York is "in debt $6.1 billion."
rationale: The claim presents fixed, absolute figures without a fiscal year or definition of “debt.” While Texas and Florida have constitutional balanced-budget requirements and typically enact budgets that are balanced on paper, they can still face cash-flow issues, off‑budget liabilities, or projected shortfalls. The specific numbers for California ($54 billion) and New York ($6.1 billion) do not match a single, clearly documented statewide debt figure and likely confuse different concepts (budget shortfall, rainy-day/borrowed amounts, or long‑term liabilities). Without a cited year and definition, the assertion is misleading and not verifiably accurate as stated.

claim: Cannabis reform "is supported by the majority of the residents of our state, including a majority of Republicans."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks the specific state and timing; national and state-level polling show overall public support for cannabis reform is often a majority, but Republican support varies and is frequently below 50% in many states. Without a named state, a poll source, and a clear definition of "cannabis reform," the assertion that a majority of residents and a majority of Republicans in that state support reform cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I remember landing under sniper fire."
rationale: This is a bare first-person recollection with no corroborating details (who, when, where, witnesses or records) provided, so it cannot be independently verified. Without additional context or evidence, the claim must be treated as unsubstantiated rather than established fact.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: Investigations and studies have documented that a portion of Amazon full-time warehouse and fulfillment employees are enrolled in government food assistance programs (SNAP). Even after Amazon's $15 minimum-wage announcement, employees in high-cost areas, with larger households, or limited hours can remain eligible for and rely on food assistance.

claim: "Currently, 23 percent of our military's infrastructure is graded as 'poor' while 9 percent is 'failing.'"
rationale: The exact figures (23% poor, 9% failing) have appeared in past U.S. Department of Defense facility-condition reports for specific years, but presenting them as 'currently' accurate is misleading without a date or source. DoD condition percentages are updated annually and depend on definitions and inventory changes, so the claim as stated lacks the necessary context to be verified.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as a definitive fact because counts of where 'ISIS' operates vary widely over time and by definition (core ISIS, affiliated groups, cells, or inspired attackers). Credible government and international reports list different numbers of countries and generally do not assert a stable figure of exactly 32 countries; therefore the absolute claim is misleading.

claim: Milwaukee "incarcerates 1.2% of white men" and has "incarcerated over 50% of black men in their 30s."
rationale: Both parts of the claim are unsupported by available incarceration data and likely stem from a misreading or conflation of measures (e.g., 'ever incarcerated' vs 'currently incarcerated', city vs county). Current incarceration prevalence in a city population is typically well below 1–2% for any racial group, and the assertion that over 50% of black men in their 30s in Milwaukee are incarcerated is implausibly high even for lifetime prevalence.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The statement is vague and there is no clear, documented evidence that Jason Kander routinely attended 'fancy dinners all over the country.' While candidates often travel for fundraising and may attend high-end events, the claim asserts a broad, nationwide pattern that is unsubstantiated. Without a verified list of such events showing regular attendance across the country, the assertion overstates what is known.

claim: Virginia voters are being turned away from polling locations because they were told they already requested absentee ballots when they haven’t.
rationale: There is no evidence of a systematic practice in Virginia of turning away in-person voters on the basis that they 'already requested' absentee ballots. State election officials and contemporary fact-checking found only isolated incidents and poll-worker or database errors; voters who have requested absentee ballots are generally still permitted to cast provisional or in-person ballots under Virginia rules.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: DHS guidance and internal communications explicitly warned that the SAVE system is not designed to be a definitive or foolproof tool for determining citizenship for voter registration. Reports and fact-checks document DHS language that SAVE records can be incomplete or contain errors and should not be used as the sole basis for removing people from voter rolls.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: I am not aware of any verified, widely reported instance in my training data where Amazon removed an educational game specifically about Gettysburg. Claims about removals of individual titles on Amazon frequently lack context (marketplace seller removal, app store takedown, or individual moderation action) and no clear corroborating reports appear for this precise claim.

claim: After hearing "the frustrations parents and teachers have with the FCAT," next year "we begin improving our testing system."
rationale: The statement presents a quoted promise but provides no speaker, date, or source to verify it. Without attribution or supporting evidence, the quote cannot be confirmed as an actual public statement and is therefore treated as unverified/false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Texas mothers are dying during childbirth at the highest rates in the nation."
rationale: National vital‑statistics data and CDC state comparisons do not show Texas as having the single highest maternal mortality rate in recent reported years; some states (for example Louisiana) have had higher rates. Texas has had elevated maternal mortality relative to many states historically, but it is not consistently or currently the highest in the nation.

claim: Says the Republican "state convention is actually larger than the Republican National Convention."
rationale: A Republican state convention represents delegates and party activists from a single state and is therefore much smaller than the Republican National Convention, which brings delegates, alternates, party officials, media, and guests from all states and territories. National conventions routinely involve thousands of delegates and many more attendees, far exceeding any single-state convention.

claim: "The State Department asked all secretaries of state to send their emails over." Hillary Clinton's "the only one who’s done it."
rationale: The State Department did ask living former secretaries of state to preserve and provide personal or work-related email records in 2015, but Hillary Clinton was not uniquely the only one who complied. Media reporting at the time noted the Department requested records from multiple former secretaries and that others had either already turned over records or were subject to the same request.

claim: Exporters are using a federal loophole to "deceptively sell products made from cat and dog fur" to U.S. consumers.
rationale: U.S. law prohibits the import and sale of products made from cat and dog fur, but enforcement and reporting have documented instances where exporters and importers mislabel or disguise trim and fur components to evade that ban. Investigations by customs authorities and media outlets have found shipments and finished goods containing cat/dog fur entering U.S. commerce through labeling or classification workarounds.

claim: "I have 2 and a half million more votes than he (Sanders) does."
rationale: The claim omits which election and who 'I' refers to, and known popular-vote margins involving Bernie Sanders do not match +2.5 million. For example, in the 2016 Democratic primary Hillary Clinton led Sanders by roughly 3.6 million votes, and in 2020 Joe Biden's lead over Sanders was larger than 2.5 million. Without a specific contest or dataset, the statement as written is inconsistent with the widely reported totals.

claim: "This is the same (farm) bill we voted on a few weeks ago, with the exception of one or two sentences."
rationale: Absent a side-by-side comparison of the official texts, claiming the farm bill is identical except for 'one or two sentences' is unlikely and potentially misleading. Legislative bills typically undergo numerous edits, substitutions, and amendment insertions between versions, so such a minimal-change claim requires documentary evidence.

claim: Says Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year.
rationale: Official reporting from state health departments and the CDC show Texas has had annual abortion totals in the tens of thousands, not exceeding 80,000 in recent years; totals fell further after major legal restrictions in 2021–2022. The claim of more than 80,000 per year is higher than recent annual counts in available official data.

claim: "Trump on revamping the military: We’re bringing back the draft."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of President Trump formally announcing 'We’re bringing back the draft' as a policy commitment. Reinstating a military draft would require Congressional legislation and has not been proposed or enacted under Trump; public statements and campaign materials instead emphasize recruitment and military strengthening rather than a reinstated draft.

claim: "Since 2011, we have documentation of 1,671 dead bodies we have recovered in Texas, many in Brooks County."
rationale: The specific figure of 1,671 documented dead bodies recovered in Texas since 2011 is not supported by authoritative public records or reporting. Official counts of migrant and other deaths along the Texas border are tracked by Border Patrol, county coroners, and state medical examiners but available datasets and media accounts do not corroborate this exact number; Brooks County is a known hotspot for deaths but does not clearly account for 'many' of that total as stated. The claim provides no source and uses an ambiguous pronoun 'we,' so it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: This quotation is widely misattributed to Albert Einstein and does not appear in his collected writings or recorded speeches. Fact-checkers and the Einstein Archives find no primary-source evidence for it; it appears to be a modern internet-era aphorism applied retroactively to Einstein.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: I cannot find evidence from major reputable polling organizations that a poll showed exactly 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid. Public opinion in Egypt about the United States and foreign assistance has varied by year and question wording, and claims citing a precise 80% figure are not corroborated by well-known sources. Without a named poll, date, or methodology this specific statistic appears unverified.

claim: "Trump’s tax reform plan was nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."
rationale: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act included broad provisions such as large corporate tax cuts, lower individual tax rates, and a doubled standard deduction that delivered tax cuts for many households. Independent analyses (CBO, JCT, Tax Policy Center) found the largest net benefits flowed to higher-income households, while middle-income households on average saw modest cuts though some experienced increases due to the SALT cap or because many individual provisions expire after 2025.

claim: "Torture is illegal by our laws. It's illegal by international laws."
rationale: The claim is too broad and ambiguous. While international law broadly prohibits torture (e.g., the UN Convention Against Torture, ICCPR and customary international law), domestic legal regimes differ: many countries criminalize torture but definitions, exceptions, and enforcement vary, so the blanket statement 'illegal by our laws' cannot be confirmed without specifying the jurisdiction. In practice some states have legal gaps, reservations, or contested interpretations that complicate the absolute claim.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum has a "far left socialist platform."
rationale: Andrew Gillum's platform as a 2018 Florida gubernatorial candidate consisted of progressive Democratic policies — Medicaid expansion, a $15 minimum wage, education and criminal justice reforms — rather than calls for public ownership or abolition of capitalism. Labeling that agenda as a 'far left socialist platform' is a partisan exaggeration that conflates mainstream progressive proposals with socialism.

claim: Says Mitch McConnell voted "two times against the Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: Mitch McConnell has not twice voted against the Violence Against Women Act. Public roll-call records and contemporary reporting show he supported major VAWA reauthorizations (including the 2013 reauthorization) rather than casting two votes against the statute; claims that he voted against it two times mischaracterize his voting record or conflate opposition to particular amendments with opposing the whole bill.

claim: Says two-thirds of groups targeted for IRS scrutiny were not conservative.
rationale: Investigations into the IRS targeting scandal (notably the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration and congressional inquiries) found that a substantial share of flagged applications bore conservative identifiers such as 'Tea Party' or 'patriot.' While some non-conservative groups were also reviewed, the evidence does not support the claim that two-thirds of targeted groups were not conservative.

claim: Photo of vaccine package with 2018 date stamp shows COVID-19 outbreak was planned.
rationale: A photo of a vaccine package stamped '2018' does not demonstrate the COVID-19 outbreak was planned. Packaging often carries manufacture or expiry dates, lot codes, or can be for unrelated vaccines, and there is no credible evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 was planned prior to its emergence in late 2019. The image alone is insufficient to support a claim of deliberate planning.

claim: Says that except for foreign policy, Ron Paul’s voting record and his voting record are virtually identical.
rationale: The claim as written compares Ron Paul’s voting record to Ron Paul’s voting record and then says they differ on foreign policy; an entity compared to itself must be identical across all issue areas, so the statement is self-contradictory and false. If the speaker intended to compare Ron Paul to a different lawmaker, the sentence is ambiguous and cannot be verified as written.

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The statement is overly specific but lacks a timeframe, location, and definition of ‘moved back in.’ Surveys do show large shares of young adults living with parents at certain times (especially during recessions or the pandemic), but there is no consistent, universal finding that exactly one third of all Millennials have moved back in with their parents. Whether the claim is true depends strongly on how 'Millennials' are defined, the country, and the period measured.

claim: The number of pregnant women who have miscarried increased by "366% in just six weeks" as a result of their receiving a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: The claim is based on a misinterpretation of passive reporting data and presents no causal evidence that COVID-19 vaccines caused a 366% increase in miscarriages in six weeks. Multiple peer-reviewed studies and public-health reviews find no increased risk of miscarriage after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, and VAERS/Yellow Card-style reports cannot be used to establish incidence or causation without proper denominators and controlled study designs.

claim: "In France, they have a (surveillance) program a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States.
rationale: The claim makes a precise numeric comparison ("a thousandfold more invasive") but provides no metric or evidence. Publicly available information shows both the United States and France have significant surveillance authorities and programs, but there is no credible, quantified basis to conclude France is 1,000 times more invasive than the U.S. The statement is therefore unsupported and likely misleading.

claim: "The poorest in this country are women."
rationale: The claim is a blanket statement about an unspecified country and cannot be verified as universally true. While women are often overrepresented among the poor in many places due to pay gaps, caregiving burdens, and asset disparities, poverty patterns vary by country, definition of poverty, and subgroup (age, race, rural/urban). Without specifying the country and poverty metric, the claim is not supportable as stated.

claim: "In Harrisburg, I passed more bills than all the Democrats combined, in terms of legislation affecting the city."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible as stated because it gives no timeframe, no identified speaker, and no definition of what counts as legislation "affecting the city." Legislative records typically show many members of a party sponsoring and passing bills; it is unlikely a single lawmaker passed more relevant measures than an entire party without clear supporting evidence. Absent specific records or definitions, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: Available county-level food insecurity and poverty data from USDA, Feeding America, and Ohio state sources do not support that 70 of Ohio's 88 counties have over 25% of residents 'eligible for emergency food.' Typical county food insecurity and poverty rates across Ohio are substantially lower than 25% in most counties, and no authoritative report was found that documents the claimed 70 counties meeting that threshold. The claim appears to rely on an unclear definition of 'eligible for emergency food' and lacks corroborating evidence.

claim: "New Jersey taxpayers … will now face the highest tolls in the country."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and unsupported: while New Jersey has relatively high tolls on some roads, toll levels vary widely by route, vehicle class, and how 'highest' is measured (per-trip, per-mile, or average annual cost). Other U.S. jurisdictions and individual crossings (for example some major bridges and toll facilities in New York, California, and elsewhere) impose single tolls or per-mile rates that exceed many New Jersey charges. Without a specific metric or timeframe, the claim that New Jersey 'will now face the highest tolls in the country' is misleading.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While a few percent of Americans receive SSDI or SSI, the exact share varies by year and is not reliably "one in 19"; moreover SSI includes some elderly and blind recipients who are not classified as disabled under SSDI rules, and many people who are disabled do not receive SSDI/SSI benefits. Thus equating the program recipiency rate with the share of Americans who are disabled is inaccurate.

claim: Obama "voted for and even sponsored amendments that were intended to kill the (immigration overhaul) legislation."
rationale: There is no credible record that Barack Obama sponsored amendments whose purpose was to kill an immigration overhaul. As a U.S. senator he generally supported comprehensive immigration reform and worked on related amendments, but legislative histories and public accounts do not show him authoring or promoting 'kill' amendments to sabotage such bills. Without a specific bill or amendment identified, the broad claim is not supported.

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits which state and which month/year are being referenced; state unemployment rankings and gaps relative to the national rate change monthly. Without a specific state and timeframe you cannot establish that it was exactly fifth-highest, one percentage point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states. Because of that missing context the assertion as presented is not supportable.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders marched with Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in Cuba.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bernie Sanders ever marched alongside Fidel Castro or Che Guevara. Che Guevara was killed in 1967, long before Sanders became a public political figure, and contemporary records and news coverage do not show Sanders marching with Castro; viral photos making that claim have been debunked or miscaptioned.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: Federal energy-efficiency rules (notably the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 and subsequent DOE standards) set minimum lumen-per-watt requirements that effectively phased out many traditional incandescent bulbs, pushing consumers toward CFLs and LEDs. While the government does not specify brands or force a single technology, the regulations restrict noncompliant bulbs from being sold, which is why critics say it 'tells us which light bulbs to buy.'

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated because whether New Jersey has fewer state employees than in January 2001 depends on which payroll series and categories are counted (headcount vs. full‑time equivalents, and whether independent authorities and local workers are included) and on the specific comparison date. Independent reviews and state payroll series show different results by measure and year, so the blanket assertion that 'today' there are fewer employees and that it was done entirely without layoffs cannot be verified as universally true.

claim: "Rep. Paul Gosar asks Capitol Police to arrest illegal immigrants attending State of the Union."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Rep. Paul Gosar formally asked the U.S. Capitol Police to arrest 'illegal immigrants' attending a State of the Union. While members of Congress can ask police to remove disruptive people from the gallery, I find no record of Gosar making a documented request to arrest attendees on the basis of immigration status.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of Americans pay no income tax."
rationale: The "47%" figure is misleading as stated. Around 2010–2012 roughly 46–47% of households paid no federal individual income tax in a given year, but that statistic applies to households in specific years and ignores payroll (Social Security/Medicare) and state/local taxes—many in that group still paid other taxes.

claim: "The Simpsons" predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The Simpsons specifically predicted Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Social media clips and images reuse old jokes or generic references to Russia and are often taken out of context or retrofitted as 'predictions.' Multiple fact-checking outlets have found the cited scenes are either unrelated, misdated, or about different fictional events rather than a forecast of that real-world invasion.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: This claim is misleading and incorrect. Under the federal stimulus rules (e.g., CARES Act and later rounds) single filers with $80,000 of adjusted gross income would generally still receive a partial payment because the phase-out starts above $75,000 and completes well above $80,000, and eligibility depends on tax/benefit records rather than criminal status. Conversely, incarcerated people are not categorically guaranteed payments — eligibility was determined by IRS rules, SSNs/tax filings, and income thresholds, and some inmates did receive payments while others did not.

claim: "I believe in tax cuts. I believe in being a supply-sider. I cut the income tax I think it was 24 percent. We got 42 percent more revenues."
rationale: The claim that cutting the income tax by 24 percentage points produced a 42% increase in revenues is not supported by historical U.S. experience or mainstream analysis. Major U.S. income-tax cuts (for example in the 1980s or the 2017 tax changes) did not produce an immediate or attributable 42% rise in federal revenues; in many cases revenues fell or rose for other reasons. The statement conflates unclear measures (percent-point cut vs percent cut, nominal vs real revenues) and overstates the revenue impact attributed solely to a tax-rate cut.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the NRA has assigned Mike DeWine an overall 'F' grade; historically the NRA has endorsed or given him favorable ratings, and while DeWine has supported some gun-safety measures after mass shootings, describing that as a definitive 'flip-flop' is subjective. Without a contemporaneous NRA grade of F or a clear timeline showing a reversal, the claim is not supported.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: Available law-enforcement investigations and academic reviews of school and mass shooters do not support the blanket claim that 'many' perpetrators were drugged or put on Ritalin from kindergarten onward. While a minority of attackers have had histories of psychiatric treatment or medication, there is no consistent, well-documented pattern showing widespread, long-term Ritalin use among school shooters.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This is false: administrations long before Obama had the United States (through the Department of Justice) bring suits against states, dating back to the 19th century and continuing through many modern presidencies. Also, presidents do not personally 'file' suits—litigation is brought by the federal government/DOJ, so characterizing Obama as the first president to do so is incorrect.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Paul Manafort served as Donald Trump's campaign chairman from June to August 2016 and was a senior campaign official responsible for strategy and delegate operations; he also continued to advise informally after his resignation. Those roles and the documented responsibilities are inconsistent with describing his involvement as "very limited."

claim: Says President Barack Obama’s "own economists say the stimulus cost $278K per job ‘created.’ "
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and official analyses show the '$278,000 per job' number is a misreading or misuse of stimulus data, not a claim made by 'Obama's own economists.' The Recovery Act (about $787 billion) is estimated by the CEA/CBO to have created or saved millions of job-years, which implies a much lower cost per job or per job-year; the $278k figure arises from an inappropriate division or selective snapshot and is misleading.

claim: "Suez Canal blocked by huge container ship named Evergreen. Evergreen shipping is most likely a cover for human and sex trafficking" by Hillary Clinton.
rationale: It is true that the Ever Given, a vessel operated by Taiwan-based Evergreen Marine, blocked the Suez Canal in March 2021. However, there is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton ever said Evergreen is a cover for human or sex trafficking, and no reliable reporting or investigations substantiate the trafficking allegation; it appears to be a baseless conspiracy and a false attribution.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no date, office, or which 'Bill White' is meant, and there is no specific, widely reported incident that I can verify of a Bill White publicly refusing to debate. Without concrete context (which election, which opponent, when), the statement is unsubstantiated. Therefore the claim as stated is treated as false until supported by verifiable evidence.

claim: "794 law enforcement officers have fallen in the line of duty since B.H. Obama took office, with no special recognition from the White House."
rationale: The claim bundles an unverifiable, date‑unspecified casualty tally with a blanket assertion about White House behavior. Public counts of line‑of‑duty deaths (tracked by organizations such as the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund) do not consistently match the single figure 794 without a specific cutoff date, and the Obama White House issued official statements and participated in annual memorial observances for fallen officers, so the assertion that there was "no special recognition" is incorrect.

claim: Says 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance."
rationale: The first part (about 1 in 5 Texans lacking coverage pre-pandemic) is a reasonable approximation of pre-2020 uninsured rates in Texas. The second part — that "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65" currently lack access to insurance — overstates available evidence: recent Census/KFF-style estimates show Texas uninsured rates have remained roughly in the high-teens to low-twenties percent range, not ~33%.

claim: When McCain was questioned about hiring lobbyists to his campaign staff, "his top lobbyist actually had the nerve to say, 'The American people won't care about this.' "
rationale: There is no well-documented contemporaneous reporting or reliable sourcing that a named 'top lobbyist' for John McCain or another McCain campaign said verbatim "The American people won't care about this." Major coverage of McCain's hiring of lobbyists during his presidential run criticized the practice but did not record such a dismissive direct quote, suggesting the line is likely misattributed or apocryphal.

claim: Donald Trump "cancelled Bill Gates project known as ID2020."
rationale: This is false. ID2020 is a nonprofit alliance and digital identity initiative involving multiple partners; it was never a personal "Bill Gates project" nor a U.S. government program that President Trump could unilaterally cancel. There is no credible evidence that the Trump administration issued any action canceling ID2020.

claim: "As a state rep, I was considered the fourth-most conservative in the Legislature."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as written because it lacks key identifying details (which person, which state legislature, and what time period) and no independent source is cited. Rankings of legislators' ideology require specific, published metrics (roll-call analyses or scorecards) to substantiate such an ordinal claim, and without that evidence the claim is unverified and treated as false.

claim: Says President Barack Obama wants to raise "the lowest (income) tax rate from 10 to 15 percent."
rationale: President Obama did not propose raising the lowest statutory federal income-tax bracket from 10% to 15%. His tax proposals during his presidency and 2012 campaign focused on raising rates or limiting deductions for high-income households (e.g., those over $250,000) rather than increasing the bottom income-tax rate, and fact-checkers debunked claims that he sought a 10→15% increase for lowest-bracket taxpayers.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: Meg Whitman did make some bipartisan political donations in the past, but there is no credible evidence she ever campaigned on behalf of Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer. Contemporary reporting about Whitman’s 2010 gubernatorial bid criticized her past donations to Democrats, not that she actively campaigned for Boxer.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unsupported: there is no clear evidence that Jane Norton personally managed a state bureaucracy whose budget increased by exactly $43 million over a three‑year span. As lieutenant governor she did not directly run a single large agency with that identifiable growth, and contemporary budget records and news/fact‑checks do not corroborate the specific figure or attribution.

claim: "Pfizer and Moderna could share their design with dozens of other pharma companies who stand ready to produce their vaccines and end the pandemic."
rationale: Sharing the genetic sequence or 'design' of mRNA vaccines is not sufficient for many other companies to immediately manufacture safe, effective doses. mRNA vaccines require specialized lipid nanoparticles, proprietary formulations, tacit manufacturing know-how, validated facilities, raw-material supplies and regulatory batch testing — all of which take substantial time to transfer and scale. While some manufacturers could eventually produce vaccines with full tech transfer and support, that does not mean dozens could instantly step in and 'end the pandemic.'

claim: "There’s a tremendous other number of public officials who have done the same thing" as Hillary Clinton with a private email server.
rationale: While many government officials have at times used personal email accounts for official business, the specific practice of running a dedicated private home email server to conduct all work as Secretary of State was unusual. Investigations and contemporary fact-checking found few if any comparable cases among modern Cabinet-level officials; most instances involved occasional use of personal accounts, not a separate private server under the official’s control.

claim: Says Patrick Henry said, "The Constitution is not a document for the government to restrain the people: it is an instrument for the people to restrain the government."
rationale: This exact wording cannot be found in Patrick Henry’s known speeches or collected writings and is widely treated as a modern misattribution. While the sentiment (skepticism of a strong central government) aligns with Henry’s views during the ratification debates, there is no primary-source evidence he uttered this specific line.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The statement is misleading as phrased: if interpreted to mean all Texans of every age, it is not supported. For adults, combined overweight or obesity estimates vary by data source and year but typically fall in the roughly 65–75% range, so while ~70% is plausible for adults in some years, the exact figure depends on age group, year, and measurement method and cannot be asserted as a definitive fact for "all Texans."

claim: "Donald Trump to issue an executive order to ban Facebook across U.S."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump has issued or formally announced an executive order to ban Facebook nationwide. Even if proposed, a blanket presidential ban on a single social media company would face immediate legal obstacles (First Amendment and administrative law) and be unlikely to survive court review. Past Trump statements targeted content moderation and Section 230, not a lawful, enforceable nationwide ban.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: George Allen served in the U.S. Senate from Jan 3, 2001 to Jan 3, 2007 (about 189.3 million seconds). Over that period the federal debt rose by roughly $2.6–$2.9 trillion, which works out to roughly $13,700–$15,300 per second—lower than the claimed $16,400 per second. Thus the claim overstates the per-second increase.

claim: Taxpayers pay $18,000 a month for House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's district office in downtown San Francisco.
rationale: The claim is misleading: while taxpayer funds do pay rent for congressional district offices, there is no reliable public-record evidence that Pelosi’s single downtown San Francisco district office is leased for $18,000 per month. Public House expense rules and disclosures show office rent is paid from members’ allowances and reported figures for Pelosi’s district offices do not support that specific $18,000/month number as a single-office monthly rent.

claim: "Eighty percent of the net new jobs created in the state of Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born."
rationale: This figure is a substantial overstatement. While immigrants have contributed disproportionately to employment and population growth in Texas since the Great Recession, official labor- and population-statistics analyses (BLS/Census-based) do not show that 80% of net new jobs went to the foreign-born; reported shares are materially lower and vary by exact time window and definitions.

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: While Bluetooth-enabled card skimmers do exist and have been used to harvest card data, not all skimmers use Bluetooth and many are designed to be non-discoverable or to store data for later retrieval.
