rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau data show that roughly 35–40% of U.S. adults (age 25+) hold a bachelor's degree or higher, so about 60–65% do not — not as high as 70%. The claim overstates the share without a college degree by several percentage points.

claim: Says opponents of proposed Austin school district bonds say the district’s "debt load doubles with these new bonds."
rationale: A district’s debt load would only “double” if the new bonds equaled the entire existing outstanding debt; that is uncommon. Opponents may assert the debt doubles as a rhetorical claim, but without figures showing the proposed bond amount matches current outstanding debt, the assertion is not supported. Generally, bond proposals add a specific incremental amount rather than literally doubling total debt.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Steve Southerland cast a vote that uniquely or explicitly 'voted himself health care for life.' Members of Congress are federal employees eligible for standard federal health and retirement benefits under the Federal Employees Health Benefits and retirement systems if they meet service/age requirements, but that is not the same as a single vote granting lifetime health care to an individual member. The phrasing is therefore misleading and not supported by known legislative records.

claim: "Now, there was a time when someone like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes."
rationale: This statement is accurate: both Antonin Scalia and Ruth Bader Ginsburg received well over 95 votes in their Senate confirmation votes. Scalia was confirmed 98-0 in 1986 and Ginsburg was confirmed 96-3 in 1993, so there indeed was a time when nominees received 95-plus votes.

claim: Quotes Donald Trump as saying in 2013, "A shutdown falls on the President’s lack of leadership. He can’t even control his own party and get people together in a room. A shutdown means the president is weak."
rationale: I find no reliable record or contemporaneous news report of Donald Trump saying that exact line in 2013. Major archives of Trump’s public statements and media coverage of the 2013 shutdown do not show this quoted phrasing, suggesting the quote is likely misattributed or fabricated.

claim: "Scott Walker to cut $300 million from universities, spend $500 million on a pro basketball stadium."
rationale: Walker’s budgets did include substantial reductions to the University of Wisconsin system (on the order of a few hundred million over budget cycles), but the assertion that he would spend $500 million on a professional basketball stadium is inaccurate. The Milwaukee Bucks arena (Fiserv Forum) had a total cost of about $524 million, but the public/state contribution was roughly $200–250 million with large private and local shares; Walker did not unilaterally authorize a $500 million state stadium payment.

claim: "The United States imprisons more than any nation in the world."
rationale: The United States has one of the largest known prison populations and the highest incarceration rate among major democracies, but it is not unequivocally the single country that imprisons more people than any other. China’s detention systems and reporting are opaque and may include very large numbers of prisoners and detainees not reflected in comparable international datasets. Because of these data gaps and differing definitions (prisoners vs. detainees vs. administrative detention), the absolute claim is not reliably supportable.

claim: "Our conservative Georgia values are under attack" ... (People) are "calling for the removal of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson statues."
rationale: The opening phrase 'Our conservative Georgia values are under attack' is a subjective political opinion and not a verifiable factual claim. The specific assertion that people are calling for removal of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson statues has occurred in isolated national protests criticizing slaveholding founders, but there is no clear evidence of a widespread, coordinated campaign in Georgia specifically to remove those two statues as presented. The statement conflates opinion and an unqualified factual claim without necessary context, so it is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "wants to force residents to fund Planned Parenthood abortion business."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes Evers' position. He has backed restoring Medicaid and family‑planning reimbursements and allowing public dollars to pay for non‑abortion health services provided by Planned Parenthood, but has not proposed a policy that forces residents to personally fund abortions or directly pay for an "abortion business." Opponents often conflate paying for provider services with funding abortions, which is misleading.

claim: Photos show a photojournalist crying while capturing pictures of the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
rationale: I cannot verify any widely reported or reliably sourced photograph that clearly shows a photojournalist crying while taking pictures of the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. Images from conflict zones are frequently miscaptioned or reposted out of context, and without an original source, photographer credit, date, or agency verification the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "John McCain said...in December he was surprised there was a subprime mortgage problem."
rationale: There is no widely reported or verifiable record of John McCain saying in any December that he was surprised there was a subprime mortgage problem. During the 2007–2008 housing turmoil McCain publicly commented on and supported actions addressing mortgage issues, so a remark expressing surprise would likely have been documented but is not found in contemporary coverage or transcripts.

claim: "Newspapers have framed this election as my fight against the Illinois mafia."
rationale: The claim is presented in sweeping terms but lacks verifiable specifics; there is no widespread evidence that newspapers generally framed any recent election broadly as a candidate's "fight against the Illinois mafia." Media coverage is diverse and while individual opinion pieces or commentators might have used provocative language, that does not constitute a general newspaper framing. Without naming the election, time period, or citing multiple mainstream outlets using that exact frame, the statement overstates what the press collectively did.

claim: Says an arts tax would provide "funding for certified arts and music teachers for every elementary school serving Portland residents."
rationale: This claim is misleading: local arts tax measures typically apply only to specified school districts or public schools and include eligibility and funding limits rather than an absolute guarantee of certified arts and music teachers at every elementary that serves city residents. Without the exact ballot language, you cannot assume the tax would cover all elementary schools serving Portland residents (including charter, private, or out-of-district schools) or fully fund a certified teacher position at every site. Promotional summaries often overstate reach.

claim: Says Democratic recall opponent Mahlon Mitchell sent a letter "encouraging folks to boycott more than 100 companies."
rationale: There is no reliable, documented evidence that Mahlon Mitchell sent a letter explicitly encouraging a boycott of more than 100 companies. While Mitchell, a firefighters' union leader and Democratic activist, has supported targeted boycotts or criticized corporate actions in the past, the specific claim that he circulated a letter urging people to boycott 100+ firms is unsubstantiated.

claim: "In the 1990s, the Biden Crime Bill added 100,000 cops to America's streets. As a result, murder and violent crime rates went down eight years in a row."
rationale: The 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act did include funding to help hire 100,000 police officers, so the first clause is essentially correct. But saying murder and violent crime rates fell "eight years in a row" solely "as a result" of that bill is misleading: U.S. violent crime began declining in the early 1990s for multiple reasons, the exact multi-year trend depends on the start/end years chosen, and scholars attribute the drop to many factors (economy, policing changes, incarceration, demographics, reduced lead exposure, etc.), not just the hiring funded by the bill.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: There is no evidence in official State of the Union transcripts or contemporaneous news coverage that those exact words were spoken during the address. The quoted language appears to be a paraphrase or a later remark about Democratic reactions, not part of the formal State of the Union speech itself. Because the claim ties the quote specifically to the address, that attribution is incorrect.

claim: Says Ken Cuccinelli "attacked churches for helping the poor."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Ken Cuccinelli mounted a campaign specifically attacking churches for providing aid to the poor. His public controversies as Virginia Attorney General and later at DHS involved issues like abortion, contraception policy, immigration and voting law, rather than targeting charitable church assistance programs.

claim: Says "Barcelona terrorist" is cousins with former President Barack Obama.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any Barcelona attacker was a cousin of Barack Obama. Multiple news organizations and fact-checkers reviewed the claim and found no genealogical or documentary link between Obama's family (whose known relatives are primarily Kenyan) and the individuals involved in the Barcelona attack (reported as Moroccan/Spanish-Moroccan).

claim: As the number of vaccines administered to children has increased in the United States, so has the autism rate.
rationale: The claim implies a causal link between increasing vaccine doses and rising autism rates. Extensive large-scale epidemiological studies and authoritative reviews have found no association between vaccines or vaccine schedules and autism; increases in diagnosed autism are largely explained by changes in diagnostic criteria, awareness, and reporting.

claim: Says "Monica Lewinsky Found Dead" in a burglary.
rationale: There are no credible reports that Monica Lewinsky was found dead in a burglary; major news organizations and public records have not reported such an event. Lewinsky has continued public activity in recent years, and past death rumors about public figures have often been hoaxes or misinformation.

claim: "For every extra year that a girl stays in secondary school, her chance of getting infected with HIV/AIDS decreases by half."
rationale: The claim states a precise and universal causal effect (each extra year of secondary school halves a girl's HIV risk) that is not supported by the evidence. Research finds that more schooling is often associated with reduced HIV risk and some interventions (e.g., scholarships or fee waivers) can lower incidence, but effect sizes are heterogeneous and far smaller than a consistent 50% reduction per additional year.

claim: "Gas is high because they shut down production in the U.S." under the Biden administration.
rationale: The claim is false because U.S. oil and gas production was not shut down under the Biden administration; total U.S. crude oil production recovered after the 2020 pandemic dip and reached near-record levels during the administration. While the administration paused some new federal leasing and implemented regulatory limits, those actions did not amount to a nationwide shutdown, and gasoline prices are largely driven by global oil markets, OPEC+ decisions, demand recovery, and refinery constraints.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: Contemporary news reports and independent fact-checkers found no evidence that Tim Wolfe was driving a car through students at the MU Homecoming Parade or that he struck a student. The viral social-media claim misidentified the driver; police and media accounts did not link Wolfe to the vehicle or the alleged hitting of a student.

claim: "I do provide universal health care."
rationale: The statement "I do provide universal health care" is unverifiable as written because the speaker and the jurisdiction/timeframe are not specified. Universal health care is a defined policy outcome (coverage for all residents for needed services without financial hardship) that must be demonstrated by specific laws or programs; without that context the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: There were "$2 billion in earmarks in fiscal year 2012."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as a clear factual claim. The House imposed an earmark moratorium in 2011 and congressional totals for FY2012 depend heavily on how one defines "earmarks" or "congressionally directed spending," and official records and CRS summaries do not unambiguously show a $2 billion earmark total for FY2012.

claim: The state crime lab under Attorney General Josh Kaul "is testing significantly less items than former AG Brad Schimel and is still taking longer to test many categories of key items in comparison to Schimel, including DNA."
rationale: The claim asserts a broad, across-the-board decline in testing volume and slower turnaround under AG Kaul compared with AG Schimel, but publicly available reporting and official metrics do not support a consistent, comprehensive pattern showing significantly fewer items tested and longer times for many categories including DNA. Performance varied by category and year, and some units saw improvements while others had continuing challenges, so the blanket statement is not supported without specific datasets and timeframes.

claim: "These are radical Islamic terrorists, and (Hillary Clinton) won't even mention the word."
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion that Hillary Clinton "won't even mention" the words "radical Islamic terrorists." In practice she repeatedly condemned Islamist extremist violence and referred to Islamist or radical extremism in various ways; while she often avoided that exact phrase for political and policy reasons, she did publicly address and name Islamist terrorism and extremist groups. Therefore the absolute claim that she refuses to even mention it is not accurate.

claim: Missouri "is leading the country when it comes to improving services for mental and behavioral health. Innovation is happening right here."
rationale: The claim that Missouri is "leading the country" on improving mental and behavioral health is an unsubstantiated, sweeping assertion. National indicators and rankings (access to care, treatment rates, suicide and overdose statistics) do not consistently place Missouri at the top, and while the state has some recent initiatives and pilots, that does not support a clear nationwide leadership claim.

claim: "Vern Buchanan. His old business was caught illegally funneling over $60,000 in campaign donations to Buchanan to influence his election."
rationale: Reporting shows there were investigations and at least one guilty plea by a former employee connected to firms tied to Vern Buchanan that involved making improper or straw donations to multiple candidates. However, I find no authoritative record that Buchanan's business was officially "caught" funneling more than $60,000 specifically to his campaign or that Buchanan was charged with receiving such illegal funds. The claim overstates and presents a specific dollar figure and legal finding that is not supported by clear public records.

claim: "$700 billion was robbed (from Medicare) to pay for Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included roughly $700–716 billion in reductions to projected Medicare spending over about a decade, mostly by reducing payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and by targeting fraud and waste. Those were statutory savings and budget offsets used to help fund coverage expansions and reduce deficits, not an illegal "robbery" of Medicare benefits; the law largely prohibited cuts to beneficiary benefits. Calling it "robbed" is misleading because it conflates projected spending reductions and provider payment changes with theft or direct cuts to Medicare benefits.

claim: The church Barack Obama belongs to only admits black people.
rationale: The claim is false. Barack Obama attended Trinity United Church of Christ in Chicago, a historically African American congregation, but that church does not have a policy admitting only Black people. It is part of the United Church of Christ tradition, which broadly affirms non-discrimination and open membership.

claim: "The Coast Guard confiscated 200 tons of contraband, heroin, and so forth. At the border they collected 20 tons."
rationale: The statement gives specific seizure totals but provides no timeframe, agency definitions, or source, so the numbers cannot be verified as presented. Public seizure totals reported by agencies (Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, DOJ) vary year to year and are published in agency reports; the exact figures claimed (200 tons by the Coast Guard and 20 tons 'at the border') are not corroborated without a cited source.

claim: Under the Democratic health plan, families "will be forced to spend an additional $2,100 a year to keep their current health care."
rationale: The statement is a blanket, absolute claim that is not supported by evidence for any single, specific Democratic plan. Independent analyses of major Democratic health proposals have shown effects vary by income, employer coverage, and specific plan design; some families could pay more, many would pay less or see no change. The $2,100 figure appears to come from selective worst‑case assumptions used in political advertising rather than a uniform, mandatory increase.

claim: "15 years ago, cancer drugs cost an average of $10,000 a year. Now it’s $10,000 a month."
rationale: This statement is misleading and not supported as a general fact. While launch prices for many new cancer drugs have risen dramatically over the past decade-plus and some modern therapies can cost on the order of $100k+ per year (which would be roughly $8k–$12k per month), the claim that the average cancer drug cost $10,000 per year 15 years ago and now costs $10,000 per month overstates the change and conflates list price, regimen duration, and patient out-of-pocket costs. Many older and generic oncology drugs remained much cheaper, and published analyses report rising launch prices but not that every or the average cancer drug rose by that exact factor.

claim: 110 people a day move to Austin.
rationale: The claim is presented as a timeless fact but lacks a timeframe and clear definition (city vs. metro, net vs. gross moves). Population growth for Austin has varied year to year and no consistent, current official source supports a steady rate of exactly 110 people per day; annual totals reported by census estimates and local data do not consistently match that daily average. Therefore the blanket assertion is misleading.

claim: "Rhode Island has the highest percentage of uninsured adults of any state in New England."
rationale: Available recent data from sources like the Census American Community Survey and health-policy trackers show Rhode Island has among the lower-to-mid uninsured adult rates in New England due to Medicaid expansion and state programs; New Hampshire (and in some years Maine) typically reports the highest adult uninsured percentage in the region. Therefore the categorical claim that Rhode Island has the highest uninsured adult rate in New England is incorrect.

claim: As a senator, Hillary Clinton "has her name on three laws in eight years."
rationale: Nonpartisan fact-checkers and congressional records indicate Hillary Clinton had her name on more than three laws during her 2001–2009 Senate tenure. The "three laws in eight years" claim relies on a very narrow counting method (for example, only counting primary sponsorship of certain public laws) and ignores cosponsorships and other enacted measures that carried her name.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: Jason Carter campaigned for Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act and for using federal matching funds, but there is no clear evidence he advocated diverting Georgia tax dollars to run advertising campaigns to 'promote Obamacare.' Opponents frequently framed his support for expansion and enrollment outreach as using state money to promote the law, but his stated positions emphasized accepting federal funds and using state capacity to enroll eligible residents.

claim: "China owns about 29% of (the U.S.) debt."
rationale: China does not own 29% of U.S. debt. China’s holdings of U.S. Treasury securities have generally been in the roughly $1.0–1.3 trillion range (varying by year), which corresponds to a small single-digit or low-teens percentage depending on the denominator used, not 29%. The 29% figure is inconsistent with standard Treasury and TIC breakdowns of foreign and total U.S. debt.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: The claim is an unverified anecdote and implausible for a third-year public school teacher in Dallas public-school pay scales. Typical Dallas-area public teacher salary schedules and reported averages show early-career teachers earn well below $90,000, and reaching that level usually requires many more years, advanced degrees, or substantial extra stipends. While an individual could earn $90,000 if they work in a higher‑paying district, private school, or have substantial additional income, the statement as presented is not supported by typical Dallas teacher pay data.

claim: "Biden and most Democrats want to cap insulin prices at $35 per month. All 50 Republicans in the Senate are opposed to it."
rationale: President Biden has promoted a $35-per-month insulin cap and many Democrats have supported legislation to limit insulin costs, so the first part is broadly accurate. However the absolute claim that all 50 Republican senators are opposed is unlikely and not reliably true—Republican positions have varied by specific proposal (Medicare-only caps versus broader caps) and at least some Republicans have backed measures to lower insulin costs or signaled support for limits in certain contexts. Because the statement asserts unanimous opposition by every Republican senator, it overstates the uniformity of GOP positions.

claim: "Mayor Bloomberg was busy blaming African Americans and Latinos for the housing crisis in 2008."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Mayor Michael Bloomberg publicly blamed African American or Latino communities for causing the 2008 housing crisis. The crisis was widely attributed to predatory subprime lending, mortgage securitization, regulatory failures, and Wall Street practices, and Bloomberg's public comments focused on regulation, lending practices, and market factors rather than blaming minority groups. Characterizing him as 'busy blaming' these communities overstates and misrepresents the record.

claim: Says Nevada state Sen. Michael Roberson "forced Common Core for Nevada schools."
rationale: Nevada’s adoption of the Common Core State Standards was a multi‑actor process (state education officials, the State Board of Education and statewide policymaking around 2010), not the unilateral action of a single state senator. Michael Roberson served in the Nevada Legislature later and may have supported or opposed related legislation, but there is no clear evidence he alone “forced” Common Core on Nevada schools.

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: National polling does not consistently show a majority (>50%) identifying as "pro‑life." Major, repeated surveys (e.g., Gallup and Pew Research) typically find the public split or a plurality favoring "pro‑choice," and results swing with question wording and timing. There is no clear consensus across polls that over half of Americans identify as pro‑life.

claim: "No one beta-tested" healthcare.gov.
rationale: The claim is false: multiple kinds of testing (unit, integration, usability and some load/pilot tests) were conducted on healthcare.gov before launch. Independent reviews (GAO and HHS OIG) and contemporaneous reporting found that testing was incomplete and not an adequate end-to-end or public "beta" test, which contributed to the site’s failures.

claim: "The Chinese last year probably stole $360 billion in intellectual property from the United States."
rationale: There is no credible, authoritative evidence that China 'probably stole $360 billion' in U.S. intellectual property in a single recent year. Estimates of losses from economic espionage and IP theft vary widely, come from contested methodologies or aggregate multi-year ranges, and no major U.S. government or independent body has substantiated a $360 billion figure for last year.

claim: In Congress, "on the Democratic side of the room, you’ve got men and women of all different races; on the other side, you’ve got a bunch of white men in dark suits, all over 55 or so."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. It is true that Democratic delegations in Congress are, on average, more racially diverse and include more women, and that Republican delegations are disproportionately white men and older, but Republicans are not exclusively “a bunch of white men” nor are they all over 55. The claim ignores existing Republican women, nonwhite Republicans, and younger members and thus misstates the composition.

claim: "They eliminated the funding for community policing."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and makes a blanket claim without specifying who 'they' are or which jurisdiction and time period are meant. Funding for community policing is provided through multiple channels (federal grants, state and local budgets) and has been altered in different ways in different places; there is no general, verifiable fact that all funding for community policing was eliminated. Without a specific actor and budget to check, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship is "still the richest scholarship program in America."
rationale: Georgia's HOPE scholarship was once unusually generous when first introduced, but it has been scaled back over time and does not objectively remain the "richest" scholarship program in the United States. Numerous other state, federal, military, and private scholarship or grant programs can deliver equal or greater total benefits (full tuition plus stipends or living allowances) than HOPE currently provides.

claim: Four (maybe five) Latinos have served on the Austin City Council.
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable and is likely inaccurate. Official rosters and historical accounts of Austin City Council do not consistently categorize members by ethnicity, and counts change depending on whether you include appointed or interim members, earlier Mexican‑American officeholders, or recent councilors. Without a clear timeframe and definition of 'Latino,' the asserted fixed number (four or five) cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Fox News uses photo of a married couple promoting ‘traditional marriage’ and the photo is actually of a same-sex couple."
rationale: The claim is vague and no widely documented, verifiable instance supports that Fox News ran an image of a same-sex couple while explicitly promoting ‘traditional marriage.’ While media outlets occasionally miscaption images, searches of reputable fact-checkers and major news archives show no clear corroboration of this specific allegation. Without a date, article link or screenshot the claim cannot be verified and appears to be an unsubstantiated social-media assertion.

claim: Republicans are now "taking credit" for provisions of the health care bill "that they had tried to derail."
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsourced generalization about an entire party's behavior and cannot be verified as universally true. While there are documented cases where individual Republicans have highlighted or supported provisions they previously opposed, the claim as phrased (that Republicans are now taking credit for provisions they had tried to derail) lacks specific examples, timeframe, or context needed to confirm it.

claim: "Tommy Thompson wanted to implant data chips in humans."
rationale: As U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary in 2005, Tommy Thompson publicly endorsed researching implantable microchips/devices to store medical or vaccination data and spoke in favor of exploring their use. His comments were reported widely; he framed them as voluntary/medical tracking rather than a proposal for mandatory government implantation.

claim: Clicking on this link in a text message lets sex traffickers track you.
rationale: The blanket claim is false: merely clicking a link in a text message does not, by itself, let someone physically track you. At most the site can learn your IP address and basic device/browser signals, or the link could lead to phishing or malware that — if you then provide credentials, grant location permissions, or install an app — might enable tracking. The statement is misleading without those additional actions.

claim: "I did very well with young people in Ohio, Massachusetts, California."
rationale: The statement is too vague and lacks a speaker, timeframe, definition of 'young people,' or a measurable metric, so it cannot be verified as stated. No specific, corroborated polling or election data is presented that shows uniformly strong performance among youth in Ohio, Massachusetts, and California.

claim: "Kamala Harris is the prosecutor who refused to charge the police in the murder of Oscar Grant!"
rationale: Kamala Harris, as Alameda County District Attorney, did not refuse to charge anyone in the Oscar Grant killing — her office charged BART officer Johannes Mehserle with murder, and he was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter. The claim likely conflates criticism of Harris's handling and comments with an outright refusal to file charges, which is inaccurate.

claim: Low gas prices in Russia, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia show that Joe Biden’s decision to cancel the Keystone Pipeline project is to blame for U.S. prices.
rationale: This is misleading: low retail gasoline prices in Russia, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia are largely the result of government subsidies and domestic pricing policies, not evidence about U.S. policy effects. U.S. pump prices are driven primarily by global crude markets, OPEC decisions, refining capacity, taxes, and regional supply logistics; the cancellation of the Keystone XL pipeline would likely have had only a modest regional effect on crude flows, not been the principal cause of U.S. prices.

claim: "This is the most generous country in the world when it comes to immigration. There are a million people a year who legally immigrate to the United States."
rationale: The claim bundles a subjective value judgment and a numerical assertion. The U.S. does admit large numbers of legal migrants, but annual counts of new lawful permanent residents have typically been in the several-hundred-thousand range in recent years (and only approach or exceed one million in some years depending on definitions), so the blanket statement of "a million people a year" is misleading. Describing the U.S. as "the most generous country" on immigration is subjective and depends entirely on metrics (per capita refugee resettlement, asylum policies, family reunification, etc.), so it cannot be treated as an established fact.

claim: "It is a fact that it costs more to run the schools in August."
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal fact but costs to run schools in August vary by location and circumstances. In many regions schools are on summer break and have lower staffing and utility expenses, while in others high cooling costs or summer programs can increase August expenses. Because the statement is unqualified and not universally true, it is false as stated.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: The token 'hidden' in website code normally refers to a technical attribute or CSS/class name (e.g., hidden inputs or elements) and is not legal language that automatically makes users waive privacy rights. Legal waivers of privacy require explicit, conspicuous consent in terms or agreements and are governed by site privacy policies and applicable law; an HTML attribute or class label does not itself create or communicate a legal waiver.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Scott Walker put forward a plan to wholesale privatize all state lands or to 'sell our deer to the highest bidder.' While his administration pursued budget cuts and occasionally proposed selling specific surplus parcels or changing management arrangements, those actions are not equivalent to a program to privatize state lands or auction off wildlife. The phrasing appears to be a partisan exaggeration of limited property-sales or management proposals.

claim: COVID spelled backward is "divoc" which means "possession of the evil spirit" in Hebrew.
rationale: Reversing the English letters of 'COVID' yields 'DIVOC', but that sequence is not a Hebrew word meaning possession by an evil spirit. The Hebrew term for a possessing spirit in Jewish folklore is 'dybbuk' (Hebrew: דיבוק), commonly transliterated dybbuk or dibbuk, which is not 'divoc'. The claim conflates an English reversal with an unrelated Hebrew word.

claim: Says as GOP was picking a convention city, "I recommended Ohio."
rationale: The claim is unverified as presented: it attributes a quoted recommendation to an unspecified speaker without providing a date or context, and there is no publicly available record confirming that a particular individual said 'I recommended Ohio' during a GOP convention-site selection. Because the statement lacks attribution and corroborating evidence, it cannot be treated as a verified fact.

claim: Says Donald Trump "was one of the people who rooted for the housing crisis. He said back in 2006, ‘Gee, I hope it does collapse because then I can go in and buy some and make some money.’ "
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and later summaries attribute to Donald Trump a 2006 remark expressing that he hoped a housing downturn would allow him to buy properties cheaply. The quoted phrasing may vary slightly across reports, but the substance — that he welcomed a collapse as an investor opportunity — is supported by multiple media accounts from that period.

claim: Says protesters at the Wisconsin state Capitol on the night the state Senate passed collective bargaining changes damaged the windshield of his car.
rationale: The statement asserts that protesters at the Wisconsin state Capitol damaged the windshield of 'his' car on the night the senate passed collective bargaining changes, but no verifiable, contemporaneous public records or reliable news reports corroborate that protesters were responsible for a specific individual's windshield damage that night. Reporting from the 2011 protests documented large crowds and some property damage, but investigators and news outlets did not establish a clear, attributable incident matching this claim. Because the claim lacks identifying details and independent confirmation, it should not be treated as factual.

claim: The Foundation for Government Accountability, which supported a Florida law requiring drug testing of welfare recipients, is a "Koch brothers affiliated group."
rationale: Multiple news reports and watchdog analyses have identified the Foundation for Government Accountability as part of the network of organizations backed by Koch-aligned donors; it has received funding routed through donor-advised funds and donors associated with the Koch network and often advances the same policy agenda. Although FGA is an independent nonprofit rather than a formal subsidiary of the Koch enterprises, it is widely described as Koch-affiliated because of funding and close collaboration with Koch-backed groups.

claim: "The barber regulation here in Missouri is 10,000 words long….the book of Revelation is (also) 10,000 words long."
rationale: The claim asserts two precise equal word counts but provides no specification of which text or edition. The word count of the Book of Revelation varies by translation and edition and is not uniquely 10,000 words, and Missouri barber regulations are codified across statutes and administrative rules whose combined text length depends on what is included — making the precise figure implausible without documentation.

claim: In 2008, "only 54 percent of Latinos in Texas were registered to vote and only 35 percent actually turned out."
rationale: The statement is likely misleading: published analyses of 2008 Hispanic political participation typically distinguish between voting-age population (VAP) and voting-eligible/citizen population, and turnout measures (of eligible, of registered, or of VAP). The flat claims “54% registered” and “35% turned out” for Texas Latinos lack that context and do not match commonly cited estimates that show different percentages depending on the denominator and that Latino turnout in 2008 was higher than 35% when measured against eligible voters. Without a clear denominator or source, the phrasing is inaccurate.

claim: Wisconsin voter turnout jumped from 67% in 2016 to 89% in 2020.
rationale: Wisconsin turnout did rise in 2020 but not to 89% statewide. Official statistics and widely reported summaries put Wisconsin's 2020 turnout in the low-to-mid 70s percent range depending on the denominator (registered voters or voting-eligible population), so an 89% statewide rate is inconsistent with those totals.

claim: "The majority of minimum wage workers...are mothers."
rationale: Relevant labor-force data and multiple fact-checks show that mothers do not make up a majority of minimum-wage workers; a substantial share of low-wage workers are teens and young adults without children. Claims that 'the majority...are mothers' rely on imprecise definitions or selective subsets of data and do not reflect broader national statistics.

claim: Says state schools superintendent candidate Don Pridemore "voted for the largest cuts to public education in our state history" and for "$2.3 billion in tax breaks for corporations and the wealthy."
rationale: The claim bundles a partisan characterization and a specific dollar figure that require precise legislative and budgetary context. I cannot verify that Don Pridemore individually voted for a measure described unambiguously as "the largest cuts to public education in our state history" or that his vote directly enacted exactly $2.3 billion in corporate/wealth tax breaks; such labels are commonly used in political advertising and overstate or simplify complex budget votes.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said when "we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Obama saying 'when we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved.' His public statements after the May 2011 raid framed the operation as a significant achievement but explicitly noted the broader threat remained and that work to combat terrorism would continue. The quote is a misattribution or oversimplified paraphrase.

claim: "In a very real sense, (Oklahoma has) flattened the curve. ... The number of cases in Oklahoma — it's declined precipitously."
rationale: The claim gives no date or metric and is therefore not verifiable as stated; while Oklahoma experienced brief declines in reported COVID-19 cases at various points, its epidemic curve also showed multiple resurgences rather than a sustained, precipitous decline. Without a specific time window and accounting for testing variability and reporting lags, the assertion that Oklahoma "flattened the curve" and that cases "declined precipitously" is unsupported.

claim: "We are spending more on affordable housing than we're spending on Dix Park right now."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify — it does not define who 'we' refers to (city, county, state, or federal) or the timeframe for 'right now.' Public budget and capital-spending records are required to compare current expenditures on Dix Park versus affordable housing, and no specific evidence was provided. Because the claim lacks jurisdictional and temporal specificity and no supporting data is available, it cannot be verified as true.

claim: The Obama White House recognizes a "baby that has not been born" for security purposes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama White House implemented a policy treating an unborn fetus as a recognized person for White House security purposes (such as issuing IDs or Secret Service protection). U.S. White House and Secret Service procedures apply to living, born individuals, and claims to the contrary appear to misinterpret statements or conflate unrelated policies.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: Measured against the full executive tenures of Barack Obama (eight years as President) and Joe Biden (eight years as Vice President, plus later service as President), their combined executive experience far exceeds Sarah Palin’s relatively brief tenure as Alaska governor (about two‑to‑three years) and earlier small‑town mayoralty. Without a specified timeframe the claim is misleading; it was arguably true as a 2008 campaign talking point (before Obama and Biden held executive office), but false in general or after they took executive office.

claim: "Mexico’s Next President Calls for An Invasion Of The US"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified reporting that Mexico’s president-elect publicly called for an invasion of the United States. Mexican presidential candidates and leaders have not advocated military aggression against the U.S., and an assertion like this would have been widely reported by major news outlets. The claim likely stems from satire, misattribution, or fabricated social-media content.

claim: Says Tom Hughes supports paving over thousands of acres with over-development and sprawl.
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified: there is no specific, attributable public record showing a person named Tom Hughes explicitly endorsing 'paving over thousands of acres' for over-development and sprawl. Without identifying which Tom Hughes and citing concrete statements, votes, or policy proposals, the allegation cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton called the Trans-Pacific Partnership "the gold standard. You called it the gold standard of trade deals. You said it’s the finest deal you’ve ever seen."
rationale: Hillary Clinton did publicly describe the Trans‑Pacific Partnership as a potential “gold standard” for trade agreements while she was Secretary of State and in earlier statements, but there is no clear contemporaneous reliable record of her saying the exact phrase “it’s the finest deal you’ve ever seen.” The claimant bundles a verified “gold standard” endorsement with an unverified quotation, making the composite assertion misleading.

claim: "We have over a million (legal immigrants) a year, more than at any time in the history of this country. We have the largest percentage of immigrants, almost tied now with the historical high as a percentage of immigrants living in this country."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. Annual admissions of lawful permanent residents have exceeded one million in past decades, and the U.S. foreign‑born share of population was higher in the late 19th/early 20th centuries than it is today. While contemporary immigrant shares are high by late‑20th century standards, they do not exceed the historical peak and the counts depend on which legal-status measure is used.

claim: Polling shows that nearly 74 percent of National Rifle Association members "support requiring background checks for all gun sales."
rationale: I cannot verify a reputable, specific poll showing nearly 74% of NRA members support requiring background checks for all gun sales. While many polls consistently show a majority of NRA members and gun owners favor some form of background checks, reported percentages vary by poll and question wording and are often lower than 74%. Without a cited source, the precise 74% figure appears unsupported.

claim: Says new Medicare billing guidelines "have nine codes for (injuries by) turkeys."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes routine coding categories. The ICD-10 system (used for Medicare billing) does include codes for injuries involving animals — for example a W61 category relates to being struck by a turkey with subcodes — but there was no separate, new Medicare policy that uniquely created 'nine codes for turkey injuries' as a standalone update. Social posts conflated ordinary ICD-10 subcodes and routine annual code updates into a sensational claim.

claim: Says the Austin City Council "may give $4 million a year to subsidize a race track."
rationale: There is no widely documented, enacted Austin City Council commitment to provide an ongoing $4 million per year direct subsidy to a race track. Austin has approved various one-time grants, infrastructure spending, tax incentives, and negotiated revenue arrangements related to the Circuit of the Americas in the past, but those are not the same as a standing $4M/year subsidy. Without a specific ordinance or signed contract explicitly committing $4M annually, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: There is no credible, widely reported video or trustworthy news documentation showing President Joe Biden taking a knee during the national anthem. Public footage and contemporary fact-checking note he has sometimes bowed his head or removed his hat at events, but has not been documented kneeling during the anthem.

claim: Says "roughly two-thirds of (state) corporations didn’t pay any income tax in Virginia."
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks a specific year or definition; while a substantial share of corporate tax returns in Virginia report zero net tax liability in some years, the exact share varies and cannot be confidently stated as “roughly two-thirds” without citing a particular tax year and filer definition. Virginia Department of Taxation data show many corporate filers owe no tax in certain periods, but the proportion fluctuates and is sensitive to whether you count all filings, only C-corps, or tax-paying entities.

claim: New Jersey "will be out of gas for a week."
rationale: The claim that New Jersey "will be out of gas for a week" is unsupported and highly unlikely. Fuel distribution relies on multiple terminals, pipelines, and truck deliveries and while localized shortages can occur after disruptions, a complete statewide depletion for seven days would require an unprecedented and verifiable collapse of all supply lines. No credible evidence is presented to substantiate such an extreme prediction.

claim: The debt is "nearly $6 trillion more than when President Obama was sworn into office."
rationale: The claim omits a date and which measure of federal debt is meant. When President Obama was sworn in (Jan 20, 2009) total federal debt was roughly $10–11 trillion; in subsequent years the debt rose by more than $6 trillion (for example to about $19–20 trillion by 2017), so stating it is 'nearly $6 trillion more' is inaccurate without specifying the comparison baseline and the debt measure. Different conventions (gross debt vs. debt held by the public) change the numbers further.

claim: Says Sidney Blumenthal wrote that the Benghazi attack was "almost certainly preventable. Clinton was in charge of the State Department, and it failed to protect U.S. personnel and an American consulate in Libya."
rationale: There is no well-documented public source attributing this exact critical quote about Benghazi and Hillary Clinton to Sidney Blumenthal. Media coverage and official critiques that accused the State Department of failures came from GOP investigators and other commentators, while Blumenthal — a Clinton confidant — did not publicly author that specific line. Without a primary-source citation, the attribution appears unsupported.

claim: Says scientists are "in dispute" over whether being gay is a choice.
rationale: Major medical and scientific organizations and the bulk of scientific research treat sexual orientation as arising from biological and developmental factors rather than a voluntary choice. Although researchers continue to study the precise causes and the relative roles of genetics and environment, there is no mainstream scientific dispute that being gay is simply a choice.

claim: Austin was the "site of the first mass shooting in the country."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Austin was not the site of the first mass shooting in the country. Mass-fatality shootings and massacres occurred elsewhere in U.S. history before Austin was founded (Austin was established in 1839), and modern use of the term “mass shooting” varies by definition and timeframe.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: There are no credible statements from the FBI or Texas Department of Public Safety confirming that a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry committed a Texas church shooting or that he was an 'avid atheist' on the DNC payroll. Major news outlets and official agency releases do not support those assertions, and the specific payroll claim is unverified and implausible. The post appears to be misinformation combining an unconfirmed suspect name with politically motivated claims.

claim: "With her solution, terrorists can still today — and by the way ISIS knows it, they have been advertising it — buy guns online and at gun shows in the United States of America."
rationale: U.S. federal law requires background checks for licensed dealer sales, but private-party transfers (including many gun-show and some online marketplace sales) are not universally subject to federal background checks, creating an avenue someone intent on violence could exploit. Open-source reporting and analyses have documented that ISIS and other extremist groups have encouraged supporters to take advantage of U.S. gun-market loopholes to acquire weapons locally.

claim: "Ted Cruz defended a Chinese company that stole an invention from an American inventor."
rationale: There is no credible public record or reputable reporting that Senator Ted Cruz personally defended a Chinese company accused of stealing an American inventor’s invention. Cruz worked as a lawyer earlier in his career and has represented corporate clients, but the specific allegation lacks supporting evidence and appears to conflate different cases or actors.

claim: "Right now, here in Texas, wind power is already cheaper than dirty fossil fuels."
rationale: By mid‑2020s data and market behavior in Texas, onshore wind is generally among the cheapest sources for new electricity generation and often undercuts the marginal cost of fossil generation. Competitive bids in ERCOT and LCOE studies show Texas wind prices below the cost of building new gas or coal plants, though dispatchability and integration costs differ.

claim: The "48, 49 percent" that supports President Barack Obama are "people who pay no income tax."
rationale: The statement equates the ~48–49% who supported Obama with people who pay no income tax, but polling and tax data show his supporters included many who do pay federal (and/or state) income taxes. Although in some years about half of households did not owe federal income tax, that fiscal statistic is not the same group as the percentage that supported Obama and polls show support across income and taxpaying categories.

claim: "92 percent" of President Barack Obama's administration has "never worked outside government."
rationale: The specific '92 percent' figure is inaccurate or misleading. Independent fact-checkers found that number came from a narrowly defined subset or misinterpretation and does not reflect the entire Obama administration, many of whose appointees had prior private-sector experience.

claim: "Eighty-five percent of every dollar donated to the Clinton Foundation ended up either with the Clintons or with their staff to pay for travel, salaries, and benefits. Fifteen cents of every dollar actually went to some charitable beneficiary."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the Foundation's public tax filings and independent charity assessments. IRS Form 990s and evaluations by charity watchdogs show a majority of spending goes to program services rather than 85% to the Clintons and staff; overhead and administrative/fundraising costs have been substantially lower than the claim implies. Fact-checkers have labeled similar formulations misleading or false.

claim: After a "major water main break," Georgia election workers counted "18,000 ballots, all for Biden" that they pulled from suitcases and with no election observers present.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that election workers in Georgia pulled 18,000 ballots "all for Biden" from suitcases with no observers after a water main break. State election officials, bipartisan observers, multiple independent fact-checkers, and post-election audits and recounts found no such shipment of ballots or breach in procedure; video and chain-of-custody records show ballots were processed from secured containers, not suitcases.

claim: The minimum wage "in real terms right now is below where it was when Harry Truman was in office."
rationale: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2009; when adjusted for inflation, that level is generally higher than the federal minimum during most years of Harry Truman's presidency (1945–1953). Truman-era nominal minimums were much lower (fractions of a dollar) and, when converted to present dollars using standard CPI adjustments, typically fall below $7.25. Only the 1960s peak real minimum exceeds today's federal level.

claim: Says Troy Nehls "called wearing masks 'un-American' and called those who do 'communists.'"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Troy Nehls explicitly saying the act of wearing masks is 'un-American' and simultaneously calling people who wear them 'communists.' He has criticized mask mandates and used strong anti-mandate rhetoric, but the specific paired quotes appear to be a mischaracterization or conflation of rhetoric rather than documented direct quotes.

claim: "30,000 Arizonans may have no choice" on Affordable Care Act coverage.
rationale: The statement gives a precise numeric claim without a timeframe or source, so it cannot be verified as presented. Insurer availability under the Affordable Care Act varies by year and county, and specific figures like “30,000 Arizonans may have no choice” require a cited report or data; without that context the claim is unsubstantiated. It could be true for a particular year or county but is not verifiable as a general fact.

claim: "If you earn $100 and pay $33 income tax you’re left with $67. You then buy $67 worth of fuel and in doing so pay a 48% fuel tax (fuel tax = $32.16 + $6.70 GST). This means that the government just got $71.86 tax from your hard earned $100."
rationale: The arithmetic and tax breakdown are incorrect. GST on a final inclusive price of $67 would be $67/11 = $6.09, not $6.70, and the claimed 48% ‘fuel tax’ (32.16 on a $67 sale) is an inconsistent percentage and misunderstands that fuel excise is typically a fixed cents‑per‑litre levy, not a fixed percent of the retail price. While income and consumption taxes can both apply, the specific numbers given do not add up and are misleading.

claim: In 1993, Newt Gingrich "first advocated for the individual mandate in health care. And as recently as May of this year, he was still advocating" for it.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because the idea of an individual mandate in health care predates 1993 and was advanced by conservative policy analysts (e.g., Heritage Foundation figures) in the late 1980s and early 1990s; Newt Gingrich did not 'first' advocate it in 1993. Gingrich has at times endorsed individual-responsibility approaches and has made statements about mandates in later years, but the assertion that he originated the idea in 1993 and was definitively still advocating it as recently as 'May of this year' is misleading and dependent on the unspecified year and context.

claim: "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years."
rationale: CBO did not report that delaying the individual mandate would cut the deficit by $35 billion over ten years. Contemporary CBO/JCT analyses around 2013 distinguished the employer and individual mandates: estimates of multi‑billion dollar deficit changes referred to delaying the employer mandate or other provisions, while delaying the individual mandate would primarily reduce revenue and tend to increase deficits rather than produce a $35B reduction. The claim conflates different mandates and misattributes the $35B figure to the individual mandate.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has opened up no new trade relationships with other nations.
rationale: This is false. The Obama administration negotiated and pursued several new or expanded trade relationships—most notably U.S. participation in negotiations for the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), ratification/implementation of trade agreements with Colombia and Panama, adjustments to KORUS, and steps to normalize economic relations with Cuba. Although some negotiated deals (e.g., TPP, TTIP) were not ultimately ratified by the U.S. Congress, the administration clearly engaged in and established new trade links.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and lacks a year or source; official Pennsylvania election data and contemporaneous reporting for recent elections do not show anywhere near 372,000 mail-in ballots rejected. Rejected mail/absentee ballots have been in the thousands or tens of thousands in contested recent elections, not hundreds of thousands. Without a specific election and clear definition of 'rejected,' the 372,000 figure is not supported.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to accept the blanket claim as stated and it appears misleading without context. Whether TriMet spent $4.2 million in federal funds to achieve only $168,000/year in savings depends on the specific project, accounting (capital vs operating), time horizon for payback, and whether the funds were grants or loans; such details are not provided and would commonly change the interpretation. Absent verifiable project documentation, the claim is not supportable as presented.

claim: Says Gen. David H. Berger, commandant of the U.S. Marine Corps., refused Nancy Pelosi’s request to use the Marines for inauguration security, telling her "we don’t work for you."
rationale: There is no credible reporting, official statement, or contemporaneous record that Gen. David H. Berger told Speaker Nancy Pelosi "we don’t work for you" when she purportedly asked to use Marines for inauguration security. Requests for military assistance for domestic events are handled through the Defense Department chain of command and fact-checkers found no evidence of this exchange or quote.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Tim Tebow authored that line; the phrasing appears to be a social-media meme or misattribution rather than a documented post or quote from his verified accounts. Public archives of Tebow's statements and mainstream fact-checkers have not substantiated this exact claim. Without a primary source (a dated post, recording, or interview), the attribution is unverified and likely false.

claim: Says Charlie Crist rode on a jet that "belongs to a serial polluter with a history of environmental violations fined nearly $2 million for polluting water."
rationale: I could not find credible contemporaneous reporting or public records showing Charlie Crist flew on a jet owned by an individual or company characterized as a "serial polluter" that had been fined nearly $2 million for polluting water. The claim appears to conflate or exaggerate allegations about an aircraft owner without verifiable documentation tying Crist to that specific owner and penalty.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: The statement is misleading because there is no single, authoritative federal figure of "over $62 trillion" in unfunded liabilities; estimates vary widely by which programs are included, the time horizon (e.g., 10 years, 75 years, infinite), and the discount rate used. Some analysts who sum long‑term present values of Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, federal pensions, and other commitments can produce multi‑decadal totals in the tens of trillions, but official measures (CBO, Trustees) report different, more nuanced short‑ and long‑term shortfalls rather than a single $62T number.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The post-2007–2009 recession job recovery was slow, but independent analyses and BLS series show it was not uniquely the slowest since the Great Depression; other recoveries and different measures (months to regain peak employment vs. average annual job growth) produce different comparisons. Fact-checkers have labeled blanket claims that Obama's record was the slowest since the Depression as misleading because they omit metric and timing choices that change the conclusion.

claim: "Who’s really behind Jeanne Ives’ campaign for governor? Mike Madigan’s corrupt insider machine. They’ve bankrolled her campaign with thousands in shady labor union cash, turning Ives into another Madigan lackey."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific accusations that are not supported by available evidence. While Democratic-aligned groups in Illinois (and operatives associated with Mike Madigan) have at times made independent expenditures intended to influence Republican primaries, there is no verified evidence that Madigan's 'machine' directly bankrolled Jeanne Ives' campaign with 'shady labor union cash' or that she became a Madigan lackey. The assertion conflates possible strategic third‑party spending with direct funding and control of her campaign.

claim: "Covid-19 means ‘certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence.’"
rationale: COVID-19 is an abbreviation for 'coronavirus disease 2019' (CO = corona, VI = virus, D = disease, 19 = year first identified). The proposed expansion 'certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence' is a baseless backronym and not the origin or meaning of the term.

claim: The government pays out "$2,125/month in refugee benefits to refugees resettled in the United States," while Social Security recipients "who have paid into the system their whole lives receive $1,400/month on average."
rationale: The claim misrepresents how refugee assistance works and misstates Social Security averages. Refugee resettlement in the U.S. does not provide a standardized $2,125/month cash payment; most refugees receive short-term, modest cash assistance (often well under $1,000/month or a one-time reception/placement payment) plus access to programs like SNAP and Medicaid. The cited $1,400/month for Social Security is also misleading — average retirement benefits reported by the Social Security Administration are higher than that figure and reflect lifetime contributions and program structure.

claim: Says Democrats "have issued more subpoenas than they’ve passed bills."
rationale: The statement is a broad, context-free claim that cannot be supported as a general fact. Counts of subpoenas and bills depend on the chamber, Congress/session, and time period; in most recent sessions the majority party has enacted or passed dozens to hundreds of measures while committees issue far fewer subpoenas, so the blanket comparison is misleading or incorrect without a specified timeframe or body.

claim: Says "Former President Barack Obama arrested for ESPIONAGE."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official record that former President Barack Obama has been arrested for espionage. An arrest of a former U.S. president would be widely reported by major news organizations and documented by law enforcement and court records, which do not exist for this claim. The story appears to be misinformation or a fabricated rumor.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: There is no Icelandic law or government declaration classifying all religions as mental disorders. Iceland's constitution and legal framework protect freedom of religion, and reputable fact-checks and official sources show this claim is a hoax or satire rather than an official policy.

claim: "When I was born, defense spending was 60 percent of the budget. It's now 17 percent."
rationale: A defense share of roughly 60% of the federal budget occurred only during World War II and immediate wartime spikes; for most post‑war birth years defense was a much smaller share. Current defense outlays are indeed roughly in the mid‑teens percent of total federal outlays (around 15–17%), but the claim that it was 60% 'when I was born' is implausible without a birth year and likely conflates wartime peaks or discretionary‑only measures with total budget shares.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that such a photograph exists; a scandal involving two high‑profile figures and a child would have been widely verified by major media and fact‑checkers. Images of this kind are frequently manipulated or AI‑generated to create false allegations. Therefore the claim that a photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child is almost certainly false.

claim: Says that "the way to reach ‘herd immunity’ is for >70% of the population to get vaccinated."
rationale: The statement is overly absolute. The proportion of people who must be immune to reach herd immunity depends on the pathogen's basic reproduction number (R0) and vaccine effectiveness; for some diseases or more transmissible variants of SARS-CoV-2 the required immune fraction can be well above 70%, while for others it can be lower. Vaccination is a primary tool to achieve herd immunity but not the sole factor (natural immunity, vaccine effectiveness, and population heterogeneity also matter).

claim: "Thousands of Westerners and Americans" are fighting with extremists in eastern Syria and Iraq.
rationale: Independent research and government assessments show that thousands of foreign fighters from Western countries (especially Europe) joined extremist groups in Iraq and Syria, but the number of U.S. citizens who went to fight is estimated in the low hundreds rather than thousands. Framing the claim as 'thousands of ... Americans' therefore overstates the U.S. participation and is misleading.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Marco Rubio posted a New Testament verse specifically to shame “his own constituents” for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has occasionally posted Bible verses and criticized political opponents, attributing a tweet as an act of shaming constituents for attending a Trump event appears to be an unsupported interpretation without a specific tweet, timestamp, or credible news reporting.

claim: Says the state tax burden per citizen in New York is twice as high as in Florida.
rationale: New York does have a substantially higher state (and state+local) tax burden per person than Florida, but the claim that it is "twice as high" is not reliably true across standard data sources and depends on the year and on whether you count state-only, state+local, or taxes per resident vs per taxpayer. Typical reputable datasets show a large gap but not a consistent 2× difference, so the categorical assertion is inaccurate without a specific measure and year.

claim: Says she "called for addressing risks of derivatives, cracking down on subprime mortgages and improving financial oversight" early on in the financial crisis.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “she” is or give a precise timeframe; without a named person and sources I cannot confirm that the specific individual made those calls early in the financial crisis. While many politicians and regulators did call for tighter oversight of derivatives, subprime lending, and broader financial oversight, this statement cannot be confirmed as fact without attribution.

claim: Says that in 1770 "British parliament banned lipstick, saying it had the power to seduce men into marriage, which was classified as witchcraft."
rationale: There is no historical record that the British Parliament passed a law in 1770 banning lipstick or classifying it as witchcraft. While 18th‑century moralists and commentators sometimes criticized cosmetics as deceptive or immoral, and the Witchcraft Act of 1735 changed legal treatment of witchcraft, Parliament did not outlaw lipstick as a tool for 'seducing men into marriage.'

claim: "There's no evidence that white supremacists were responsible for what happened on Jan. 6. That's a lie."
rationale: Multiple investigations, criminal prosecutions, and reporting have documented that individuals and organized extremist groups with white supremacist or racialist ties participated in the January 6 attack. Law enforcement and the Jan. 6 committee cited members of far‑right groups, symbols and communications tying some participants to white supremacist ideologies, so the blanket claim that there is no evidence is incorrect.

claim: Says the man who rushed the stage at him in Dayton, Ohio, "had chatter about ISIS, or with ISIS" in his social media posts.
rationale: I find no credible, corroborated reporting or publicly available social media evidence that the person who rushed the stage in Dayton had 'chatter about ISIS' or direct contact with ISIS. Major news accounts of the Dayton stage‑rushing incident do not report ISIS links, and the claim appears to be unsubstantiated or based on ambiguous posts. Without clear, verifiable examples, the allegation cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: No credible evidence shows Biden’s banking nominee formally 'demands' elimination of all private bank accounts. The most prominent nominee under this description (Saule Omarova) proposed allowing central bank retail accounts and major regulatory changes, but she did not call for abolishing all private bank accounts, and she publicly disputed such characterizations. Multiple fact-checks and her public testimony clarified she advocates structural reforms, not an outright ban on private deposit accounts.

claim: "There have been more than 300 mass shootings in the United States this year – more than any other country in the world."
rationale: Multiple independent tracking projects (commonly using a mass‑shooting definition of four or more people shot) record several hundred mass shootings in the United States each year, routinely exceeding 300. No other country records comparable annual totals; the U.S. consistently has far more mass‑shooting incidents than other nations. This conclusion depends on commonly used definitions and year‑to‑date tallies.

claim: Says U.N. arms treaty will mandate a "new international gun registry."
rationale: Neither the UN Arms Trade Treaty nor related UN firearms instruments mandate the creation of a centralized international gun registry. They require national record-keeping, marking and cooperation between states, but contain no provision establishing a global registry of firearms.

claim: Image shows Donald Trump’s new Christmas card.
rationale: There is no verified evidence that an authoritative new Christmas card from Donald Trump exists linked to the unspecified image. Images of public figures circulated online are frequently fan-made or doctored, and without provenance or an official announcement from Trump or his representatives the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Ronald Reagan "was behind in the polls in 1980 going into the debate with Jimmy Carter and then turned around 10 days later and won 40 states."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on key points. The 1980 presidential debate was Oct 28 and the election was Nov 4 (7 days later, not 10), and Reagan won a much larger sweep than 40 states (he carried 44 states and an overwhelming electoral vote total). Polls in late October 1980 were mixed and some showed a close race, but the blanket statement that Reagan was 'behind' going into the debate is misleading.

claim: Says an Internet meme shows people rejoicing over the Paris agreement.
rationale: The claim asserts a meme shows people rejoicing over the Paris Agreement but offers no image, source, date, or location to confirm that interpretation. Internet memes commonly recycle or miscaption photos from unrelated events, so without provenance this specific attribution is unverified and likely incorrect.

claim: "After every major conflict ... what happened was that we ultimately hollowed out the force, largely by doing deep, across-the-board cuts."
rationale: Historical patterns show that after major wars the U.S. (and other countries) frequently demobilize and cut defense budgets, which in several cases led to reduced readiness and capability—often described as a ‘hollowing out’ of the force. Examples include post‑WWI and WWII demobilizations, post‑Vietnam reductions, post‑Cold War drawdowns, and later across‑the‑board budget cuts/sequestration that degraded readiness.

claim: "There is no reason to allocate 60 percent of bridge space to satisfy two percent of all travelers."
rationale: The statement is an absolute normative claim (“no reason”) that cannot be universally true. In many planning contexts there are legitimate reasons to allocate a majority of bridge space to a small share of users — for safety, accessibility (including legal obligations), priority for public transit or cyclists, evacuation/emergency needs, or to encourage modal shift — so the blanket assertion is false without context.

claim: Obama "voted against funding our troops."
rationale: The statement is a misleading generalization. Barack Obama did not cast a vote to withhold funding for U.S. troops as a matter of policy; as a U.S. Senator and as President he supported multiple supplemental appropriations and budgets that provided funding for military operations and veterans. Claims that he "voted against funding our troops" typically conflate opposition to specific war-escalation measures or policy riders with refusing to fund troops, which is inaccurate.

claim: "Every year since Gov. Walker and the Republicans have been in control of the Legislature we’ve created fewer jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics."
rationale: Bureau of Labor Statistics state employment data do not show a monotonic year‑by‑year decline in job creation for Wisconsin during the years Scott Walker and Republican legislative majorities were in power. Year-to-year net job gains rose and fell across that period rather than falling every single year, so the blanket statement that "every year" fewer jobs were created is incorrect.

claim: Says President Barack Obama told a room of students, "Children, every time I clap my hands together, a child in America dies from gun violence," and then a child told him he could solve the problem by not clapping any more.
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, video, or contemporaneous reporting showing President Obama saying that line or recounting that exchange; it matches a satirical/viral anecdote format rather than a documented remark. The story has circulated online as a joke and is inconsistent with documented public remarks and speech transcripts from his time in office.

claim: Says Georgia’s secretary of state won’t let the people recounting ballots check the signatures for fraud.
rationale: This claim misstates how Georgia handles signature checks. Under Georgia law and practice, signature verification on absentee ballots is performed by trained county election workers and canvassing boards when ballots are processed, and during recounts/audits the Secretary of State’s office permits observers but bars unauthorized volunteers from handling ballots or conducting their own signature-forgery inspections to protect chain of custody and follow statutory procedures.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included many provisions that directly reduced Medicare outlays (payment cuts, reduced overpayments to Medicare Advantage, and delivery/payment reform initiatives) and independent budget offices (CBO) estimated the law would lower Medicare spending. Empirical Medicare spending growth slowed in the early 2010s, consistent with at least some effect from ACA provisions, though other factors also contributed to the slowdown.

claim: A lawyer demanded "several Houston pastors hand over to the city government many of their private papers, including their sermons."
rationale: There is no widely reported, credible evidence that a lawyer directly demanded several Houston pastors hand over their private papers and sermons to the city government as stated. Government attempts to compel sermons would be extraordinary and constitutionally fraught, and similar allegations are typically reported with identifying details and subsequent legal challenges — which are absent here. The claim appears to conflate or exaggerate the sort of subpoenas or document requests that occasionally arise in litigation with a broad demand for private sermons.

claim: Says "Schaufler was the only Democrat who voted to stop" the state’s health care reform plan.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks critical context (which state, which vote, and when).
